parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is a non-wage factor that might influence a person's choice of occupation?
A overtime pay
B an annual bonus
C the chance of promotion
D commission on sales
parts.answer: C the chance of promotion
parts.working: Promotion prospects are a non-wage (non-monetary) benefit of a job. Overtime pay (A), bonuses (B) and commission (D) are all forms of payment, so they are wage factors.

practice.stem: In a football factory in Sialkot, one group of workers cuts the panels, another stitches them together and a third group prints the logos.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define specialisation of workers (division of labour).
parts.answer: Workers concentrating on a particular task or a narrow range of tasks, with production split into separate stages.
parts.working: 1 mark: concentrating on one task / particular job. 1 mark: production broken down into stages / tasks.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two advantages to the factory of its workers specialising.
parts.answer: Any two, developed: workers become more skilled and faster through repetition, so productivity rises; less time is wasted moving between tasks; training is quicker and cheaper because each worker learns only one task; it is easier to use specialist machinery; output rises and average cost falls.
parts.working: For each of two advantages: 1 mark for the advantage, 1 mark for the effect on the firm (output/costs/quality).

practice.stem: Demand for software developers in Pakistan has risen as more firms sell services to customers abroad.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two factors that influence the demand for a type of worker.
parts.answer: Any two of: demand for the product the workers make (derived demand); productivity of the workers; price of the workers (wage); price of capital that could replace them.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid factors.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain, using demand and supply, how the wage of software developers is likely to change.
parts.answer: Demand for developers increases (shifts right); with supply of skilled developers slow to rise, there is a shortage at the old wage, so the wage rises until a new equilibrium.
parts.working: Demand for developers increases/shifts right (1); supply limited in the short run because training takes time (1); shortage at old wage, firms compete for workers (1); equilibrium wage and employment rise (1).

practice.stem: In a car assembly plant in Karachi each worker fits only one component, such as a door or a seat, as cars move along a production line.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two disadvantages of specialisation for the workers.
parts.answer: Any two of: boredom/repetitive work; low job satisfaction; narrow skills, making it hard to change jobs; risk of unemployment if the task is automated; repetitive strain injuries.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid disadvantages.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two disadvantages of specialisation for the firm.
parts.answer: If one worker is absent the whole line stops; bored workers make mistakes and leave, raising costs.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two developed points: interdependence – absence or a strike at one stage stops the whole line; boredom lowers quality/raises errors; higher labour turnover raises recruitment and training costs; inflexible workforce when demand changes.

practice.stem: A garment worker in Lahore is paid a piece rate of Rs 35 for each shirt she stitches. She stitches 40 shirts a day and works 26 days a month.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate her monthly earnings.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The piece rate rises to Rs 38 a shirt. Calculate the percentage increase in her monthly earnings if her output does not change. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one disadvantage to the worker of being paid by piece rate.
parts.answer: Earnings vary and fall if she is ill, the machine breaks or there are power cuts; pressure to work fast.
parts.working: Disadvantage (1) explained (1), e.g. income is uncertain because it depends on output, which falls through illness or power cuts.

practice.stem:
The table shows the average monthly wage of two occupations in a country.
Occupation | Average monthly wage (Rs)
Airline pilot | 960 000
Farm labourer | 40 000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the pilot's average wage is than the farm labourer's.
parts.answer: 24 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why airline pilots are paid more than farm labourers.
parts.answer: Pilots need long, expensive training and rare skills, so the supply of pilots is small, whereas almost anyone can do farm labouring, so supply is large. Demand for pilots is high because each pilot produces a very valuable service (high revenue per flight) and carries great responsibility for passengers' safety.
parts.working: For each of two reasons: 1 mark for the reason (training/skills, limited supply, high demand/productivity, responsibility, risk), 1 mark for linking it to the wage.

practice.stem: Nadia has been offered two jobs: one as an economist in a government ministry and one, with a 25% higher salary, at a private bank.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two non-wage factors that Nadia might consider when choosing between the jobs.
parts.answer: Any two of: job security; pension; working hours; holidays; promotion prospects; working conditions; location/travel time; job satisfaction; training opportunities.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two non-wage factors.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Nadia might choose the lower-paid government job.
parts.answer: Government jobs often offer greater job security, so she is less likely to become unemployed; they may provide better pensions and fringe benefits; shorter or more regular working hours give a better work–life balance; she may value serving the public; together these benefits may outweigh the higher salary at the bank.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark per relevant non-wage benefit explained (max 3), 1 mark for the idea that total benefits/net advantages outweigh the higher wage.

practice.stem: A factory worker in Faisalabad is paid Rs 400 an hour for a basic week of 40 hours. Any extra hours are paid at time-and-a-half (1.5 times the basic rate). In one week he works 48 hours.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate his gross earnings for the week.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the employer pays a higher rate for overtime hours.
parts.answer: Workers value their leisure time more after a long working day, so a higher rate is needed to persuade them to work extra hours; it is cheaper for the firm than hiring and training extra workers for a short period.
parts.working: 1 mark: incentive to give up leisure / compensate for longer hours. 1 mark: cheaper or more flexible than recruiting more workers.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which change is most likely to increase the supply of nurses?
A a fall in the wages paid to nurses
B more government-funded places on nurse training courses
C an increase in the number of hospitals
D more nurses moving abroad to work
parts.answer: B more government-funded places on nurse training courses
parts.working: More funded training places make it easier and cheaper to qualify, increasing the number of nurses available. A reduces the incentive to be a nurse (a movement along supply); C increases the demand for nurses, not supply; D reduces supply.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define derived demand.
parts.answer: Demand for a factor of production, such as labour, that depends on the demand for the product it helps to make.
parts.working: Demand for a factor/labour (1) that comes from demand for the good or service it produces (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse how a large increase in the number of engineering graduates is likely to affect the wages of engineers.
parts.answer: Supply of engineers increases (shifts right); at the old wage there is a surplus of engineers, so the equilibrium wage falls and employment rises; the effect is smaller if demand for engineers is also rising.
parts.working: More graduates increases the supply of engineers (1), supply curve shifts right (1); surplus of engineers at the original wage (1); competition for jobs pushes the wage down (1) while the number employed rises (1); the wage may not fall if demand for engineers is rising at the same time (e.g. construction boom) or graduates emigrate (1).

practice.stem: An electrician in Karachi earns more than an electrician doing the same job in a small town in rural Sindh.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two reasons why wages for the same job may differ between a large city and a small town.
parts.answer: e.g. higher cost of living in the city; greater demand for electricians in the city; more firms competing for workers; workers unwilling to move.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid reasons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse why skilled workers usually earn more than unskilled workers.
parts.answer: Supply of skilled workers is limited because training takes time and money; demand is high because they are more productive; so the equilibrium wage is higher. Unskilled workers are in plentiful supply and easier to replace, so wages are lower.
parts.working: Skilled: supply is low/inelastic because of long, costly training and ability needed (1+1); demand is high because their productivity and value of output are high (1+1). Unskilled: large supply of workers, easily replaced, so wage low (1). Diagram/comparison of two labour markets with higher equilibrium wage for skilled (1).

practice.stem: A government raises the national minimum wage by 20%. Many workers in shops, restaurants and small factories are paid at the minimum wage.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define a national minimum wage.
parts.answer: The lowest wage rate per hour (or per month) that employers are legally allowed to pay workers, set by the government.
parts.working: 1 mark: lowest wage that can be paid. 1 mark: set by law/government.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not raising the minimum wage benefits low-paid workers.
parts.answer: Benefits those who keep their jobs, but may cost some jobs.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for 'benefits': higher income for those employed; reduces poverty and inequality; may motivate workers and raise productivity; encourages people into work. Up to 3 marks for 'may not': higher labour costs may make firms employ fewer workers, raising unemployment among the low-skilled; firms may replace workers with machines; prices may rise, reducing real gains; firms may cut hours or move into the informal sector, where the law is not enforced. Max 5 without a conclusion; 1 mark for a justified conclusion (e.g. depends on the size of the rise and the elasticity of demand for labour).

practice.stem: In a country the average monthly wage of men is Rs 80 000 and the average monthly wage of women is Rs 62 400.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gap between men's and women's average wages as a percentage of men's average wage.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not the difference between men's and women's average wages is caused only by discrimination.
parts.answer: Discrimination can explain part of it (lower pay for the same work, fewer promotions). Other causes: women may work in lower-paid occupations or sectors, work part-time, have career breaks for childcare, have less access to training or education, or be less geographically mobile. Conclusion: discrimination is one cause, but not the only one, though some other causes may themselves reflect social barriers.
parts.working: Discrimination (up to 4): employers pay women less for the same job; fewer promotions to senior posts; barriers to entering some well-paid occupations. Other causes (up to 4): occupational differences (more women in lower-paid sectors such as teaching assistants, garment work); part-time work/career breaks reduce experience; less education/training in some regions; lower geographical mobility; less membership of strong trade unions. Levels: 1–3 limited/one-sided; 4–6 both sides developed; 7–8 both sides developed plus a justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two parts of a worker's pay other than the basic wage.
parts.answer: e.g. overtime pay, bonuses, commission, allowances, fringe benefits such as free transport.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid items.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not a worker's earnings are likely to rise throughout their working life.
parts.answer: Likely to rise: experience and skills increase productivity; promotion; pay scales based on length of service; further qualifications. Not always: earnings may fall in later years in physical jobs; skills can become out of date with new technology; the industry may decline; ill-health, part-time work or career breaks; real earnings fall if inflation is higher than pay rises. Conclusion: earnings usually rise in early and middle working life, then level off or fall.
parts.working: Rise (up to 4): experience and training raise productivity; promotion to more senior posts; annual increments in pay scales (e.g. government jobs); more qualifications. Not always (up to 4): physical strength declines in manual jobs; technology makes skills obsolete; structural decline of the industry; illness, part-time work or career breaks; pay rises below inflation cut real earnings. Levels: 1–3 limited/one-sided; 4–6 both sides developed; 7–8 both sides developed plus a justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one reason why specialisation by workers increases output.
parts.answer: Workers become skilled and quick at one task through repetition, so more is produced per hour.
parts.working: Reason (1) explained (1): e.g. repetition increases skill and speed; no time lost moving between tasks; workers can do the task they are best at.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not specialisation benefits an economy.
parts.answer: For: higher productivity and output, lower average costs and prices, use of machinery, more trade. Against: boredom and lower quality, dependence on others (a breakdown at one stage stops production), narrow skills cause structural unemployment when demand changes, regions that specialise are vulnerable. Conclusion: benefits usually outweigh costs if workers can retrain.
parts.working: For (up to 4): higher labour productivity and total output; lower costs and prices; higher incomes and living standards; workers choose jobs that match their abilities; regions/countries can trade surpluses. Against (up to 4): repetitive work lowers motivation; interdependence — strikes or absence at one stage halt others; workers with narrow skills face occupational immobility and unemployment when industries decline; over-dependence on a few industries. Levels: 1–3 limited/one-sided; 4–6 both sides developed; 7–8 both sides developed plus a justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A car manufacturer in Japan merges with a car manufacturer in Germany. What type of merger is this?
A conglomerate merger
B horizontal merger
C vertical backward merger
D vertical forward merger
parts.answer: B horizontal merger
parts.working: A horizontal merger joins two firms at the same stage of production in the same industry, as here (two car makers); the countries do not matter. A vertical merger (C, D) joins firms at different stages, e.g. a car maker and a tyre supplier; a conglomerate merger (A) joins firms in unrelated industries.

practice.stem: A rice mill in Punjab buys a chain of grocery shops that sells rice and other food to consumers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the type of merger.
parts.answer: Vertical forward merger
parts.working: B1: vertical forward (the mill moves towards the consumer, the next stage of production).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two benefits to the rice mill of this merger.
parts.answer: Any two, developed: guaranteed outlets for its rice, so it can plan production; it gains the retail profit margin that the shops used to earn; it can control how its rice is displayed and priced; it can prevent rival mills selling through the shops; it receives direct information about consumer demand.
parts.working: For each of two benefits: 1 mark for the benefit, 1 mark for development.

practice.stem: Three businesses in Pakistan: a cotton farm in Sindh, a textile mill in Faisalabad that makes cloth, and a bank in Karachi. The textile mill is a private company; the national railway that carries its cloth is owned by the government.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the sector of production (primary, secondary or tertiary) of each of the three businesses.
parts.answer: Cotton farm – primary; textile mill – secondary; bank – tertiary.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct sector.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two differences between a private sector firm and a public sector organisation.
parts.answer: Ownership: private sector firms are owned by individuals/shareholders, public sector by the government. Aims: private firms usually aim for profit, public sector for providing services/social welfare.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two developed differences: ownership (private individuals/shareholders vs government); main aim (profit vs public service/welfare); source of finance (owners, shares, loans vs taxes/government); control (owners/directors vs government ministers).

practice.stem: Two furniture firms: Firm X employs 40 workers and has yearly sales revenue of Rs 80 million. Firm Y employs 250 workers and has yearly sales revenue of Rs 300 million.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two ways of measuring the size of a firm.
parts.answer: Any two of: number of workers; sales revenue; output; capital employed; market share; number of branches/shops.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid measures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the sales revenue per worker of each firm.
parts.answer: Firm X Rs 2 million; Firm Y Rs 1.2 million.
parts.working: 80 ÷ 40 = Rs 2 million (1); 300 ÷ 250 = Rs 1.2 million (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the number of workers may not be a good measure of the size of a firm.
parts.answer: Capital-intensive firms may produce or sell a lot with few workers, while labour-intensive firms employ many workers but sell less.
parts.working: Firms use different methods of production (1); e.g. a capital-intensive firm can have high sales with few workers, as Firm X shows higher revenue per worker (1).

practice.stem: A family-owned restaurant in Lahore has grown over ten years from one branch to six branches. It has not bought or merged with any other business.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define internal growth.
parts.answer: When a firm grows by increasing its own output/size, e.g. opening new branches or buying more capital, rather than by joining with another firm.
parts.working: Growth from within the firm/using its own resources (1), not through mergers or takeovers (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which a firm can grow internally.
parts.answer: e.g. opening new branches or factories; selling new products; selling in new markets (online, exports); reinvesting profits in new capital.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two developed ways: new branches/locations; increasing capacity with more capital and workers; developing new products; entering new markets (other cities, exports, online sales); advertising to increase market share.

practice.stem: A dairy company in Punjab closes several small milk-processing units and builds one large, highly automated plant.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define economies of scale.
parts.answer: The fall in average (unit) cost of production that occurs as a firm increases its scale of production / grows larger.
parts.working: 1 mark: fall in average cost. 1 mark: as the firm increases its scale/size of output (long run).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two internal economies of scale that the company might gain.
parts.answer: Any two, developed: technical – large automated machines produce much more output per worker, lowering cost per litre; purchasing (bulk-buying) – buying milk, packaging and fuel in large quantities gets discounts; financial – a large firm can borrow more cheaply from banks; marketing – advertising costs are spread over more output; managerial – specialist managers can be employed.
parts.working: For each of two economies: 1 mark for naming/identifying it, 1 mark for explaining why average cost falls.

practice.stem: A dairy company expands its milk-processing plant. Before expanding, the plant produced 10 000 litres a day at a total cost of Rs 1 500 000. After expanding, it produces 40 000 litres a day at a total cost of Rs 4 800 000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the average cost per litre before and after the expansion.
parts.answer: Before Rs 150 per litre; after Rs 120 per litre

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one diseconomy of scale that might occur if the company grows much larger.
parts.answer: e.g. communication problems: with many layers of management, messages are slow or distorted, decisions are delayed and mistakes are made, so average cost rises. Also: poor motivation of workers who feel unimportant; difficulty coordinating/controlling a very large firm.
parts.working: 1 mark: identifies a diseconomy. 1 mark: explains why it raises average cost.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is an example of an external economy of scale?
A A firm receives discounts for buying raw materials in bulk.
B A technical college opens near an industrial area and trains skilled workers for local firms.
C A firm employs specialist managers as it grows.
D A large firm can borrow at a lower interest rate than a small firm.
parts.answer: B A technical college opens near an industrial area and trains skilled workers for local firms.
parts.working: External economies come from the growth of the industry or area, benefiting all firms in it, such as a local supply of trained workers. A, C and D are internal economies, which arise from the growth of one firm (purchasing, managerial and financial economies).

practice.stem: A cement company buys a chain of pharmacies.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the type of merger.
parts.answer: Conglomerate merger
parts.working: Conglomerate (diversifying) merger (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the cement company might make this merger.
parts.answer: To spread risk across unrelated markets (diversification); to use its spare profits to earn more; to grow and gain financial economies of scale.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two developed reasons: diversification spreads risk if demand for cement falls (e.g. construction slump); growth in size and profit; financial economies of scale; using surplus funds; entering a growing market.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one possible disadvantage of this merger for the cement company.
parts.answer: Managers lack experience in running pharmacies, so poor decisions and higher costs (diseconomies of scale).
parts.working: Disadvantage (1) explained (1), e.g. lack of expertise in the new market; management becomes harder; high cost of the purchase.

practice.stem: A chocolate manufacturer in Switzerland buys a cocoa farm in Ghana.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the type of merger.
parts.answer: Vertical backward merger
parts.working: Vertical (backward) merger (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse the possible benefits of this merger to the chocolate manufacturer.
parts.answer: A secure, reliable supply of cocoa; control over quality; cuts out the supplier's profit margin, lowering costs; information about harvests; can deny supply to rivals.
parts.working: Up to 6 marks for developed points: secure supply of cocoa beans, so production not interrupted (2); control over quality of beans, improving the product (1); lower costs as supplier's profit no longer paid (1); more control over prices and less exposure to price rises (1); may restrict rivals' supplies, increasing market power (1).

practice.stem:
The table shows a firm's total cost at different levels of output.
Output (units) | Total cost (Rs 000)
1 000 | 50
2 000 | 80
4 000 | 140
8 000 | 320

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the average cost per unit at each level of output.
parts.answer: Rs 50, Rs 40, Rs 35 and Rs 40.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the level of output at which average cost is lowest.
parts.answer: 4 000 units
parts.working: 4 000 units (B1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two causes of the change in average cost between 4 000 and 8 000 units.
parts.answer: Average cost rises because of diseconomies of scale, e.g. communication problems, poor coordination, low worker motivation.
parts.working: Average cost rises from Rs 35 to Rs 40 (diseconomies of scale). 2 marks each for two developed causes: communication problems across many layers of management; difficulties coordinating/controlling a large firm; low morale of workers in a large organisation; rising raw material prices as the firm buys large quantities.

practice.stem: In many towns, small family-run shops and workshops operate alongside large supermarket chains and manufacturers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two reasons why a firm might choose to stay small.
parts.answer: Any two of: the owner wants to keep control; the owner wants to avoid risk or extra work; the market is small or local; the product is a personal/specialised service; lack of finance for expansion; to avoid diseconomies of scale.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid reasons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not small firms can survive in competition with large firms.
parts.answer: Many can survive, especially in niche or local markets, but they face disadvantages.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for 'can survive': offer personal service and flexibility; serve small or niche markets that large firms ignore; located close to customers; can give credit to regular customers; can respond quickly to changes; may supply large firms (subcontracting); government support schemes. Up to 3 marks for 'cannot': higher average costs because they lack economies of scale, so higher prices; harder and more costly to raise finance; cannot afford advertising or research; large firms may cut prices to drive them out. Max 5 without a conclusion; 1 mark for a justified conclusion.

practice.stem: Many textile mills are located close together in Faisalabad. Firms benefit from local suppliers of yarn and dyes, but also face traffic congestion and rising land rents.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between internal and external economies of scale.
parts.answer: Internal economies arise from the growth of an individual firm; external economies arise from the growth of the industry or area and benefit all firms in it.
parts.working: Internal: from growth of the firm itself (1); external: from growth of the industry/concentration in an area (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not a firm benefits from locating in an area where many firms in the same industry are found.
parts.answer: Benefits: external economies – skilled labour pool, specialist suppliers, training colleges, good infrastructure, reputation of area, shared services. Drawbacks: external diseconomies – congestion, higher rents and wages as firms compete, pollution, competition for customers. Conclusion depends on the balance and the firm's needs.
parts.working: Benefits (up to 4): pool of skilled workers reduces training costs; nearby suppliers of yarn and dyes lower transport costs; specialist services (repairs, banks, transport); area's reputation attracts buyers; colleges and infrastructure. Drawbacks (up to 4): traffic congestion raises transport time and costs; rising land rents and wages; workers poached by rivals; pollution and pressure on water/power; intense competition for sales. Levels: 1–3 limited/one-sided; 4–6 both sides developed; 7–8 both sides developed plus a justified conclusion.

practice.stem: Two of a country's four mobile phone network companies are planning to merge.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two reasons why firms in the same industry may merge.
parts.answer: e.g. to gain economies of scale; to increase market share; to reduce competition; to share technology or networks; to cut duplicate costs.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid reasons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not this merger will benefit consumers.
parts.answer: Benefits: economies of scale lower costs, which could mean lower prices; investment in better networks/5G; wider coverage. Drawbacks: fewer competitors (three), so the merged firm may raise prices, reduce quality and choice; less incentive to innovate. Conclusion depends on whether regulators control prices and whether cost savings are passed on.
parts.working: Benefit (up to 4): lower average costs from combining networks/towers; more profit to invest in coverage and new technology; better service in rural areas; a stronger firm to compete with the market leader. Not benefit (up to 4): less competition, so higher prices; less choice; reduced quality/customer service; job losses; possible collusion among the few remaining firms. Levels: 1–3 limited/one-sided; 4–6 both sides developed; 7–8 both sides developed plus a justified conclusion.

practice.stem: A furniture maker has expanded. Before expanding it employed 300 production workers and 12 managers. After expanding it employs 1 200 production workers and 60 managers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of production workers per manager before and after the expansion.
parts.answer: Before 25 workers per manager; after 20 workers per manager.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not a firm should try to grow as large as possible.
parts.answer: For: internal economies of scale (bulk buying, specialist machinery, cheaper finance), higher market share and profit, more security. Against: diseconomies of scale, e.g. more layers of management (here fewer workers per manager, so higher management cost per worker), communication and coordination problems, loss of control, need for finance and risk, market may be small, competition rules. Conclusion: grow to the size where average cost is lowest and the market allows.
parts.working: For (up to 4): lower average costs from purchasing, technical, financial economies; lower prices and higher market share; more profit for investment; survival against rivals. Against (up to 4): diseconomies of scale – more managers per worker (as here), communication and coordination problems raise average cost; owners lose control; small markets or demand for personal/custom products; risk of borrowing to expand; competition authorities may block growth. Levels: 1–3 limited/one-sided; 4–6 both sides developed; 7–8 both sides developed plus a justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is a characteristic of a monopoly?
A many small sellers of the same product
B a single seller protected by barriers to entry
C firms that have no control over the price they charge
D easy entry of new firms into the market
parts.answer: B a single seller protected by barriers to entry
parts.working: A monopoly is a single seller (dominating the market) with barriers that stop new firms entering. Many sellers (A), no control over price (C) and free entry (D) are features of a highly competitive market.

practice.stem: At a large fruit and vegetable market (sabzi mandi) in Lahore, hundreds of traders sell very similar tomatoes, onions and potatoes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define a competitive market.
parts.answer: A market in which there are many firms competing to sell similar products, so no single firm can control the price.
parts.working: 1 mark: many buyers and sellers / firms competing. 1 mark: no single firm controls the price / similar products.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify two characteristics of a highly competitive market shown in the information.
parts.answer: Many sellers (hundreds of traders); similar (identical) products. (Also accept: price takers; easy entry.)
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two characteristics, ideally linked to the information.

practice.stem: A pharmaceutical company develops a new medicine and is granted a patent, giving it the sole right to make and sell the medicine for 20 years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define a monopoly.
parts.answer: A market with a single seller (or a firm with a very large share of the market) with high barriers to entry.
parts.working: Single seller/dominant firm (1); barriers to entry stop rivals (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a patent gives the company monopoly power and why governments grant patents.
parts.answer: The patent is a legal barrier to entry: no other firm may make the medicine, so the company is the only seller and can set a high price. Governments grant patents to reward the high cost and risk of research, encouraging new inventions.
parts.working: Patent is a legal barrier to entry (1); no rival can sell the same medicine, so the firm controls price/supply (1). Governments grant patents to reward research and development costs/risk (1), giving an incentive for firms to invent new products (1).

practice.stem:
The table shows the yearly sales of the four cement firms in a country.
Firm | Sales (thousand tonnes)
P | 420
Q | 280
R | 180
S | 120

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the market share of firm P.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the combined market share of the two largest firms.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State whether this market is highly competitive, and give a reason.
parts.answer: Not highly competitive: only four firms and two have 70% of sales.
parts.working: Not highly competitive (1); few firms / large firms dominate the market (1).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain one benefit to consumers if more firms entered the cement market.
parts.answer: More competition would push prices down / improve quality and service as firms compete for customers.
parts.working: Benefit (1) explained (1), e.g. lower prices because firms compete for buyers; more choice; better quality.

practice.stem: Outside a university in Lahore, more than 20 food stalls sell similar snacks. New stalls open whenever the owner of a spare space decides to start one.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a barrier to entry.
parts.answer: Anything that makes it difficult or impossible for a new firm to enter a market, e.g. high start-up costs or legal restrictions.
parts.working: Obstacle to new firms entering a market (1); example (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two benefits to students of buying from a highly competitive market such as this one.
parts.answer: Low prices because each stall must match rivals; better quality and choice because stalls compete for customers.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two developed benefits: low prices, as any stall charging more loses customers; quality/hygiene and service improve to attract buyers; wide choice; new ideas from new stalls entering easily.

practice.stem: In a small town, 30 shops repair mobile phones. They all offer similar services at similar prices.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why one repair shop cannot charge much more than the others.
parts.answer: Customers can easily go to another shop offering the same service at a lower price.
parts.working: Many close substitutes/similar services (1); customers switch to cheaper shops, so it loses sales (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways a repair shop could try to attract more customers without cutting its price.
parts.answer: e.g. faster service or home collection; warranty on repairs; better customer service; advertising on social media; selling accessories.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two developed ways: differentiate the service (faster repairs, guarantee); better location or opening hours; promotion/advertising; loyalty discounts or extra services such as accessories.

practice.stem: A single company supplies all the electricity to the homes and businesses in a city.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two barriers to entry that could stop new firms supplying electricity in the city.
parts.answer: Any two of: very high start-up costs (power stations, cables); economies of scale enjoyed by the existing firm; legal barriers such as a government licence; control of the distribution network.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two barriers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two disadvantages of this monopoly for consumers.
parts.answer: Any two, developed: higher prices, because consumers have no alternative supplier; poor quality of service such as power cuts, because there is little pressure to improve; less choice; the firm may be inefficient, so costs and prices are higher; little incentive to innovate.
parts.working: For each of two disadvantages: 1 mark for identifying it, 1 mark for explaining why it arises from monopoly.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In a highly competitive market, one seller raises its price above the price charged by all the other sellers of the identical product. What is most likely to happen?
A It will lose most of its customers to other sellers.
B Its total revenue will rise.
C All the other sellers will raise their prices too.
D Consumers will keep buying from it because they have no choice.
parts.answer: A It will lose most of its customers to other sellers.
parts.working: In a highly competitive market there are many sellers of the same product and buyers know the prices, so customers switch to cheaper sellers. B and D would only be true for a firm with market power (e.g. a monopoly); C is unlikely because rivals gain customers by keeping prices low.

practice.stem: In most cities, a single company supplies piped water. Laying a second set of pipes to every building would be very costly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two ways a government could stop a water-supply monopoly from charging high prices.
parts.answer: e.g. set a maximum price/price cap through a regulator; take the company into public ownership; require approval for price rises; subsidise the supplier in return for low prices.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid ways: price regulation/maximum price; nationalisation/state ownership; a regulator that must approve price changes; subsidy linked to lower prices; quality and service standards with fines.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why it may be cheaper for one firm, rather than several, to supply piped water to a city.
parts.answer: Very high fixed costs of pipes and treatment plants; one firm spreads these over all customers, getting large economies of scale and low average cost; several firms would duplicate the network and each have high average cost.
parts.working: Very high fixed costs of the pipe network (1); one firm spreads them over many customers (1), so average cost is low/economies of scale (1); competing firms would duplicate pipes, wasting resources and raising average cost (1).

practice.stem: A monopoly supplier sells 2 million units a year at a price of Rs 50 each. Its average total cost is Rs 30 a unit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the monopoly's yearly profit.
parts.answer: Rs 40 million
parts.working: Profit per unit 50 − 30 = Rs 20 (M1); × 2 million = Rs 40 million (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse why a monopoly may have less incentive than a firm in a competitive market to keep its costs low.
parts.answer: With no rivals and barriers to entry, it can earn high profits even with inefficiency; customers cannot switch; it can pass higher costs on as higher prices. A competitive firm that lets costs rise would lose customers and make losses.
parts.working: No close competitors/barriers to entry (1); consumers cannot switch to a cheaper supplier (1); higher costs can be passed on as higher prices (1); profits remain high even if costs rise, so less pressure to be efficient (1). In contrast, a competitive firm with higher costs than rivals would lose sales and could be forced out (1). Possible limit: the threat of regulation or new technology may still push the monopoly to control costs (1).

practice.stem: For many years only one airline flew between Karachi and Islamabad. After a second airline began flying the route, the average fare fell from Rs 32 000 to Rs 24 000 and the number of passengers a year rose from 600 000 to 780 000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in the average fare and in the number of passengers.
parts.answer: Fare −25%; passengers +30%.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which passengers may have benefited from the entry of the second airline.
parts.answer: Lower fares; more choice of flight times; better service quality as the airlines compete.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two developed benefits: lower fares (25% fall) let more people fly; more flights/choice of times; better service and quality as airlines compete for passengers; innovation such as online booking.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one reason why a monopoly can charge a higher price than a firm in a highly competitive market.
parts.answer: Consumers have no close substitutes and rivals cannot enter the market, so the monopoly can raise price without losing all its customers; a competitive firm that raised its price would lose customers to rivals.
parts.working: 1 mark: no close substitutes / barriers to entry. 1 mark: so demand does not fall to zero / it is a price maker, unlike a competitive firm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not a monopoly is always worse for consumers than a competitive market.
parts.answer: Not always: economies of scale and research can benefit consumers, but higher prices and less choice are common.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for 'worse': higher prices and lower output; less choice; less incentive to be efficient or improve quality; high profits at consumers' expense. Up to 3 marks for 'not always': economies of scale may mean lower costs and prices; high profits can fund research and new products; avoids wasteful duplication (natural monopoly, e.g. water pipes); can be regulated or state-owned to protect consumers. Max 5 without a conclusion; 1 mark for a justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one advantage of a monopoly for consumers.
parts.answer: e.g. economies of scale may lead to lower average costs and lower prices; high profits can fund research and new products; avoids wasteful duplication.
parts.working: Advantage (1) explained (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not a government should break up a large monopoly into several smaller competing firms.
parts.answer: For: more competition lowers prices, raises output, quality and choice, gives an incentive to be efficient and innovate. Against: smaller firms lose economies of scale, so average costs and possibly prices rise; less profit for research; in natural monopolies duplication is wasteful; costly and slow to do. Alternatives: regulate prices. Conclusion depends on the industry.
parts.working: For (up to 4): lower prices and higher output; more choice and quality; firms must be efficient to survive; consumer exploitation ends; more innovation from rivalry. Against (up to 4): loss of economies of scale; less funds for research; duplication of infrastructure (e.g. power grids); the smaller firms may collude; regulation of the monopoly may achieve the same result more cheaply. Levels: 1–3 limited/one-sided; 4–6 both sides developed; 7–8 both sides developed plus a justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why firms in a highly competitive market are unlikely to earn high profits for long.
parts.answer: High profits attract new firms because there are no barriers to entry; extra supply and competition push prices and profits down.
parts.working: No barriers to entry/new firms attracted by profit (1); more competition lowers prices and profits (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not firms in a highly competitive market are likely to produce goods and services of high quality.
parts.answer: Likely: customers can easily switch, so firms that sell poor quality lose sales; firms compete on quality and service as well as price. Not likely: low profits leave little money to improve products; firms may cut corners to keep prices low; buyers may lack information about quality; small firms cannot afford research. Conclusion depends on how well consumers can judge quality and on regulation.
parts.working: Likely (up to 4): consumers switch away from poor-quality sellers; reputation and repeat custom matter; new entrants with better products win customers; firms differentiate through service. Not likely (up to 4): intense price competition and low profits leave little for investment or research; firms may use cheaper materials or ignore safety; consumers may not be able to judge quality before buying; small scale limits technology. Levels: 1–3 limited/one-sided; 4–6 both sides developed; 7–8 both sides developed plus a justified conclusion.

practice.stem: When a market was supplied by a monopoly, the price was Rs 900 and 10 000 units were sold each month. After new firms entered, the price fell to Rs 600 and 16 000 units were sold each month.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in the price and in the quantity sold. Give your answers to 1 decimal place where necessary.
parts.answer: Price −33.3%; quantity +60%.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not a monopoly is likely to spend more on research and development than firms in a competitive market.
parts.answer: More: high profits protected by barriers to entry give funds and allow the firm to keep the rewards of new products; can afford risky long-term projects. Less: with no rivals there is little pressure to innovate; competitive firms innovate to gain an advantage over rivals. Conclusion: monopolies have the means but not always the incentive; depends on threat of new entrants or technology.
parts.working: More (up to 4): large profits provide finance; barriers/patents mean the firm keeps the reward from its inventions; economies of scale in research; can take long-term risks. Less (up to 4): lack of competition reduces pressure to improve; complacency/inefficiency; competitive firms innovate to survive and win customers; small firms can be very inventive (start-ups). Levels: 1–3 limited/one-sided; 4–6 both sides developed; 7–8 both sides developed plus a justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is a measure of labour productivity?
A the total output of a firm
B output per worker per hour
C total wages paid divided by the number of workers
D the number of workers divided by total output
parts.answer: B output per worker per hour
parts.working: Labour productivity is output per worker (or per worker-hour). Total output (A) is production, not productivity – a common confusion; C is the average wage; D is the inverse of productivity (workers per unit of output).

practice.stem: Hand-knotted carpets made in Pakistan are produced mainly by workers using simple looms, while carpets in some other countries are made on large automated machines.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between labour-intensive and capital-intensive production.
parts.answer: Labour-intensive production uses a high proportion of labour relative to capital; capital-intensive production uses a high proportion of capital (machinery) relative to labour.
parts.working: 1 mark: labour-intensive = more labour than capital. 1 mark: capital-intensive = more machinery/capital than labour.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why hand-knotted carpet production remains labour-intensive.
parts.answer: Labour is relatively cheap compared with expensive machinery; consumers pay a high price for hand-made quality and designs that machines cannot copy; production is in small workshops that cannot afford or finance machinery; skilled weavers are available.
parts.working: For each of two reasons: 1 mark for the reason, 1 mark for development.

practice.stem: On farms in Sindh, labour productivity in growing rice is lower than on rice farms in some other Asian countries.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define labour productivity.
parts.answer: Output per worker (per period of time, e.g. per hour).
parts.working: Output (1) per worker/per worker-hour (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two factors that could increase the productivity of rice farm workers.
parts.answer: e.g. more and better capital (tractors, irrigation); education and training; better seeds and fertilisers; better management/organisation.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two developed factors: more/better machinery and irrigation; training in modern methods; higher-quality inputs (seeds, fertiliser); better organisation and management; better health of workers; better roads and storage reducing waste.

practice.stem: Cotton grown in Punjab is spun into yarn, woven into cloth, made into shirts in Karachi and then sold in shops.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify which stages in this chain are secondary production.
parts.answer: Spinning the cotton into yarn, weaving cloth and making shirts.
parts.working: Recognises manufacturing/processing stages (1); names them: spinning, weaving, making shirts (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how each stage of production adds value.
parts.answer: Each stage turns inputs into a product consumers value more (e.g. cloth worth more than yarn); value added = value of output − cost of bought-in inputs, which pays wages, rent, interest and profit.
parts.working: Production changes the form/location of goods to satisfy wants (1); output at each stage sells for more than the inputs bought (1); value added = sales value minus bought-in inputs (1); this pays factor rewards: wages, rent, interest, profit (1). Credit retail adding value by making goods available (tertiary).

practice.stem:
The table shows the weekly output of a small furniture workshop with a fixed number of machines as more workers are employed.
Number of workers | Total output (chairs per week)
1 | 10
2 | 24
3 | 36
4 | 44
5 | 48

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate output per worker when 2 workers and when 4 workers are employed.
parts.answer: 2 workers: 12 chairs; 4 workers: 11 chairs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the extra output produced by the fifth worker.
parts.answer: 4 chairs

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the extra output from each additional worker falls after the second worker.
parts.answer: The number of machines and space is fixed, so extra workers have less equipment each; they wait to use machines and get in each other's way.
parts.working: Capital/space is fixed (1); each extra worker has less capital to work with (1); workers wait for machines or crowd the workshop, so each adds less output (1).

practice.stem: Rising wages for farm labourers in Punjab have led many farmers to hire combine harvesters instead of employing workers to cut wheat by hand.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two advantages to a farmer of using a combine harvester rather than cutting wheat by hand.
parts.answer: e.g. faster harvesting; less crop lost to bad weather; lower cost per hectare; fewer workers to recruit and manage.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid advantages: speed; less crop loss/damage from rain; lower average cost when wages are high; does not depend on finding seasonal labourers; consistent quality.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a rise in the price of labour affects a firm's demand for capital.
parts.answer: Labour becomes relatively more expensive, so firms substitute machines for workers; demand for capital rises and demand for labour falls.
parts.working: Higher wages raise the cost of labour (1); capital becomes relatively cheaper (1); firms switch to more capital-intensive methods, e.g. combine harvesters (1); demand for capital rises while demand for labour falls (1).

practice.stem:
The table shows information about a textile mill in Faisalabad.
Year | Number of workers | Weekly output (metres of cloth)
2025 | 200 | 50 000
2026 | 180 | 54 000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate labour productivity (metres per worker per week) in each year.
parts.answer: 2025: 250 metres; 2026: 300 metres

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in labour productivity between 2025 and 2026.
parts.answer: +20% (increase)
parts.working: (300 − 250) ÷ 250 × 100 = 20% increase (B1, own figures from (a)).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two ways in which the mill may have increased labour productivity.
parts.answer: Any two, developed: training workers so they work faster and make fewer mistakes; installing more modern machinery; better organisation or division of labour; incentives such as bonuses linked to output; better working conditions that improve motivation.
parts.working: For each of two ways: 1 mark for the method, 1 mark for explaining how it raises output per worker.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A firm increases its workforce from 40 to 48 workers, and its output rises from 2 000 to 2 640 units a week. What happens to labour productivity?
A It rises by 5 units per worker a week.
B It rises by 20%.
C It rises by 32%.
D It falls because more workers are employed.
parts.answer: A It rises by 5 units per worker a week.
parts.working: Productivity = output per worker: 2 000 ÷ 40 = 50 and 2 640 ÷ 48 = 55, a rise of 5 units (10%). B is the rise in workers, C the rise in total output.

practice.stem: A car manufacturer in Japan uses robots on most of its production line. A hair salon in Islamabad employs eight stylists and uses only simple equipment.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify which business is capital-intensive and which is labour-intensive.
parts.answer: Car manufacturer: capital-intensive; hair salon: labour-intensive.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse why these two businesses use different methods of production.
parts.answer: Cars are standardised and made in large quantities, so expensive robots spread over large output lower average cost; wages in Japan are high. Hairdressing is a personal service, tailored to each customer, needs human skill and cannot be easily automated; small scale.
parts.working: Car maker: large-scale output of standard products allows capital costs to be spread (1); high wages in Japan make labour relatively expensive (1); robots give precision and consistent quality (1). Salon: personal service, each job different, needs human judgement (1); small scale, so expensive machinery would not be worthwhile (1); labour relatively cheap / customers value personal contact (1).

practice.stem: A packaging firm needs to increase output. It can either employ 10 extra workers at Rs 45 000 a month each, or lease a machine for Rs 300 000 a month that needs 2 operators paid Rs 60 000 a month each. Both options would give the same extra output.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the monthly cost of each option and state which is cheaper.
parts.answer: Workers Rs 450 000; machine Rs 420 000; the machine option is cheaper by Rs 30 000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two factors, other than cost, that the firm should consider before choosing the machine.
parts.answer: e.g. reliability/breakdowns and power cuts; flexibility if demand falls (workers can be moved, lease contract fixed); quality of output; effect on staff morale and union reaction; skills needed to operate it.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two developed factors: risk of breakdowns or electricity shortages stopping output; flexibility – workers can do several tasks, machine only one; quality/consistency of output; availability of trained operators; reaction of existing workers and unions; length of the lease contract.

practice.stem: After training and new equipment, output per worker at a fish-processing plant rose from 8 tonnes to 10 tonnes a month.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in labour productivity.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse how an increase in labour productivity can benefit a firm.
parts.answer: Lower labour cost per unit, so lower average cost; firm can cut prices or earn higher profit; more competitive, including in export markets; can afford higher wages, improving morale; extra profit for investment.
parts.working: Higher output with the same workers (1) lowers labour cost per unit/average cost (1); the firm can lower its price and sell more, increasing market share (1), or keep price and earn more profit (1); more competitive against foreign rivals (1); profit can be reinvested / pay higher wages to retain staff (1).

practice.stem: A biscuit manufacturer is deciding whether to replace 60 packing workers with automated packing machines.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two influences on a firm's demand for a factor of production.
parts.answer: Any two of: the price (cost) of the factor, e.g. the wage rate; the productivity of the factor; the demand for the product it makes (derived demand); the price and productivity of other factors that could replace it.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid influences.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not the firm should replace the workers with machines.
parts.answer: Depends on relative costs, productivity and the firm's market.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for 'should': machines work faster and longer without breaks, raising productivity; lower average cost in the long run; more consistent quality and hygiene; fewer labour problems such as strikes. Up to 3 marks for 'should not': high initial cost and maintenance; machines may break down and need skilled technicians; workers are cheap and flexible; if demand falls, idle machines still have to be paid for; loss of goodwill and redundancy costs. Max 5 without a conclusion; 1 mark for a justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two ways a firm can increase labour productivity.
parts.answer: e.g. training; better or more capital; better management; incentives such as bonuses; better working conditions.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid ways.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not an increase in productivity always benefits workers.
parts.answer: Benefits: higher wages possible because each worker produces more; more secure jobs as the firm is more competitive; better conditions; training raises skills. Not always: firms may need fewer workers, causing redundancy; gains may go to profits not wages; more intense, stressful work; jobs deskilled by machines. Conclusion depends on demand for the product and bargaining power.
parts.working: Benefit (up to 4): higher pay/bonuses; firm more competitive so jobs safer; new skills from training increase future earnings; lower prices for workers as consumers. Not always (up to 4): same output needs fewer workers – redundancies; employers keep gains as profit; work intensifies, raising stress; machines replace skills; benefits depend on trade union strength and demand growth. Levels: 1–3 limited/one-sided; 4–6 both sides developed; 7–8 both sides developed plus a justified conclusion.

practice.stem: A firm is choosing where to locate a call centre. In Country A, workers are paid $400 a month and handle 30 calls an hour. In Country B, workers are paid $2 000 a month and handle 60 calls an hour. In both countries each worker works 160 hours a month.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the labour cost per call in each country. Give your answers to 3 decimal places.
parts.answer: Country A $0.083; Country B $0.208.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not firms should always locate production where wages are lowest.
parts.answer: For: lower labour cost per unit, as here, if productivity is not too low; more competitive prices; higher profit. Against: low wages may come with low productivity, poor skills, weak infrastructure, language or quality problems, political risk, transport costs, distance from customers; reputation if workers are exploited. Conclusion: what matters is cost per unit, not the wage alone.
parts.working: For (up to 4): lower labour cost per call/unit (A's is less than half of B's); lower prices and higher profit; large supply of workers; may get government incentives. Against (up to 4): lower productivity can cancel the wage advantage; quality, language and skills; poor infrastructure/power; transport costs and distance from markets; political and currency risk; ethical concerns and damage to brand. Levels: 1–3 limited/one-sided; 4–6 both sides developed; 7–8 both sides developed plus a justified conclusion.

practice.stem: Many firms are introducing artificial intelligence (AI) software that can write reports, answer customer emails and process invoices.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two reasons why a firm might introduce AI software to process its invoices.
parts.answer: e.g. lower cost per invoice than paying clerks; faster processing; fewer errors; can work 24 hours a day.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid reasons: lower costs; speed; accuracy; works continuously without breaks; easy to expand when the firm grows.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not the introduction of AI software will reduce the demand for office workers.
parts.answer: Reduce: AI is a substitute for routine office tasks, often cheaper than wages, so firms employ fewer clerks. Not necessarily: AI may complement workers, raising productivity and lowering costs, so firms expand output and demand; new jobs in managing and checking AI; some tasks need human judgement and personal contact; adoption takes time and costs money. Conclusion: demand for routine roles likely falls, while demand for skilled roles may rise.
parts.working: Reduce (up to 4): AI substitutes for labour in routine tasks; lower cost than wages; works without breaks; firms seeking profit cut staff. Not reduce (up to 4): AI complements workers, raising productivity and so the value of their output; lower costs and prices increase sales and derived demand; new occupations (AI supervisors, data specialists); customers prefer human contact for some services; cost of software and training slows adoption; trade unions may resist. Levels: 1–3 limited/one-sided; 4–6 both sides developed; 7–8 both sides developed plus a justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is a function of a central bank rather than a commercial bank?
A accepting deposits from households
B acting as the banker to the government
C lending money to small businesses
D providing loans to people buying houses
parts.answer: B acting as the banker to the government
parts.working: A central bank is the government's banker (it also issues the currency, is lender of last resort and conducts monetary policy). Accepting household deposits (A) and lending to firms (C) and house buyers (D) are functions of commercial banks.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A shop in Quetta shows the price of every item in rupees, so customers can compare the value of different goods. Which function of money does this show?
A medium of exchange
B unit of account (measure of value)
C standard of deferred payment
D store of value
parts.answer: B unit of account (measure of value)
parts.working: Pricing goods in a common unit so values can be compared is the unit of account / measure of value function. A would be using money to pay for the goods; C is settling debts in the future; D is keeping money to spend later.

practice.stem: In a remote mountain village, families still exchange goats, wheat and woollen shawls directly with one another, without using money.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define barter.
parts.answer: The direct exchange of goods and services for other goods and services, without money.
parts.working: Exchange of goods/services (1) directly for other goods/services without using money (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two problems the villagers face from using barter.
parts.answer: e.g. need a double coincidence of wants; hard to divide a goat; difficult to agree relative values; hard to store wealth.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two developed problems: double coincidence of wants (each must want what the other has); indivisibility (a goat cannot be split to buy a small amount of wheat); no common measure of value, so many exchange rates; difficulty storing wealth as perishable goods; difficult to arrange future payments.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two characteristics that an item needs in order to act as good money.
parts.answer: Any two of: acceptable, durable, portable, divisible, homogeneous (uniform), scarce/limited in supply, recognisable, hard to forge.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid characteristics.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why paper banknotes are better money than sacks of wheat.
parts.answer: Banknotes are portable and divisible; wheat is heavy, perishable and varies in quality.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two developed comparisons: portability (notes light, wheat bulky); durability (wheat rots or is eaten by pests); divisibility (notes come in many values); homogeneity (each note the same, wheat varies in quality); limited supply controlled by the central bank, so value is more stable; general acceptability.

practice.stem: The State Bank of Pakistan is the central bank of Pakistan.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two functions of a central bank.
parts.answer: Any two of: issues notes and coins; banker to the government; banker to commercial banks; lender of last resort; controls the money supply/sets interest rates; manages foreign exchange reserves; supervises banks.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid functions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a central bank acts as the banker to commercial banks.
parts.answer: Commercial banks keep reserves at the central bank, settle payments with each other through it, and can borrow from it when short of cash (lender of last resort), which keeps the banking system stable.
parts.working: Commercial banks hold accounts/reserves at the central bank (1); used to settle payments between banks (1); central bank lends to banks short of liquidity, as lender of last resort (1); this prevents bank failures/maintains confidence in the system (1).

practice.stem: In many countries, including Pakistan and Kenya, people pay shopkeepers and send money to relatives using balances held in mobile phone wallets.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two functions of money.
parts.answer: Any two, developed: medium of exchange – money is accepted in payment for goods, avoiding the need for a double coincidence of wants in barter; unit of account/measure of value – prices of different goods can be compared in one unit; store of value – money can be saved and used later; standard for deferred payment – debts can be agreed now and repaid in future.
parts.working: For each of two functions: 1 mark for the function, 1 mark for explanation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why mobile-wallet balances can act as money.
parts.answer: They are generally acceptable to sellers as payment and have the characteristics of money: portable, divisible into small amounts and durable, so they can act as a medium of exchange.
parts.working: 1 mark: generally accepted as payment / medium of exchange. 1 mark: a relevant characteristic (portable, divisible, durable, hard to forge).

practice.stem: A young tailor in Hyderabad opens a current account and a savings account at a commercial bank. The bank pays 9% a year on savings and charges 16% a year on loans to small businesses.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two functions of a commercial bank.
parts.answer: Any two of: accepting deposits; lending (loans/overdrafts); providing ways to make payments (cards, transfers, cheques); exchanging currency; safekeeping.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid functions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The bank receives deposits of Rs 500 000 and lends all of this money to small businesses for one year. Calculate the difference between the interest it receives and the interest it pays.
parts.working: Interest received 16% × 500 000 = Rs 80 000; interest paid 9% × 500 000 = Rs 45 000 (M1); difference Rs 35 000 (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how this difference helps the bank to make a profit.
parts.answer: The gap between lending and saving rates is the bank's income, from which it pays its costs (staff, buildings); what is left is profit.
parts.working: Interest earned on loans is greater than interest paid on deposits (1); this margin covers running costs and leaves a profit (1).

practice.stem: Farah borrows Rs 400 000 from a bank to buy a motor rickshaw. The bank charges simple interest of 18% a year, and the loan lasts 2 years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total amount Farah must repay.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Farah repays in 24 equal monthly instalments. Calculate each instalment to the nearest rupee.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons why banks often charge higher interest rates to small businesses than to large companies.
parts.answer: Small businesses are riskier (more likely to fail, less collateral) and the costs of arranging small loans are higher relative to their size.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two developed reasons: higher risk of default because small firms fail more often; little collateral/security; short or no credit history; administration cost is high relative to a small loan; large firms can borrow elsewhere (e.g. shares, bonds), so banks compete for them with lower rates.

practice.stem: A savings account pays interest of 7% a year. Over the same year, prices in the country rise by 10%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of savings of Rs 200 000 after one year in this account.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the saver may be worse off at the end of the year despite earning interest.
parts.answer: Goods costing Rs 200 000 now cost Rs 220 000, more than the Rs 214 000 saved, so the savings buy less (real value falls).
parts.working: Prices rise by more than the interest rate (1); the same goods now cost Rs 220 000 (1); so savings of Rs 214 000 buy fewer goods: purchasing power/real value has fallen (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two other reasons why households keep money in bank accounts.
parts.answer: Safety from theft and loss; convenience of making payments (cards, transfers); access to loans; earning some interest.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two developed reasons: safety compared with keeping cash at home; easy payments by card/app/transfer; salaries paid into accounts; a record with the bank helps when applying for a loan; interest is better than nothing even when below inflation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two forms of money used in a modern economy.
parts.answer: e.g. coins, banknotes, bank deposits (current accounts), mobile-wallet/electronic balances.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid forms.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the use of money encourages specialisation.
parts.answer: Money removes the need for a double coincidence of wants, so people can concentrate on one job, earn money and buy everything else they need.
parts.working: Without money, people must find someone who wants exactly what they make (1); money as a medium of exchange makes trade easy (1); workers can specialise in one task and be paid a wage (1); they use the money to buy many goods from other specialists, raising total output (1).

practice.stem: Commercial banks in a country raise the interest rate they pay on savings accounts from 8% to 11% a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the interest earned in one year on savings of Rs 250 000 at the new rate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not the growth of commercial banking benefits an economy.
parts.answer: Benefits through saving, lending and payments, but there are risks.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for benefits: safe place for savings and interest for savers; loans to firms finance investment and growth; loans to households for housing/cars raise living standards; efficient payment systems help trade. Up to 3 marks for problems: banks aim for profit, so they may charge high interest or ignore small firms/poor households; excessive lending can cause debt problems, inflation or asset bubbles; bank failures can harm savers and the whole economy; banks may concentrate in cities. Max 5 without a conclusion; 1 mark for a justified conclusion (e.g. benefits depend on regulation by the central bank).

practice.stem: In a country, the share of shop payments made digitally (by card, bank app or mobile wallet) rose from 30% in 2022 to 55% in 2026.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in the share of payments made digitally between 2022 and 2026. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: (55 − 30) ÷ 30 × 100 (M1) = 83.3% (A1). (A rise of 25 percentage points.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse how the growth of digital payments may affect commercial banks.
parts.answer: More transaction fees and deposits kept in accounts; data on customers helps lending; lower costs of handling cash and fewer branches needed; but competition from mobile-wallet firms and costs of cyber security.
parts.working: Up to 6 marks for developed points: more money held as bank deposits, giving more funds to lend and more interest income (2); fees from card and transfer payments (1); lower costs of handling and transporting cash, so fewer branches (1); data on spending helps assess borrowers (1); competition from non-bank mobile-wallet firms could reduce market share (1); higher spending on IT and fraud protection (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two characteristics that money must have to act as a store of value.
parts.answer: It must be durable and keep its purchasing power (stable value / limited supply).
parts.working: 2 marks each: durable (does not wear out or rot, so can be kept) (1+1); stable value / limited supply, so its purchasing power is kept over time (1+1). Accept recognisable/acceptable in the future with development.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not a country should replace cash completely with digital money.
parts.answer: For: lower costs of printing and handling cash, faster payments, less theft, harder to evade tax, easier to trace crime. Against: people without bank accounts, phones or internet are excluded; risk of power and network failures and cyber-attacks; loss of privacy; elderly and rural people may struggle. Conclusion: move gradually while keeping some cash.
parts.working: For (up to 4): cheaper and safer than handling notes; quick, convenient payments; records make tax evasion and corruption harder; less robbery; easier for government to make transfers to the poor. Against (up to 4): financial exclusion of the poor, elderly and rural households; depends on electricity and mobile networks; fraud and hacking; loss of privacy; small traders face fees. Levels: 1–3 limited/one-sided; 4–6 both sides developed; 7–8 both sides developed plus a justified conclusion.

practice.stem: A government wants commercial banks to lend more to small firms, which receive only a small share of all bank loans.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two ways in which a commercial bank can lend to a firm.
parts.answer: e.g. a loan; an overdraft; credit card; trade finance.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid methods.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not commercial banks should lend more to small firms.
parts.answer: For: small firms create jobs, competition and growth; banks earn higher interest. Against: higher risk of default, lack of collateral, higher administration costs; banks must protect depositors' money. Conclusion: more lending is useful with guarantees or careful assessment.
parts.working: For (up to 4): finance lets small firms expand, buy capital and employ more workers; more competition benefits consumers; higher interest rates can raise bank profit; spreads lending across many borrowers. Against (up to 4): small firms are more likely to fail, so bad debts rise; little security; costly to assess many small loans; banks have a duty to protect deposits and keep liquidity; may reduce lending to safer large firms. Levels: 1–3 limited/one-sided; 4–6 both sides developed; 7–8 both sides developed plus a justified conclusion.

practice.stem: A commercial bank has customer deposits of $800 million. It keeps 10% of its deposits as cash reserves, lends 75% to customers and uses the rest to buy government bonds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount the bank holds as reserves, lends to customers and holds in government bonds.
parts.answer: Reserves $80 million; loans $600 million; bonds $120 million.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not the bank should increase its lending to 85% of its deposits.
parts.answer: For: loans pay the highest interest, so profit rises; supports firms and households. Against: lower reserves and bonds mean less liquidity, so the bank may not be able to repay depositors who withdraw; more bad-debt risk. Conclusion depends on how stable deposits are and on regulation.
parts.working: For (up to 3): loans earn more interest than cash or bonds, raising profit; more credit helps spending and investment; satisfies borrowers' demand. Against (up to 3): less cash and liquid bonds to meet withdrawals (liquidity risk); bank run risk; more loans to riskier borrowers; central bank rules may require reserves. Max 5 without a conclusion; 1 for a justified conclusion.

practice.stem:
A café sells meals at Rs 250 each. The table shows its total cost per day at different outputs.
Meals per day | Total cost (Rs)
0 | 8 000
50 | 13 000
100 | 17 000
150 | 22 500

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the café's fixed cost per day.
parts.working: B1: Rs 8 000 (total cost when output is zero).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the average total cost per meal when 100 meals are sold.
parts.answer: Rs 170

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the café's profit when it sells 150 meals.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why average fixed cost falls as output increases.
parts.answer: Fixed cost stays the same (Rs 8 000) whatever the output, so as more meals are produced it is spread over a larger number of units, so the fixed cost per meal falls.
parts.working: 1 mark: total fixed cost does not change with output. 1 mark: divided by more units, so AFC falls.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is a variable cost for a bakery?
A the rent of the shop
B the flour used to make bread
C the yearly insurance on the building
D the interest on a bank loan
parts.answer: B the flour used to make bread
parts.working: A variable cost changes with output: the more bread baked, the more flour used. Rent, insurance and loan interest (A, C, D) are fixed costs that must be paid whatever the output.

practice.stem: A small factory making plastic buckets has fixed costs of Rs 40 000 a month. The variable cost is Rs 120 per bucket. In March it made 500 buckets.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define fixed cost.
parts.answer: A cost that does not change with the level of output (in the short run), e.g. rent.
parts.working: Cost that does not vary with output (1); example such as rent or insurance (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the factory's total cost in March.

parts.label: c
