parts.text: Calculate the average total cost per bucket in March.
parts.answer: Rs 200

practice.stem: A shoe shop sells 1 200 pairs of sandals a month at Rs 350 a pair. It cuts the price to Rs 300 and sales rise to 1 500 pairs a month.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define total revenue.
parts.answer: The total income a firm receives from selling its output: price × quantity sold.
parts.working: Income from sales (1); = price × quantity (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the shop's total revenue before and after the price cut.
parts.answer: Before Rs 420 000; after Rs 450 000.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a rise in total revenue does not necessarily mean the shop's profit has risen.
parts.answer: Selling more pairs also raises total cost (more sandals bought in), so profit (TR − TC) may rise, fall or stay the same.
parts.working: Profit = total revenue − total cost (1); extra 300 pairs add to costs, which may exceed the Rs 30 000 rise in revenue (1).

practice.stem: A new mobile-phone accessories business opened in Rawalpindi this year. Its owner says that for the first year its aims are to survive and to win customers from established rivals.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by survival as an objective of a firm.
parts.answer: Staying in business by covering costs (at least in the long run) and having enough cash to pay bills, rather than closing.
parts.working: Continue trading/avoid closure (1); by covering costs/having enough cash to pay debts (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a new firm might aim to increase its market share rather than maximise profit.
parts.answer: To build a customer base and brand loyalty, it may set low prices and spend on promotion; a larger share later gives economies of scale and market power, allowing higher long-run profits.
parts.working: New firms need to attract customers from established rivals (1), so may charge low prices/spend on advertising even if profit is low (1); a larger market share builds loyalty and reputation (1) and later allows lower average costs and higher long-term profit (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A firm has fixed costs of Rs 60 000. At an output of 3 000 units its average variable cost is Rs 25. What is its average total cost at this output?
A Rs 20
B Rs 25
C Rs 45
D Rs 85
parts.answer: C Rs 45
parts.working: Total cost = 60 000 + 25 × 3 000 = 135 000; average total cost = 135 000 ÷ 3 000 = Rs 45 (= AFC 20 + AVC 25). Rs 20 (A) is only average fixed cost and Rs 25 (B) only average variable cost.

practice.stem: A rickshaw driver in Rawalpindi rents his rickshaw for Rs 31 200 a month and pays Rs 6 000 a month for maintenance. On each day he works he spends Rs 1 800 on fuel and collects Rs 4 500 in fares.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Classify the rickshaw rent, the maintenance and the fuel as fixed or variable costs.
parts.answer: Rent and maintenance: fixed costs; fuel: variable cost.
parts.working: Rent and maintenance fixed (1); fuel variable (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate his profit in a month in which he works 26 days.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate his average fixed cost per working day if he works 26 days and if he works 24 days, to the nearest rupee.
parts.answer: 26 days: Rs 1 431; 24 days: Rs 1 550.

practice.stem:
A printing firm produces 5 000 school notebooks a week and sells each one for Rs 50. Its weekly costs are:
Rent of premises: Rs 60 000
Interest on a bank loan: Rs 15 000
Paper and ink: Rs 90 000
Wages paid at Rs 7 per notebook: Rs 35 000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the firm's total fixed cost and total variable cost per week.
parts.answer: Total fixed cost Rs 75 000; total variable cost Rs 125 000.
parts.working: Fixed = rent + interest = 60 000 + 15 000 = Rs 75 000 (1); variable = paper and ink + piece-rate wages = 90 000 + 35 000 = Rs 125 000 (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the firm's average total cost per notebook and its weekly profit.
parts.answer: Average total cost Rs 40; profit Rs 50 000 a week.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The landlord raises the rent by Rs 25 000 a week. Output does not change. Explain how this affects the firm's average variable cost and its average total cost.
parts.answer: Average variable cost is unchanged at Rs 25, because rent is a fixed cost; average total cost rises by Rs 5 to Rs 45.
parts.working: Rent is a fixed cost, so variable costs and AVC (125 000 ÷ 5 000 = Rs 25) do not change (1); fixed cost rises to Rs 100 000 (1); ATC = 225 000 ÷ 5 000 = Rs 45, a rise of Rs 5 (1).

practice.stem: A firm making solar lamps has fixed costs of Rs 600 000 a month. Each lamp sells for Rs 1 500 and has a variable cost of Rs 900.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of lamps the firm must sell each month for total revenue to equal total cost.
parts.answer: 1 000 lamps
parts.working: Each lamp contributes 1 500 − 900 = Rs 600 towards fixed costs (M1); 600 000 ÷ 600 = 1 000 lamps (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the firm's profit if it sells 1 400 lamps in a month.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how a rise in the price of the lamps would affect the number the firm must sell to cover its costs.
parts.answer: Each lamp would contribute more above its variable cost, so fewer lamps are needed to cover the fixed costs.
parts.working: Higher price raises revenue per lamp relative to variable cost (1); so fewer lamps are needed to cover fixed costs (1).

practice.stem: A drinks company in Lahore has set a target of halving the plastic waste from its bottles within five years, even though this will raise its costs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define profit.
parts.answer: Total revenue minus total cost.
parts.working: Total revenue (1) minus total cost (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse why a profit-seeking firm might choose an objective such as reducing its environmental impact.
parts.answer: It improves the firm's image and brand loyalty, so sales rise; attracts customers and workers who care about the environment; avoids future fines, taxes or regulations; may cut costs in the long run (less material); so it can support long-run profit.
parts.working: Up to 6 marks for developed points: better reputation increases demand/brand loyalty (2); helps recruit and keep motivated workers (1); avoids fines, taxes or bans on plastic in future (1); may reduce costs by using less material (1); satisfies shareholders/investors and retailers who want sustainable suppliers (1); owners may genuinely value social responsibility (1).

practice.stem: A large food company says its main aim is to maximise profit. A social enterprise selling low-cost water filters says its main aim is to improve health in poor villages.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two objectives a firm might have other than profit maximisation.
parts.answer: Any two of: survival; growth / increasing sales; increasing market share; social welfare / helping the community; providing a good service; protecting the environment.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid objectives.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not a firm should always aim to maximise profit.
parts.answer: Profit is important, but other aims may be more suitable at times.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for 'should': rewards owners/shareholders for risk; provides funds for investment and growth; shows efficient use of resources; attracts finance. Up to 3 marks for 'not always': a new firm may aim to survive or grow first; cutting prices to gain market share may be better long term; social enterprises and public-sector firms aim at welfare; pursuing profit may harm reputation (pollution, poor treatment of workers); owners may want a comfortable life rather than maximum profit. Max 5 without a conclusion; 1 mark for a justified conclusion.

practice.stem:
A firm can choose its output. The table shows the price it can charge and its total cost at each output.
Output (units) | Price (Rs) | Total cost (Rs)
100 | 500 | 30 000
200 | 450 | 55 000
300 | 400 | 80 000
400 | 350 | 125 000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit at each output and identify the profit-maximising output.
parts.answer: Profits: Rs 20 000, Rs 35 000, Rs 40 000, Rs 15 000; profit is maximised at 300 units.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not the firm should produce 400 units in order to maximise its sales revenue.
parts.answer: For: highest revenue (Rs 140 000) and market share, may deter rivals, gain economies of scale later, satisfy managers. Against: profit falls from Rs 40 000 to Rs 15 000, owners/shareholders lose, less profit to reinvest. Conclusion depends on the firm's long-term aims.
parts.working: For (up to 3): revenue Rs 140 000 is the highest; bigger market share and brand recognition; may squeeze out rivals and allow higher prices later; managers' pay may depend on sales. Against (up to 3): profit falls by Rs 25 000; owners want profit; lower funds for investment; lower price may harm the brand image. Max 5 without a conclusion; 1 mark for a justified conclusion.

practice.stem: An airline flies between Karachi and Dubai.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give one example of a fixed cost and one example of a variable cost for the airline.
parts.answer: Fixed: e.g. lease of aircraft, airport office rent, insurance, salaries of head-office staff. Variable: e.g. fuel, in-flight meals, landing fees per flight.
parts.working: Valid fixed cost (1); valid variable cost (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not a firm's average total cost always falls as it increases its output.
parts.answer: Falls: average fixed cost falls as fixed costs are spread over more units; internal economies of scale (bulk buying, specialisation, cheaper finance) lower costs. Not always: in the short run, fixed capacity leads to overcrowding, overtime pay and breakdowns, raising average variable cost; in the long run diseconomies of scale (communication, coordination, motivation) can raise average cost. Conclusion: average cost usually falls at first but can rise beyond a point.
parts.working: Falls (up to 4): spreading fixed costs (AFC falls continuously); purchasing, technical, financial, managerial economies; e.g. a fuller aircraft has lower cost per passenger. Not always (up to 4): capacity limits – overtime, crowding, more breakdowns; prices of inputs rise when buying large quantities in a scarce market; diseconomies of scale – communication, coordination, worker morale; external diseconomies such as congestion. Levels: 1–3 limited/one-sided; 4–6 both sides developed; 7–8 both sides developed plus a justified conclusion.

practice.stem: A state-owned railway company carries passengers and freight. It makes a loss every year and receives a subsidy from the government.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two objectives a public-sector organisation might have.
parts.answer: e.g. providing an affordable service to the public; serving remote areas; providing jobs; breaking even; safety; reducing road congestion and pollution.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid objectives.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not the state-owned railway should aim to make a profit.
parts.answer: For: profit removes the need for subsidy, freeing tax revenue for other uses (opportunity cost); encourages efficiency and cost control; funds investment. Against: profit aim may mean higher fares or closing unprofitable rural routes, hurting poorer people; external benefits (less congestion, pollution, road accidents) are not counted in profit; railways are a public service. Conclusion: aim to cover costs or reduce losses while keeping social objectives.
parts.working: For (up to 4): subsidy has an opportunity cost; efficiency incentive; money for new trains and safety; could be privatised more easily. Against (up to 4): higher fares reduce access for low-income passengers; unprofitable routes to remote areas closed; external benefits of rail over road; essential freight for the economy; social objectives such as jobs. Levels: 1–3 limited/one-sided; 4–6 both sides developed; 7–8 both sides developed plus a justified conclusion.

practice.stem: A road transport firm has fixed costs of Rs 2.4 million a month. Its variable cost is Rs 80 per kilometre and it charges customers Rs 160 per kilometre. It drives 40 000 km a month. A rise in fuel prices then increases its variable cost by 25%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the firm's monthly profit before and after the rise in fuel prices, assuming its prices and distance driven do not change.
parts.answer: Before Rs 800 000; after Rs 0 (it just breaks even).
parts.working: TR = 160 × 40 000 = Rs 6.4 million; TC before = 2.4m + 80 × 40 000 = Rs 5.6 million, profit Rs 0.8 million (M1 A1); new VC Rs 100 per km, TC = 2.4m + 4.0m = Rs 6.4 million, profit Rs 0 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not the firm should raise its prices in response to the higher fuel costs.
parts.answer: For: restores profit; rivals face the same fuel costs and may also raise prices; customers may have few alternatives. Against: customers may switch to rivals or rail, so revenue may fall if demand is price elastic; could lose long-term contracts; alternative is to cut other costs or improve fuel efficiency. Conclusion depends on competition and price elasticity.
parts.working: For (up to 3): without a rise profit is zero; cost rise is industry-wide so rivals likely to raise prices; demand may be inelastic if few substitutes. Against (up to 3): customers switch to cheaper rivals/rail; contract customers may leave; better to cut other costs, use fuel-efficient vehicles or plan routes better. Max 5 without a conclusion; 1 mark for a justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which change is most likely to cause a household to save more of its income?
A a fall in the household's income
B a rise in the interest rate paid on savings
C easier access to credit cards
D greater confidence that the household's jobs are secure
parts.answer: B a rise in the interest rate paid on savings
parts.working: A higher interest rate increases the reward for saving, so households tend to save more. Lower income (A) usually reduces saving; easy credit (C) encourages borrowing and spending; job security (D) reduces the need for precautionary saving.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two influences on the amount a household spends.
parts.answer: Any two of: disposable income; wealth; interest rates; confidence about the future; availability of credit; size and age of household; taxes.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid influences.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why a household might spend less even though its income has not changed.
parts.answer: e.g. higher interest rates make borrowing dearer and saving more rewarding; fear of losing jobs makes it save more; fall in wealth.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two developed reasons: a rise in interest rates (dearer loans, more reward for saving); lower confidence/fear of unemployment; fall in wealth, e.g. house or share prices; credit harder to get; saving for a planned future purchase such as a wedding or house.

practice.stem: A young married couple in Islamabad put aside Rs 20 000 of their income every month.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define saving.
parts.answer: Disposable income that is not spent on consumption.
parts.working: Income (1) not spent (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two motives the couple may have for saving.
parts.answer: e.g. to buy a house or car in the future; for emergencies such as illness; for children's education; to earn interest.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two developed motives: a future large purchase (house, car, wedding); a precaution against illness, job loss or emergencies; children's education; retirement/old age; to earn interest.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two sources from which a household can borrow.
parts.answer: e.g. commercial bank, microfinance bank, credit card company, relatives/friends, shop credit, moneylender.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid sources.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two factors that influence how much a household borrows.
parts.answer: e.g. interest rates; confidence about future income; availability of loans; level of existing debt; wealth to use as collateral.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two developed factors: interest rate (cost of borrowing); confidence/job security; banks' willingness to lend; income to repay; wealth/collateral; existing debts.

practice.stem: A family in Multan has a monthly income of Rs 150 000. The father is 45 and the grandmother, who is retired, lives with the family.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two factors, other than the level of income, that affect the proportion of income a household saves.
parts.answer: e.g. age; interest rates; confidence; availability of credit; social or religious attitudes; size of family; pension schemes.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid factors.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a retired person usually saves a smaller proportion of income than a worker aged 45.
parts.answer: A 45-year-old is near peak earnings and saves for retirement; a retired person's income is lower (pension) and they draw on past savings to pay for living costs and healthcare.
parts.working: Workers in middle age earn more (1) and save for retirement and children's education (1); retired people have lower income (1) and run down savings/spend a larger share on needs such as health care (1).

practice.stem: A household in Lahore has a monthly disposable income of Rs 180 000. It spends Rs 153 000 a month and saves the rest.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the household's saving as a percentage of its disposable income.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why a high-income household usually saves a larger proportion of its income than a low-income household.
parts.answer: Low-income households must spend almost all their income on necessities such as food, rent and fuel, so little is left to save. High-income households can meet their needs with a smaller share of income, so they can save more; they also have better access to banks and saving schemes and may save for large future purchases or investments.
parts.working: For each of two reasons: 1 mark for the reason, 1 mark for development.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A household's monthly disposable income rises from Rs 100 000 to Rs 120 000, and its spending rises from Rs 90 000 to Rs 104 000. What happens to its saving?
A Saving falls by Rs 6 000.
B Saving rises by Rs 6 000.
C Saving rises by Rs 14 000.
D Saving stays at 10% of income.
parts.answer: B Saving rises by Rs 6 000.
parts.working: Saving = income − spending: Rs 10 000 before and Rs 16 000 after, a rise of Rs 6 000. C is the rise in spending, and D is wrong because saving rises to 13.3% of income.

practice.stem: A household in Karachi has a monthly income of Rs 250 000. It spends 35% of its income on food.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the household's monthly spending on food.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The household's income rises by 20% and its spending on food rises by 10%. Calculate the new percentage of income spent on food. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why low-income households spend a higher proportion of their income on food than high-income households.
parts.answer: Food is a necessity, so poor households must spend most of their income on it; as income rises spending on food rises by less than income, and more goes on luxuries and saving.
parts.working: Food is a necessity that takes a large share of a small income (1); as income rises, the extra is spent on other goods or saved, so the food share falls (1).

practice.stem: House prices in a large city rose by 25% over two years. Most households in the city own their homes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between income and wealth.
parts.answer: Income is a flow of money received over a period (e.g. wages per month); wealth is the stock of assets owned at a point in time (e.g. houses, savings).
parts.working: Income: flow of money over a period (1); wealth: stock/value of assets owned (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse how the rise in house prices may affect household spending and saving.
parts.answer: Homeowners feel wealthier and more confident, so they spend more and save less; they can borrow more using the house as security. But renters and first-time buyers must save more for a deposit and may cut spending.
parts.working: Higher house prices increase homeowners' wealth (1); feeling richer and more confident, they spend more (1) and save a smaller proportion of income (1); higher value as collateral makes borrowing easier, raising spending (1). Other side: people who rent or want to buy must save more for a deposit/pay higher rents (1) so their spending falls (1).

practice.stem:
The table shows the interest rate on savings and the average saving ratio (saving as a percentage of disposable income) in a country.
Year | Interest rate (%) | Saving ratio (%)
2022 | 8 | 9
2023 | 12 | 11
2024 | 15 | 13
2025 | 11 | 12

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the change in the saving ratio between 2022 and 2024, in percentage points.
parts.answer: 4 percentage points (rise)
parts.working: 13 − 9 = 4 percentage points (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the relationship between the interest rate and the saving ratio shown in the data.
parts.answer: Positive/direct: when the interest rate rises the saving ratio rises, and when it falls the saving ratio falls, though not proportionately.
parts.working: Positive relationship (1); supported with data, e.g. rate 8→15% and saving ratio 9→13% / both fell in 2025 (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons, other than the interest rate, why the saving ratio might change.
parts.answer: e.g. changes in income; confidence/fear of unemployment; inflation; availability of credit; changes in age structure; pension rules.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two developed reasons, e.g. falling confidence leads to precautionary saving; higher incomes allow a larger proportion to be saved; easier credit reduces saving; high inflation encourages buying now.

practice.stem: Rubina borrows Rs 150 000 from a microfinance bank at an interest rate of 24% a year to buy a sewing machine for a home business.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the interest Rubina pays in one year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Rubina may decide to borrow even though the interest rate is high.
parts.answer: She expects the extra income from sewing to be more than the interest; she has no savings and cannot get cheaper loans.
parts.working: The machine lets her earn income/profit from selling clothes (1); if this exceeds Rs 36 000 a year the loan is worthwhile (1); she may have no savings or collateral for a cheaper bank loan (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how borrowing to buy a sewing machine differs from borrowing to buy a television in its effect on the household's future income.
parts.answer: The sewing machine is capital that produces income which can repay the loan and raise future income; the television is a consumer good that gives satisfaction but no income, so repayments reduce future spending.
parts.working: Sewing machine: productive asset/capital (1) that generates income to repay the loan and raise living standards (1). Television: consumer good giving no income (1), so future income is reduced by repayments/less available to spend later (1).

practice.stem: The central bank of a country cuts its interest rate from 15% to 12%, and commercial banks reduce the interest they charge on loans.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two reasons why a household might borrow.
parts.answer: Any two of: to buy a house; to buy expensive durable goods such as a car or motorcycle; to pay for education; to pay for a wedding or emergency; to start a small business.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid reasons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not the fall in interest rates will cause households to borrow more.
parts.answer: Borrowing is likely to rise but depends on other influences.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for 'will': loans are cheaper, so repayments fall; more households can afford house or car loans; saving is less rewarding, so spending financed by credit rises. Up to 3 marks for 'may not': households worried about job security or a recession may not borrow; they may already have high debts; banks may not lend if they think borrowers are risky; a cut of 3 percentage points may be too small to change decisions; religious or cultural reasons may discourage interest-based borrowing. Max 5 without a conclusion; 1 mark for a justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define disposable income.
parts.answer: Income after direct taxes have been deducted (and state benefits added), available to spend or save.
parts.working: Income after direct taxes (1) available for spending and saving (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not an increase in income will always lead a household to spend more.
parts.answer: Usually yes: more income allows more spending, especially for poorer households with unmet needs. But not always: the rise may be saved (high-income households, uncertainty), used to repay debts, or offset by higher taxes or prices; a temporary rise may be saved. Conclusion: spending usually rises, but by less than income and not in every case.
parts.working: Will (up to 4): more income means more purchasing power; low-income households spend most of any rise on needs; confidence rises, encouraging large purchases; easier to borrow. Not always (up to 4): higher-income households save more of a rise; uncertainty/expected job loss leads to precautionary saving; income used to repay loans; higher income tax may cut disposable income; if prices rise faster, real income falls; a one-off bonus may be saved. Levels: 1–3 limited/one-sided; 4–6 both sides developed; 7–8 both sides developed plus a justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two ways a government could encourage households to save more.
parts.answer: e.g. higher interest rates; tax-free savings schemes; national savings certificates; compulsory pension schemes; public campaigns.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid methods.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not households should be encouraged to save more.
parts.answer: For: provides funds for banks to lend for investment, security against emergencies, less borrowing, provision for old age. Against: less spending reduces firms' sales, output and jobs in the short run; poor households cannot afford to save; saving may sit idle. Conclusion depends on the state of the economy.
parts.working: For (up to 4): savings are lent to firms for investment, raising future productive capacity; households are protected against illness or job loss; less reliance on government in old age; lower debt. Against (up to 4): lower consumer spending means less demand, lower sales and possible unemployment, especially in a recession; firms may cut investment if sales fall; low-income households need to spend on necessities; money saved at home is not lent. Levels: 1–3 limited/one-sided; 4–6 both sides developed; 7–8 both sides developed plus a justified conclusion.

practice.stem: A country's central bank raises its interest rate, and commercial banks raise the interest rate on home loans from 10% to 14% a year. One household has an interest-only home loan of Rs 6 million.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the increase in the household's monthly interest payment.
parts.answer: Rs 20 000 a month
parts.working: Yearly interest rises from Rs 600 000 to Rs 840 000, an increase of Rs 240 000 (M1); ÷ 12 = Rs 20 000 a month (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not the rise in interest rates will reduce total household spending in the country.
parts.answer: Likely to reduce: borrowers pay more interest and cut other spending; loans for cars and houses become dearer; saving becomes more rewarding; falling house prices reduce wealth. May not: savers receive more interest income and may spend more; many loans may be at fixed rates; spending on necessities continues; confidence and rising incomes may outweigh the rise. Conclusion depends on how many households are borrowers rather than savers.
parts.working: Reduce (up to 4): higher repayments, e.g. Rs 20 000 a month for this household, leave less to spend; dearer credit discourages buying cars, appliances and houses; higher reward for saving encourages saving instead of spending; lower house prices reduce wealth and confidence. Not reduce (up to 4): savers and retired people gain more interest income; fixed-rate loans are not affected at once; necessities still bought; effect is small if incomes or confidence are rising; households may borrow anyway for essential purchases. Levels: 1–3 limited/one-sided; 4–6 both sides developed; 7–8 both sides developed plus a justified conclusion.

practice.stem: Workers at brick kilns near Lahore have formed a trade union. Many of them work long hours in hot, dusty conditions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two functions of a trade union.
parts.answer: Any two of: negotiating wages; improving working conditions; protecting jobs; representing members in disputes; improving health and safety; providing training, legal advice or benefits; influencing government policy.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid functions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which the union could improve working conditions for the kiln workers.
parts.answer: Negotiate with owners for shorter hours, breaks and safety equipment such as masks; press the government to enforce labour laws; represent workers who are treated unfairly.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two developed ways: collective bargaining for shorter hours/rest breaks; demand protective equipment and clean drinking water; report breaches of safety laws and lobby government; represent individual members in disputes; threaten industrial action if demands ignored.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define collective bargaining.
parts.answer: Negotiation between a trade union, on behalf of all its members, and employers over pay and working conditions.
parts.working: Negotiation between union (representing workers as a group) and employer(s) (1) over pay/conditions (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two forms of industrial action a trade union might use.
parts.answer: e.g. strike – workers stop working; work-to-rule – doing only the minimum required; overtime ban; go-slow; sit-in.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two forms, each identified (1) and explained in terms of how it puts pressure on the employer (1): strike (output stops, sales lost); work-to-rule; overtime ban; go-slow; picketing.

practice.stem: In an industry with 180 000 workers, 45 000 are members of a trade union. In one year the union recruits 9 000 new members while the number of workers in the industry stays the same.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of workers who were union members before the recruitment drive.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of workers who are union members after the recruitment drive.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a higher membership rate may increase the union's bargaining power.
parts.answer: With more members, a strike would stop more of the industry's output, so employers lose more and are more likely to agree; the union also has more subscription income to support members during action.
parts.working: A strike or action would affect a larger share of workers/output (1), so employers would lose more revenue (1); more income from subscriptions/strike funds, and stronger claim to represent workers (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two costs to a worker of being a member of a trade union.
parts.answer: e.g. membership subscription fees; lost pay during strikes; pressure to follow union decisions; possible tension with the employer.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid costs: subscription fees; loss of wages while on strike; must follow collective decisions they may disagree with; possible poor relations with managers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why a worker may decide to join a trade union.
parts.answer: To get higher pay and better conditions through collective bargaining; for protection against unfair dismissal and help in disputes; for benefits such as legal advice and training.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two developed reasons: stronger bargaining power as a group; protection of job security and help with disputes or unfair treatment; better health and safety; access to legal advice, training, insurance or welfare benefits.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define a trade union.
parts.answer: An organisation of workers that acts on behalf of its members to protect and improve their pay and working conditions.
parts.working: 1 mark: association/organisation of workers. 1 mark: aims to improve pay/conditions/job security of members.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two factors that affect the strength of a trade union.
parts.answer: Any two, developed: the proportion of workers who are members – a high membership gives more bargaining power; the skills of members – skilled workers are hard to replace during a strike; the state of the economy – when unemployment is low, firms find it harder to replace workers; laws on strikes and union activity; the financial health of the employer; public support.
parts.working: For each of two factors: 1 mark for the factor, 1 mark for explaining how it affects bargaining power.

practice.stem: A union representing textile workers asks for a 15% pay rise. The employer offers 6%. Prices in the country are rising at 9% a year. The average monthly wage is currently Rs 70 000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the new average monthly wage under the union's claim and under the employer's offer.
parts.answer: Union claim Rs 80 500; employer offer Rs 74 200.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the union is likely to reject the employer's offer.
parts.answer: A 6% rise is below 9% inflation, so workers' real wages (purchasing power) would fall.
parts.working: Offer is less than the rate of inflation (1); so wages buy fewer goods – real wage falls (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two effects on the firm if the workers go on strike.
parts.answer: Lost output and sales revenue; orders delayed or lost to rivals; damaged reputation and relations with workers.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two developed effects: output stops, so revenue and profit fall; customers (e.g. foreign buyers) switch to rivals, losing future orders; fixed costs still have to be paid; poorer relations/lower morale after the strike.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two reasons why an employer might agree to a union's pay claim.
parts.answer: e.g. to avoid a strike; high profits; to keep and attract workers; workers' productivity has risen; shortage of skilled workers.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid reasons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse how a successful pay claim by a trade union could affect employment in an industry.
parts.answer: Higher wages raise firms' costs, so they may employ fewer workers or replace them with machines, and may raise prices so sales fall; but if productivity rises or demand is strong and profits are high, employment may not fall.
parts.working: Higher wage raises the cost of labour (1); firms demand fewer workers – movement up the demand curve for labour (1); firms may substitute capital for labour (1); higher costs may lead to higher prices and lower sales, reducing derived demand (1). However: if productivity rises/the firm is very profitable or demand is growing, jobs may be kept (1); higher pay may improve motivation and reduce labour turnover (1).

practice.stem: A union at a cement factory agrees to the introduction of new machinery. In return, every worker receives a 10% pay rise. As a result, output per worker rises by 25%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in the labour cost of producing each tonne of cement.
parts.answer: A fall of 12%
parts.working: New labour cost per unit = 1.10 ÷ 1.25 = 0.88 of the old cost (M1); a fall of 12% (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which a trade union may benefit the firm that employs its members.
parts.answer: e.g. one organisation to negotiate with saves time; agreements on productivity/new technology; communicates workers' views and reduces disputes; helps training and safety.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two developed ways: employer bargains with one body rather than each worker; helps introduce change (new machines) with less resistance; channels complaints, reducing labour turnover and unofficial action; supports training and health and safety, raising productivity.

practice.stem: After a fire in a garment factory, a trade union campaigns for better fire exits and safety training.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two aims of a trade union other than higher pay.
parts.answer: e.g. better health and safety; job security; shorter hours; better holidays/pensions; training; equal opportunities.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid aims.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why an employer might agree to spend more on safety after the union's campaign.
parts.answer: e.g. to avoid a strike and lost output; to avoid fines or legal claims; to protect its reputation with buyers; fewer accidents mean less lost output and lower labour turnover.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two developed reasons: avoid industrial action and the lost output/revenue it causes; avoid fines, closure or compensation claims under safety laws; foreign buyers/brands may stop orders from unsafe factories; fewer accidents reduce lost working time and costs; better morale lowers labour turnover and recruitment costs.

practice.stem: 2 000 workers at a fertiliser plant go on strike for 5 days. Each worker normally produces output worth Rs 12 000 a day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of output lost during the strike.
parts.answer: Rs 120 million (Rs 120 000 000)
parts.working: 2 000 × 12 000 = Rs 24 million a day (M1); × 5 = Rs 120 million (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two possible effects of the strike on the workers who take part.
parts.answer: Lose wages for the strike days; may win higher pay or better conditions; risk of losing their jobs if the firm loses customers; relations with managers may worsen.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two developed effects: lose pay for 5 days, reducing household income; may gain a pay rise or better conditions afterwards; job losses if customers switch to imports/rivals; stress and poorer relations with employer; (credit) farmers face fertiliser shortages, harming public support.

practice.stem: A teachers' union asks for an increase in its members' average monthly pay from Rs 90 000 to Rs 103 500. Prices in the country rose by 12% over the past year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage pay rise that the union is asking for.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not a trade union is always beneficial for its members.
parts.answer: Usually beneficial, but not always.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for 'beneficial': collective bargaining wins higher pay (e.g. protecting real wages when prices rise 12%); better working conditions, safety and job security; legal advice and representation; training. Up to 3 marks for 'not always': members pay subscriptions; strikes mean lost pay; high wage rises may cause employers to cut jobs or replace workers with machines; a weak union may achieve little; members may disagree with the union's decisions. Max 5 without a conclusion; 1 mark for a justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two ways in which trade unions might reduce the efficiency of firms.
parts.answer: e.g. strikes disrupt output; resisting new technology; restrictive practices/overmanning; wage rises above productivity raise costs.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid ways.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not trade unions benefit an economy.
parts.answer: Benefits: fairer pay, better conditions and safety, more skilled and motivated workers, smoother introduction of change, reduced inequality. Costs: strikes lose output and exports, higher wage costs can raise prices and unemployment, resistance to new technology, may protect members at the expense of non-members. Conclusion depends on how unions behave and on the economic situation.
parts.working: Benefit (up to 4): protect workers from exploitation; higher wages raise spending; health and safety gains; training and productivity agreements; easier collective negotiation; less inequality. Not benefit (up to 4): strikes lose output and harm exporters; cost-push inflation; unemployment if wages exceed productivity; resistance to change reduces competitiveness; foreign investors may be deterred. Levels: 1–3 limited/one-sided; 4–6 both sides developed; 7–8 both sides developed plus a justified conclusion.

practice.stem: Junior doctors in government hospitals in a country have gone on strike several times over pay. Some politicians want to ban strikes in essential services.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two essential services other than health care.
parts.answer: e.g. fire service, police, electricity supply, water supply, ambulance services.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid examples.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not the government should ban strikes by workers in essential services such as hospitals.
parts.answer: For a ban: strikes put lives at risk, harm the poor who cannot pay for private care, and hit the whole economy. Against: workers lose their main bargaining power, pay and conditions may fall, staff may leave the profession or emigrate, causing shortages; a ban may be ignored. Alternatives: independent pay review bodies, arbitration. Conclusion: a ban could be justified only with fair alternative ways of setting pay.
parts.working: For (up to 4): risk to patients' lives; poor households most affected; public services have no alternative supplier; disruption to the wider economy. Against (up to 4): removes workers' strongest bargaining tool, so pay may fall behind; low morale, staff shortages, brain drain; may lead to unofficial action; basic right of workers; better to use arbitration/minimum service rules. Levels: 1–3 limited/one-sided; 4–6 both sides developed; 7–8 both sides developed plus a justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why trade union membership may fall during a recession.
parts.answer: Many workers lose their jobs, so they leave the union or stop paying; others cannot afford the subscription or feel the union cannot protect them.
parts.working: Unemployment rises, so fewer workers are employed to be members (1); unemployed or low-income workers stop paying subscriptions / believe unions are weak during a recession (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not a trade union is likely to win a pay rise for its members during a recession.
parts.answer: Less likely: demand and profits are falling, firms are cutting jobs, unemployment means workers are easy to replace, and members fear losing jobs so are less willing to strike. More likely if: the union is large and well-organised, workers are skilled and hard to replace, the firm or sector is still profitable (e.g. essential services), or inflation is high and the case for a rise is strong. Conclusion: possible but usually small.
parts.working: Unlikely (up to 4): falling demand and profits limit the firm's ability to pay; unemployment is high, so firms can find replacement workers; members fear redundancy; government may freeze public-sector pay. Likely (up to 4): strong, large membership; skilled workers in short supply; some firms still profitable; good negotiating skills or public support; high inflation erodes real wages, strengthening the claim. Levels: 1–3 limited/one-sided; 4–6 both sides developed; 7–8 both sides developed plus a justified conclusion.

practice.stem: A car plant employs 3 000 union members. The union asks for a pay rise of Rs 2 000 a month for every member. The firm says it can afford to increase its total yearly wage bill by only Rs 54 million.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the yearly cost of the union's claim and the monthly pay rise per worker that the firm can afford.
parts.answer: Claim costs Rs 72 million a year; the firm can afford Rs 1 500 a month per worker.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not the union should accept the firm's offer.
parts.answer: Accept: avoids strike and lost wages, protects jobs if the firm really cannot afford more, and a Rs 1 500 rise is three-quarters of the claim. Reject: if profits are high or inflation is high, members' real pay may fall; holding out may win more. Conclusion depends on the firm's finances, inflation and members' views.
parts.working: Accept (up to 3): 75% of the claim; avoids loss of pay during a strike; higher costs could lead to job cuts or automation; keeps good relations. Reject (up to 3): firm may be able to pay more (check profits); rise may not keep up with inflation; union has strong bargaining power if workers are skilled; could negotiate other benefits. Max 5 without a conclusion; 1 mark for a justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A country has a labour force of 60 million people, of whom 4.2 million are unemployed. What is the unemployment rate?
A 7.0 %
B 7.5 %
C 6.5 %
D 70 %
parts.working: Unemployment rate = unemployed ÷ labour force × 100 = 4.2 ÷ 60 × 100 = 7.0 %. B divides by the number employed (55.8 million), giving about 7.5 %, instead of by the whole labour force.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define unemployment.
parts.answer: Being of working age, willing and able to work, actively seeking work, but without a job.
parts.working: 1 mark: willing and able to work/of working age; 1 mark: without a job but looking for one.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify and explain two types of unemployment.
parts.answer: e.g. frictional – people between jobs; structural – mismatch caused by long-term decline of an industry
parts.working: 1 mark each for naming two types + 1 mark each for explanation: frictional (between jobs, searching); structural (decline of an industry/change in skills needed); cyclical (lack of demand in a recession); seasonal (demand varies with seasons, e.g. tourism, harvest).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A country has a working-age population of 30 million, a labour force of 19.5 million and 1.17 million unemployed people. What is its unemployment rate?
A 3.9%
B 6.0%
C 6.4%
D 0.06%
parts.working: Unemployment rate = unemployed ÷ labour force × 100 = 1.17 ÷ 19.5 × 100 = 6.0%. A divides by the working-age population (1.17 ÷ 30 × 100 = 3.9%), not the labour force. C divides by the employed workers (19.5 − 1.17 = 18.33 million) instead. D forgets to multiply by 100.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define frictional unemployment.
parts.answer: Unemployment that exists when workers are between jobs or searching for a suitable vacancy. It is short term, because it takes time to match workers with jobs.
parts.working: 1 mark: workers between jobs or searching for work; 1 mark: short term, or time taken to match workers to vacancies.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one cause of frictional unemployment.
parts.answer: Any one: lack of information about job vacancies; time spent moving home or changing jobs.
parts.working: 1 mark for any one valid cause.

practice.stem: A country has a working-age population of 35 million, a labour force of 22 million and 3.3 million unemployed people.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the activity rate (labour force as a percentage of the working-age population). Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: 1 mark for the method (labour force ÷ working-age population × 100); 1 mark for 62.9%.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of people in employment.
parts.working: 1 mark for labour force minus unemployed.

practice.stem: In a country, the working-age population is 130 million. The labour force is 75 million, of whom 69 million are employed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of people unemployed.
parts.answer: 6 million
parts.working: B1 75 − 69 = 6 million.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the unemployment rate. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the working-age population that is in the labour force. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain two consequences of unemployment for the government.
parts.answer: Lower income tax revenue; higher spending on unemployment benefits/welfare
parts.working: 1 mark each for two consequences + 1 mark each for development: less tax revenue (income and indirect taxes); more spending on benefits; larger budget deficit/more borrowing; opportunity cost – less to spend on schools/hospitals; social problems such as crime raise costs; loss of votes/popularity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why automation in textile mills in Faisalabad could cause structural unemployment.
parts.answer: Machines replace workers; the displaced workers' skills no longer match the jobs available, so they stay unemployed for a long time.
parts.working: 1 mark: machines replace labour/fewer workers needed; 1 mark: workers' skills do not match jobs elsewhere (occupational immobility); 1 mark: long-term unemployment linked to a change in the structure of the industry.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two government policies that could reduce this type of unemployment.
parts.answer: Retraining schemes to give workers new skills; subsidies/grants for firms that set up in the area or employ these workers
parts.working: 1 mark each for two policies + 1 mark each for explanation: retraining/vocational courses improve occupational mobility; relocation grants/housing help geographical mobility; subsidies to firms that hire; better job information centres; attracting new industries to the region.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a recession leads to cyclical unemployment.
parts.answer: Total spending (aggregate demand) falls, so firms sell less and produce less output. They reduce hiring, cut overtime or make workers redundant, so unemployment rises.
parts.working: 1 mark: fall in aggregate demand or spending; 1 mark: firms sell less and produce less; 1 mark: fewer workers needed, so hiring stops or workers are made redundant.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one government policy to reduce cyclical unemployment.
parts.answer: Any one, e.g. expansionary fiscal policy such as higher government spending on roads or schools, a cut in income tax, or lower interest rates to raise spending.
parts.working: 1 mark for any policy that raises aggregate demand.

practice.stem: A country has a labour force of 40 million. Its unemployment rate was 5.2% last year and rose to 6.8% this year. Assume the labour force stays at 40 million.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of unemployed people last year.
parts.answer: 2.08 million (5.2% × 40 million = 2 080 000)
parts.working: 1 mark for the method (unemployment rate × labour force); 1 mark for 2.08 million.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the increase in the number of unemployed people this year.
parts.answer: 0.64 million (6.8% of 40 million = 2.72 million; 2.72 − 2.08 = 0.64 million)
parts.working: 1 mark for 2.72 million; 1 mark for the difference of 0.64 million.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways in which a rise in the minimum wage could increase unemployment.
parts.answer: Any two, each explained: (1) firms facing higher labour costs employ fewer workers or cut hours; (2) some firms close or replace workers with machines; (3) more people want jobs at the higher wage than there are jobs (labour supply exceeds demand); (4) low-skilled workers are the most likely to lose their jobs.
parts.working: 2 marks for each reason fully explained (1 for the reason, 1 for the link to labour demand or supply).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether a rise in unemployment is always bad for an economy.
parts.answer: Usually harmful (lost output, lower incomes, lower tax revenue, social costs), but may be short-term frictional, can reduce inflationary pressure and may reflect structural change that raises productivity later.
parts.working: Up to 5 marks for harm: output below potential/lost GDP; lower incomes and living standards; lower tax revenue and higher benefit spending; skills lost; poverty, crime, health problems. Up to 5 marks for why not always bad: frictional unemployment may be short and improve job matching; lower wage pressure may reduce inflation; labour available for new expanding industries; firms may become more efficient. Max 8; conclusion required for top band, e.g. depends on type and duration.

practice.stem:
Real GDP growth (%) and unemployment rate (%) for five countries in one year:
Country A: growth 6.1, unemployment 4.0
Country B: growth 3.5, unemployment 6.2
Country C: growth 1.2, unemployment 8.9
Country D: growth −0.8, unemployment 11.5
Country E: growth 4.0, unemployment 7.8

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the country with the highest unemployment rate.
parts.answer: Country D (11.5 %)
parts.working: B1 Country D.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse the relationship between economic growth and the unemployment rate shown in the table.
parts.answer: Generally an inverse relationship: higher growth, lower unemployment (A highest growth 6.1 %, lowest unemployment 4.0 %; D negative growth, highest unemployment). Exception: E has higher growth than B but higher unemployment, so other factors (e.g. structural unemployment, labour force growth) matter.
parts.working: 1 mark: inverse/negative relationship; 1 mark: data comparison using two countries (A and D); 1 mark: reason – growth raises demand for goods and so for labour (derived demand); 1 mark: exception identified (E vs B); 1 mark: explanation of exception, e.g. growth driven by capital-intensive industries, fast-growing labour force, structural or frictional factors.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether governments should give higher priority to reducing unemployment than to controlling inflation.
parts.answer: A balanced discussion. For priority to unemployment: lost output and income, social and health costs, rising inequality, political pressure; moderate inflation may be tolerable. Against: high inflation erodes savings and real incomes, creates uncertainty that reduces investment, and can cause unemployment later. The trade-off is mainly short run. A reasoned conclusion is needed.
parts.working: 5–6 marks: developed arguments on both sides, clear use of the unemployment–inflation trade-off, and a justified conclusion. 3–4 marks: one side well developed or a limited link to the trade-off. 1–2 marks: unsupported assertions.

practice.stem:
Unemployment data for four countries in one year (hypothetical)
Country | Overall unemployment rate (%) | Youth unemployment rate, ages 15–24 (%)
A | 4.5 | 9.0
B | 12.0 | 27.6
C | 7.8 | 15.6
D | 3.1 | 6.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the country with the highest youth unemployment rate.
parts.answer: Country B (27.6%)
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times larger the youth unemployment rate is than the overall unemployment rate in Country B. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: 1 mark for the division; 1 mark for 2.3.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why youth unemployment is often higher than overall unemployment.
parts.answer: Any two: young people have less work experience; fewer skills or qualifications; they change jobs more often, so they are often between jobs; employers may prefer experienced workers; young workers are often the first to be dismissed.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why an economy can have frictional and structural unemployment even when the number of job vacancies is high.
parts.answer: Any four, each explained: workers lack the skills the vacancies need (structural); workers live far from the jobs and cannot easily move (geographical immobility); it takes time to search for and start a new job (frictional); workers do not know about the vacancies; wage expectations of workers are above what firms offer for the vacancies.
parts.working: 1 mark per valid point with an explanation, maximum 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is a progressive tax?
A a tax that takes a higher proportion of income as income rises
B a tax that takes the same proportion of income at all income levels
C a tax that takes the same amount from everyone
D a tax that takes a lower proportion of income as income rises
parts.answer: A a tax that takes a higher proportion of income as income rises
parts.working: A progressive tax has an average rate that rises with income. B is a proportional tax; D is a regressive tax.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between a direct tax and an indirect tax, giving one example of each.
parts.answer: Direct tax is levied on income or wealth and paid directly to the government by the person taxed (e.g. income tax). Indirect tax is levied on spending on goods and services (e.g. sales tax/GST).
parts.working: 1 mark: direct tax on income/wealth; 1 mark: valid example (income tax, corporation tax, property tax); 1 mark: indirect tax on spending/goods and services; 1 mark: valid example (sales tax, GST/VAT, excise duty, customs duty).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two reasons why governments impose taxes.
parts.answer: To raise revenue for public spending; to redistribute income
parts.working: 1 mark each, any two: raise revenue; redistribute income; discourage consumption of demerit goods/reduce external costs; protect domestic industries (tariffs); influence aggregate demand/manage the economy.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following is an example of an indirect tax?
A income tax paid by employees on their wages
B value added tax (VAT) charged on goods bought in shops
C corporation tax on the profits of companies
D a tax paid by a property owner on the value of a house
parts.answer: B value added tax (VAT) charged on goods bought in shops
parts.working: Indirect taxes are charged on spending; VAT is added to the price of goods. A, C and D are direct taxes on income, profits or property.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define fiscal policy.
parts.answer: The use of government spending and taxation to influence the level of aggregate demand and economic activity.
parts.working: 1 mark: uses government spending and/or taxation; 1 mark: to influence aggregate demand or economic activity.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define a budget surplus.
parts.answer: A situation in which government revenue is greater than government spending in a year.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two sources of government revenue.
parts.answer: Any two: income tax; corporation tax; indirect taxes such as VAT or sales taxes; customs duties on imports; property taxes.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct source.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two examples of government spending.
parts.answer: Any two: education; health care; defence; welfare payments such as pensions; building roads or other infrastructure.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct example.

practice.stem:
A country's income tax bands are:
first $10 000 of income: 0 %
next $20 000 (from $10 001 to $30 000): 10 %
income above $30 000: 25 %

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the income tax paid by a person earning $50 000 a year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate this person's average rate of tax.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A person earning $20 000 pays $1 000 in tax. Explain whether this income tax system is progressive.
parts.answer: Yes: the average rate rises from 5 % at $20 000 to 14 % at $50 000.
parts.working: 1 mark: average rate at $20 000 = 5 %; 1 mark: rising average rate with income, so progressive.

practice.stem: In one year, a government's revenue is $120 billion and its spending is $138 billion. The country's GDP is $450 billion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the budget deficit.
parts.answer: $18 billion

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the budget deficit as a percentage of GDP.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two ways in which the government could reduce the budget deficit.
parts.answer: Raise tax revenue (e.g. higher tax rates, wider tax base); cut government spending (e.g. on subsidies)
parts.working: 1 mark each for two ways + 1 mark each for explanation: increase tax rates; widen tax base/reduce tax evasion; cut current spending (subsidies, wages); delay capital projects; privatise state firms to raise revenue; encourage economic growth which raises tax revenue automatically.

practice.stem:
A country has these income tax bands:
First $8 000 of income: 0%
Next $17 000 (income from $8 001 to $25 000): 15%
Income above $25 000: 25%
A worker earns $31 000 a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the income tax the worker pays.
parts.working: 1 mark for the 15% band ($2 550); 1 mark for the total of $4 050 including the 25% band ($1 500).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the worker's average rate of tax as a percentage of income. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: 1 mark for the method; 1 mark for 13.1%.

practice.stem: In one year, a government's tax revenue is $96 billion and its spending is $103 billion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the budget balance and state whether it is a surplus or a deficit.
parts.answer: −$7 billion: a budget deficit of $7 billion (96 − 103 = −7)
parts.working: 1 mark for the calculation of −7; 1 mark for stating a deficit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the government can finance this deficit and give one effect on the national debt.
parts.answer: It borrows, for example by selling government bonds to domestic or foreign lenders. National debt rises as the borrowing builds up, and the government must pay more interest in future years, which can limit future spending.
parts.working: 1 mark: borrowing (e.g. issuing bonds); 1 mark: national debt rises; 1 mark: higher interest repayments or pressure on future budgets.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how an increase in income tax can help to reduce inflation.
parts.answer: Higher income tax reduces households' disposable income, so consumer spending falls. Aggregate demand therefore shifts to the left. With less pressure on prices, the rate of inflation falls.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: lower disposable income; lower consumer spending; lower aggregate demand; reduced pressure on prices or lower inflation. Maximum 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether a cut in income tax rates will increase economic growth.
parts.answer: Could raise disposable income and spending, and improve incentives to work and invest; but extra income may be saved or spent on imports, supply may not respond if near capacity, and lower revenue may force cuts in public investment or more borrowing.
parts.working: Up to 5 marks for why it may: higher disposable income → more consumption → higher aggregate demand → more output; stronger incentive to work/more hours; more saving available for investment; attracts skilled workers. Up to 5 marks for why it may not: income saved (low confidence); spending on imports; inflation if economy near full capacity; lower government revenue → less spending on infrastructure/education or bigger deficit; small effect if many workers earn below the tax threshold. Max 8; judgement needed for top band.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how expansionary fiscal policy can reduce unemployment during a recession.
parts.answer: Higher government spending and/or lower taxes raise aggregate demand; firms sell more and need more workers (labour is a derived demand), reducing cyclical unemployment.
parts.working: 1 mark: increase spending/cut taxes; 1 mark: aggregate demand rises; 1 mark: firms raise output; 1 mark: demand for labour rises, cyclical unemployment falls.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why expansionary fiscal policy may fail to reduce unemployment.
parts.answer: e.g. time lags in planning and spending; unemployment may be structural, so extra demand does not match workers' skills
parts.working: 1 mark each for two reasons + 1 mark each for explanation: time lags; structural/frictional unemployment not caused by low demand; extra income saved or spent on imports; government cannot afford more borrowing/debt; firms use spare capacity or machines rather than hiring.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether a government should finance a major infrastructure project through a budget deficit during a recession.
parts.answer: A balanced discussion. For: the multiplier effect raises output; the project creates jobs; borrowing costs may be low in a recession; the infrastructure gives long-term benefits. Against: national debt and interest payments rise, limiting future spending; if the economy is near full capacity the project could cause inflation or crowd out private spending; time lags delay the effect; the project may be badly chosen. The conclusion depends on existing debt levels, the size of the multiplier and the quality of the project.
parts.working: 5–6 marks: developed arguments on both sides, uses the recession context, and a justified conclusion. 3–4 marks: one side well developed. 1–2 marks: unsupported statements.

practice.stem: Country Z has a GDP of $200 billion. Its government spending is 32% of GDP and its tax revenue is 27% of GDP.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the budget deficit in $ billion.
parts.answer: $10 billion (spending $64 billion; revenue $54 billion)
parts.working: 1 mark for spending of $64 billion and revenue of $54 billion; 1 mark for a deficit of $10 billion.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a rise in the share of tax revenue that comes from indirect taxes can be regressive.
parts.answer: An indirect tax such as VAT takes the same amount on a good whatever the buyer's income. Low-income households spend a larger share of their income on taxed goods, so the tax takes a higher proportion of their income than of richer households' income.
parts.working: 1 mark: same tax on the same good whatever the income; 1 mark: poorer households spend a larger share of income on taxed goods; 1 mark: so the tax takes a larger share of income from the poor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why fiscal policy can be difficult to use effectively to stabilise the economy.
parts.answer: Any two, each explained: time lags, since it takes time to recognise a problem, plan and carry out tax or spending changes, and for their effects to appear; political pressure may lead to decisions that are not best for the economy; forecasting errors may mean the policy is applied at the wrong time; existing debt and borrowing limits restrict how much the government can spend.
parts.working: 2 marks for each reason explained (1 for the reason, 1 for why it makes the policy less effective).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define inflation.
parts.answer: A sustained rise in the general price level over a period of time.
parts.working: 1 mark: rise in general price level; 1 mark: sustained/over time (fall in value of money).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two causes of inflation.
parts.answer: Demand-pull: aggregate demand rises faster than output. Cost-push: higher costs of production (wages, imported oil) passed on as higher prices.
parts.working: 1 mark each for naming two causes + 1 mark each for explanation: demand-pull (spending > output capacity); cost-push (higher wages, raw materials, energy, import costs after depreciation); increase in money supply; higher indirect taxes.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A basket of goods costs $240 in Year 1 and $250.80 in Year 2. What is the rate of inflation between Year 1 and Year 2?
A 10.8%
B 4.3%
C 4.5%
D 0.45%
parts.working: (250.80 − 240) ÷ 240 × 100 = 4.5%. A is the rise in dollars, not a percentage. B divides by the Year 2 price instead of the Year 1 price. D forgets to multiply by 100.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define cost-push inflation.
parts.answer: A rise in the general price level caused by an increase in the costs of production, such as wages, raw materials or energy, which firms pass on to consumers.
parts.working: 1 mark: rise in the general price level; 1 mark: caused by higher costs of production.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define demand-pull inflation.
parts.answer: A rise in the general price level caused by total demand in the economy rising faster than the economy's ability to supply goods and services.
parts.working: 1 mark: total demand exceeds or outpaces supply; 1 mark: prices rise as a result.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two groups who lose out when inflation is higher than people expected.
parts.answer: Any two: people on fixed incomes such as pensioners; savers whose money loses value; lenders who are repaid in money that is worth less; workers whose wages rise more slowly than prices.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid group.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one way in which higher inflation than in other countries can reduce a country's exports.
parts.answer: Its goods become more expensive for foreign buyers, so demand for exports falls.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A consumer price index has three categories. In the base year each category had an index of 100. One year later: food (weight 0.5) has an index of 112, transport (weight 0.3) 120 and other items (weight 0.2) 105. What is the rate of inflation?
A 13 %
B 12.3 %
C 37 %
D 11.3 %
parts.working: Weighted index = 0.5 × 112 + 0.3 × 120 + 0.2 × 105 = 56 + 36 + 21 = 113, so prices rose 13 %. B is the unweighted average (112.3), which ignores the weights.

practice.stem:
A country's consumer price index (CPI):
Year 1: 150
Year 2: 162
Year 3: 170.1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of inflation in Year 2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate of inflation in Year 3.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A newspaper says 'prices fell in Year 3'. Explain why this statement is wrong.
parts.answer: Inflation fell (disinflation) but was still positive, so prices continued to rise, only more slowly.
parts.working: 1 mark: index still rose/inflation still positive; 1 mark: rate of increase slowed – this is not deflation.

practice.stem: The price of a fixed basket of groceries was Rs 1 350 in January, Rs 1 404 in July and Rs 1 445 in December.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of inflation between July and December. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: 1 mark for the method; 1 mark for 2.9%.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one reason why economists measure inflation with a price index, such as a basket of goods, rather than the price of one good.
parts.answer: A price index averages the price changes of many goods, so it shows the typical change in what households buy, not the change in one good.
parts.working: 1 mark for a valid reason, e.g. it reflects average spending across many goods and services.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways in which deflation can reduce the profits of firms.
parts.answer: Any two, each explained: falling prices reduce a firm's revenue per unit sold; consumers delay purchases in the expectation of lower prices, so sales fall; the real value of firms' debts rises; firms cut investment because expected profits are lower.
parts.working: 2 marks for each way fully explained.

practice.stem: A teacher's monthly salary rises from Rs 60 000 to Rs 64 800 over one year. In the same year, the price index of goods rises from 108 to 111.6.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in the teacher's nominal (money) salary.
parts.working: 1 mark for the method; 1 mark for 8.0%.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in the teacher's real salary. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: A 4.5% rise in real salary. Prices rose by 3.3% (111.6 ÷ 108 = 1.0333), so the Year 2 salary is worth Rs 64 800 ÷ 1.0333 = Rs 62 709.68 at Year 1 prices; (62 709.68 − 60 000) ÷ 60 000 × 100 = 4.5%.
parts.working: 1 mark for the price rise of 3.3% (or the ratio 1.0333); 1 mark for a real salary of Rs 62 709.68 at Year 1 prices; 1 mark for 4.5%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether deflation is harmful to an economy.
parts.answer: Harmful if caused by falling demand: consumers delay purchases, profits fall, unemployment rises, real debt burden rises. Less harmful if caused by lower costs/higher productivity: real incomes rise and exports become more competitive.
parts.working: Up to 5 marks for harm: postponed spending lowers aggregate demand; firms cut output and jobs; real value of debts rises, so borrowers suffer and spending falls; falling profits reduce investment; difficult for central bank to cut interest rates further. Up to 5 marks for not harmful: 'good' deflation from lower costs/new technology; higher real incomes, especially for people on fixed incomes and savers; improved international competitiveness. Max 8; judgement on cause/size/length needed for top band.

practice.stem: A worker's monthly wage rises from Rs 40 000 to Rs 44 000 over a year in which inflation is 12 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in the worker's money (nominal) wage.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in the worker's real wage. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how inflation affects savers and borrowers.
parts.answer: Savers lose if inflation exceeds the interest rate, as the real value of savings falls; borrowers gain because the real value of their debts falls.
parts.working: Savers: 1 mark real value of savings falls, 1 mark if interest rate < inflation (negative real interest). Borrowers: 1 mark real value of debt falls, 1 mark repay with money worth less.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether a central bank should aim for zero inflation rather than a low positive rate of inflation.
parts.answer: A balanced discussion. For zero inflation: price stability gives certainty, reduces the costs of inflation (menu costs, loss of savings value). Against: at zero inflation the risk of deflation is higher in a downturn; deflation raises real debts and can cause spending to be postponed; with low inflation, real wages can adjust more easily and the central bank has room to cut real interest rates. Conclusion needs judgement.
parts.working: 5–6 marks: developed arguments on both sides and a justified conclusion. 3–4 marks: one side well developed. 1–2 marks: unsupported statements.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a sharp rise in the price of imported oil can cause cost-push inflation.
parts.answer: Fuel and energy are used by most firms, so their production costs rise; firms pass these higher costs on as higher prices; workers may demand higher wages to protect their real incomes, which raises costs and prices again.
parts.working: 1 mark: higher costs of production (energy); 1 mark: firms pass costs on to consumers; 1 mark: wage demands create a further cost increase.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify one government policy that could reduce this cost-push pressure.
parts.answer: Any one relevant policy, e.g. a temporary tax cut or subsidy on fuel, or supply-side measures such as investment in energy efficiency or alternative energy supply.
parts.working: 1 mark for a policy that acts on costs or supply.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the official consumer price index may not reflect the inflation experienced by a particular household.
parts.answer: Any two, each explained: the index uses an average basket, while a household may spend more on items whose prices rose fastest (e.g. health care or rent); a household with children or pensioners buys a different mix of goods; prices differ between regions and shops; changes in quality are difficult to measure.
parts.working: 2 marks for each reason explained.

practice.stem: The price index of a country falls from 112.0 in Year 1 to 106.4 in Year 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of change in the price level between Year 1 and Year 2, as a percentage.
parts.working: 1 mark for the method; 1 mark for −5.0%.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether this is inflation or deflation, and explain why falling prices can harm borrowers.
parts.answer: Deflation. Debts are fixed in money terms, so their real value rises. Borrowers must repay money that is worth more, so the real burden of their debt increases and the risk of default rises.
parts.working: 1 mark: deflation (prices fall); 1 mark: real value of debt rises; 1 mark: repayments become harder or default risk increases.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Economic growth is best measured by an increase in which of the following?
A real GDP
B nominal (money) GDP
C the size of the population
D the money supply
parts.answer: A real GDP
parts.working: Economic growth is an increase in real GDP, i.e. output adjusted for inflation. B can rise just because prices rise.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define a recession.
parts.answer: A fall in real GDP for two consecutive quarters (six months or more).
parts.working: 1 mark: fall in real GDP/negative economic growth; 1 mark: for two consecutive quarters/six months.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two consequences of a recession.
parts.answer: Rising unemployment as firms cut output; lower tax revenue and higher benefit spending for the government
parts.working: 1 mark each for two consequences + 1 mark each for explanation: unemployment rises; incomes and living standards fall; firms' profits fall and some close; government tax revenue falls/benefit spending rises; inflation usually falls; imports fall.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following would be most likely to increase an economy's long-run productive potential?
A a rise in consumer spending on imported goods
B an improvement in the education and training of the workforce
C a rise in the rate of interest
D a fall in the number of new businesses being set up
parts.answer: B an improvement in the education and training of the workforce
parts.working: Better education and training raise labour productivity, shifting long-run aggregate supply to the right. A affects demand and the trade balance, not productive capacity. C raises the cost of investment. D reduces the economy's capacity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between actual economic growth and potential economic growth.
parts.answer: Actual growth is the increase in real output (real GDP) that the economy actually produces. Potential growth is the increase in the maximum output the economy could produce at full employment, i.e. its productive capacity.
parts.working: 1 mark for actual growth as a rise in real output produced; 1 mark for potential growth as a rise in productive capacity or maximum sustainable output.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two causes of an increase in an economy's productive capacity.
parts.answer: Any two: improved technology; a larger or better-trained labour force; more investment in capital goods; discovery of new natural resources.
