parts.working: 1 mark for each valid cause.

practice.stem: A country's real GDP rose from $380 billion to $395.2 billion in one year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of economic growth.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The population grew by 2.5 % in the same year. Calculate the percentage change in real GDP per head. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two causes of economic growth.
parts.answer: Investment in capital goods; improvements in education and training (human capital)
parts.working: 1 mark each for two causes + 1 mark each for explanation: more investment in machinery and infrastructure; better education/skills raise productivity; new technology; discovery of natural resources; more workers (e.g. immigration, higher participation); higher aggregate demand using spare capacity.

practice.stem: Real GDP of a country was $52.4 billion in Year 1 and $54.1 billion in Year 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of economic growth between Year 1 and Year 2. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: 1 mark for the method; 1 mark for 3.2%.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why the figures must be measured in real terms when comparing the two years.
parts.answer: To remove the effect of price changes (inflation), so that only changes in output are compared.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: A country's real GDP grows by 3.6% in one year. Its population grows by 1.8% in the same year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the approximate growth rate of real GDP per head. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: 1.8% (1.036 ÷ 1.018 − 1 = 1.77%; the simple difference 3.6% − 1.8% also gives 1.8%)
parts.working: 1 mark for dividing 1.036 by 1.018 (or subtracting 1.8% from 3.6%); 1 mark for 1.8%.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why growth in real GDP per head is a better indicator of living standards than growth in total real GDP.
parts.answer: Real GDP per head divides output by population, so it shows how much each person gets. Total GDP can grow even when each person's share falls because population grows faster.
parts.working: 1 mark: divides by population so shows output per person; 1 mark: total growth can hide a fall in output per person.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why rapid economic growth may cause inflation.
parts.answer: Any two, each explained: total demand grows faster than the economy can supply, so prices are pushed up (demand-pull); labour shortages lead to higher wages, which firms pass on in higher prices; capacity limits mean firms raise prices when they cannot increase output; rapid money supply growth can increase spending.
parts.working: 2 marks for each reason fully explained.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what usually happens to real GDP, unemployment and inflation during the boom stage of the business cycle.
parts.answer: Real GDP grows rapidly; unemployment falls as firms take on more workers; inflation tends to rise because demand is strong and capacity is stretched.
parts.working: 1 mark each for real GDP, unemployment and inflation, correctly described.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether economic growth always benefits the people of a country.
parts.answer: Growth can raise incomes, jobs and tax revenue for public services, but may damage the environment, deplete resources, widen inequality, cause inflation or longer working hours, and benefits depend on population growth.
parts.working: Up to 5 marks for benefits: higher real incomes and living standards; more jobs/lower unemployment; more tax revenue for schools and hospitals without raising tax rates; reduced poverty. Up to 5 marks for costs: pollution and climate damage; depletion of non-renewable resources; inequality – gains go to a few; inflation; stress/longer hours; GDP per head may not rise if population grows faster. Max 8; judgement needed for top band.

practice.stem:
Real GDP growth and carbon dioxide (CO₂) emissions per head for four countries in one year (hypothetical data)
Country | Real GDP growth (%) | CO₂ emissions per head (tonnes)
P | 6.2 | 1.4
Q | 2.1 | 9.8
R | 3.8 | 4.3
S | 1.1 | 12.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the average real GDP growth rate of the four countries. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: 1 mark for a total of 13.2 divided by 4; 1 mark for 3.3%.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the country with the highest CO₂ emissions per head.
parts.answer: Country S (12.5 tonnes)
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Discuss whether high economic growth is consistent with environmental sustainability.
parts.answer: A balanced discussion using the data. Country S has the highest emissions but the slowest growth, so high emissions do not by themselves produce growth. Country P grows quickly with low emissions, showing that cleaner technology can separate growth from emissions. Growth can also pay for clean energy and environmental protection. High growth is consistent with sustainability only if production methods and policies change.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid point that uses the data; 1 mark for a justified conclusion. Maximum 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether a government should give priority to faster economic growth or to a more equal distribution of income in a middle-income economy.
parts.answer: A balanced discussion. Growth: raises incomes and tax revenue, which can fund public services; creates jobs; a larger output means more to share. Equality: reduces poverty and social tension; higher incomes for poorer groups can raise demand and productivity through better health and education; very high inequality can slow growth. Against: some redistribution (e.g. high taxes) may reduce incentives. The conclusion must consider how the two goals interact.
parts.working: 5–6 marks: developed arguments on both sides and a justified conclusion. 3–4 marks: one side well developed. 1–2 marks: unsupported statements.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why nominal GDP figures can give a misleading picture of economic growth over time.
parts.answer: Nominal GDP rises when prices rise, even if the quantity of goods and services produced does not change, so it overstates growth. Real GDP removes the effect of price changes by valuing output at constant (base-year) prices.
parts.working: 1 mark: nominal GDP can rise because of inflation; 1 mark: output may not have increased; 1 mark: real GDP uses constant prices to remove price effects.

practice.stem: A price index (base year = 100) is 112.5 in Year 1 and 120.0 in Year 2. Nominal GDP is $900 billion in Year 1 and $975 billion in Year 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate real GDP in Year 1, in $ billion.
parts.working: 1 mark for dividing by the price index as a decimal (112.5 ÷ 100 = 1.125); 1 mark for $800 billion.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate real GDP in Year 2, in $ billion.
parts.working: 1 mark for the method; 1 mark for $812.5 billion.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the rate of economic growth between Year 1 and Year 2. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: 1 mark for the method; 1 mark for 1.6%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two monetary policy measures.
parts.answer: Changing interest rates; changing the money supply
parts.working: 1 mark each, any two: interest rate changes; changes in the money supply; changes in the exchange rate (managed by the central bank).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a cut in interest rates can increase consumer spending.
parts.answer: Borrowing becomes cheaper so more people take loans for cars and homes; the reward for saving falls so people save less; existing borrowers with variable-rate loans pay less interest and have more disposable income.
parts.working: 1 mark: borrowing cheaper; 1 mark: more spending on credit (e.g. cars, appliances); 1 mark: saving less attractive so more spent; 1 mark: lower repayments on existing loans raise disposable income.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the most likely effect of a central bank buying government bonds from commercial banks?
A interest rates rise and bank lending falls
B the money supply falls
C the money supply rises and interest rates tend to fall
D prices fall immediately
parts.answer: C the money supply rises and interest rates tend to fall
parts.working: Buying bonds gives commercial banks money in exchange, increasing the funds available for lending, so the money supply rises and the interest rates on bonds and loans tend to fall. A and B are the effects of selling bonds. D is wrong because prices adjust slowly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the role of a central bank in managing the banking system and the economy. Give two roles.
parts.answer: Any two: controls the money supply and sets interest rates; acts as banker to the government and commercial banks; acts as lender of last resort to banks in difficulty; manages the exchange rate and foreign currency reserves.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid role described.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two reasons why a central bank might reduce interest rates.
parts.answer: Any two: to encourage households and firms to borrow and spend; to increase investment; to raise aggregate demand and reduce unemployment in a recession; to prevent deflation.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A central bank raises its interest rate. What is the most likely effect?
A consumers borrow and spend less
B firms increase investment
C the country's currency depreciates
D the rate of inflation rises
parts.answer: A consumers borrow and spend less
parts.working: Higher interest rates make loans more expensive and saving more rewarding, so consumer borrowing and spending fall. The currency usually appreciates (C wrong) as foreign savers are attracted, and investment falls (B wrong).

practice.stem: A household has a loan of Rs 1 500 000 at an annual interest rate of 14%. The interest rate rises to 15.5% a year. Assume the loan balance is unchanged during the year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the extra interest the household pays in one year.
parts.working: 1 mark for the increase of 1.5 percentage points; 1 mark for Rs 22 500.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one way in which a rise in the interest rate can reduce a firm's spending.
parts.answer: Borrowing to buy new machinery becomes more expensive, so the firm invests less.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how an increase in interest rates can reduce the rate of inflation.
parts.answer: Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive, so households and firms borrow and spend less; saving becomes more attractive; aggregate demand falls; with less pressure on prices, inflation falls. A stronger currency can also reduce import prices.
parts.working: 1 mark each for four linked points, maximum 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a central bank may lower interest rates during a recession.
parts.answer: Lower borrowing costs encourage households to borrow and spend on goods and services, and firms to borrow for investment. Aggregate demand rises, so output and employment increase.
parts.working: 1 mark: lower borrowing costs; 1 mark: spending and investment increase; 1 mark: aggregate demand, output and jobs rise.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a fall in interest rates may cause the value of a currency to fall.
parts.answer: Lower interest rates reduce the return on savings held in that currency, so investors move their funds to other countries. Demand for the currency falls, so its value depreciates.
parts.working: 1 mark: lower return on savings in the currency; 1 mark: funds move abroad or demand for the currency falls; 1 mark: the currency depreciates.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one difference between monetary policy and fiscal policy in who makes the decisions.
parts.answer: Monetary policy is decided by the central bank, which is often independent of government. Fiscal policy is decided by the government through its budget on taxation and spending.
parts.working: 1 mark: monetary policy set by the central bank; 1 mark: fiscal policy set by the government through the budget.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A country's central bank raises its interest rate to reduce inflation. Discuss whether higher interest rates will reduce inflation.
parts.answer: Likely to reduce demand-pull inflation by cutting borrowing and spending and by appreciating the currency; less effective against cost-push inflation, if many people do not borrow from banks, if time lags are long, or if the higher rates cut investment and growth.
parts.working: Up to 5 marks for why it may work: dearer loans → less consumption and investment → lower aggregate demand; more saving; currency appreciation lowers import prices; reduced expectations of inflation. Up to 5 marks for why it may not: inflation is cost-push (e.g. imported oil prices); many households use cash/informal credit; time lags; government spending financed by borrowing keeps demand high; side effects – unemployment, lower growth, higher cost of government debt. Max 8; judgement needed for top band.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why an increase in interest rates to reduce inflation may cause the currency to appreciate and reduce exports.
parts.answer: Higher interest rates attract foreign funds, so demand for the currency rises and it appreciates. Exports become more expensive for foreign buyers, so demand for exports falls. Imports become cheaper, so domestic producers face more competition.
parts.working: 1 mark: higher rates attract foreign funds, raising demand for the currency; 1 mark: currency appreciates; 1 mark: exports become more expensive, so demand for exports falls; 1 mark: cheaper imports increase competition for domestic producers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether a central bank should be independent of the government.
parts.answer: A balanced discussion. For independence: avoids pressure to cut interest rates before elections; gives credibility to the inflation target, so expectations stay stable; decisions are made with a long-term view. Against: the central bank is not directly accountable to voters; it may focus only on inflation and ignore unemployment or growth; coordination with fiscal policy may be poor. The conclusion should weigh credibility against accountability.
parts.working: 5–6 marks: developed arguments on both sides and a justified conclusion. 3–4 marks: one side well developed. 1–2 marks: unsupported statements.

practice.stem: A bank offers a loan of $200 000. For this question, assume that the monthly interest is one-twelfth of the annual interest on the full $200 000, and that the balance is not repaid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the monthly interest payment when the annual interest rate is 6%.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in the monthly interest payment when the annual rate rises to 8%. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: 33.3% (monthly payment rises from $1 000 to $1 333.33)
parts.working: 1 mark for the new monthly payment of $1 333.33; 1 mark for 33.3%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why an increase in interest rates may cause house prices to fall.
parts.answer: Higher interest rates raise mortgage repayments, so fewer people can afford to buy; demand for houses falls, and sellers must lower prices to attract buyers.
parts.working: 1 mark: higher mortgage repayments; 1 mark: fewer buyers or lower demand for houses; 1 mark: prices fall to sell houses.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following is a supply-side policy?
A investment in vocational training
B an increase in interest rates
C an increase in unemployment benefits
D an increase in import tariffs
parts.answer: A investment in vocational training
parts.working: Supply-side policies aim to raise the productive capacity of the economy; training raises labour productivity. B is monetary policy and D is protectionism.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following policies is most likely to increase the productive capacity of an economy in the long run?
A an increase in the indirect tax on petrol
B a reduction in regulations that make it costly to start a new business
C an increase in unemployment benefits
D an increase in the interest rate charged on business loans
parts.answer: B a reduction in regulations that make it costly to start a new business
parts.working: Lower barriers to entry increase the number of firms and the economy's capacity over time, which is a supply-side policy. A and D raise firms' costs. C is a welfare transfer that does not increase productive capacity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define supply-side policy.
parts.answer: A government measure aimed at increasing the productive capacity of the economy, shifting long-run aggregate supply to the right.
parts.working: 1 mark: government measure to increase productive capacity; 1 mark: shifts aggregate supply to the right or increases long-run output.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two supply-side policies that aim to improve labour productivity.
parts.answer: Any two: spending on education and vocational training; improved health services for workers; retraining schemes for workers whose skills are out of date; apprenticeship schemes.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid policy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two government policies that can improve the quality of the labour force.
parts.answer: Any two: free or subsidised education; vocational and apprenticeship training schemes; free or subsidised health care; adult literacy programmes.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid policy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how better health can increase labour productivity.
parts.answer: Healthier workers are absent less often because of illness; they have more energy and concentration, so they produce more output per hour; fewer long-term disabilities mean more years of productive work.
parts.working: 1 mark for fewer days lost to illness; 1 mark for higher output per worker from more energy or concentration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how two supply-side policies could increase labour productivity.
parts.answer: Education and training raise workers' skills; tax incentives or subsidies for investment give workers better capital equipment
parts.working: 1 mark each for two policies + 1 mark each for explanation: education/training; better health care; subsidies/tax allowances for investment in machinery and technology; improved infrastructure (roads, power supply); deregulation/privatisation increasing competition and efficiency.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why supply-side policies may take a long time to have an effect.
parts.answer: e.g. education and infrastructure projects take years to complete before output rises.
parts.working: 1 mark: long time to train workers/build infrastructure; 1 mark: so productive capacity increases only in the long run.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how investment in transport infrastructure, such as new roads and ports, can increase an economy's productive capacity.
parts.answer: Any four, each explained: lower transport costs for firms; goods reach markets faster and more cheaply; workers can reach jobs more easily, improving labour mobility; new firms and foreign investors are attracted; access to raw materials and markets allows output to grow.
parts.working: 1 mark per valid explained point, maximum 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a cut in corporation tax may encourage firms to invest.
parts.answer: Lower tax leaves firms with higher after-tax profits, giving them more funds to invest; the expected return on new capital rises, so firms are more willing to buy new equipment; the country becomes more attractive to foreign investors.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three explained points.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways in which the deregulation of a state-run industry could increase competition.
parts.answer: Any two, each explained: new private firms are allowed to enter the market, so there are more competitors; barriers such as licences are reduced; firms compete on price, quality and service, which benefits consumers; competition encourages cost cutting and innovation.
parts.working: 2 marks for each way fully explained.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a reduction in regulations that make it costly for firms to hire and dismiss workers could increase the productive capacity of an economy.
parts.answer: Firms can take on workers when demand grows and reduce their workforce when it falls, so labour is used more fully and output rises. Workers can move more easily to the jobs where they are most productive, which improves the allocation of labour. Firms that can adjust more easily are more willing to invest and expand, so productive capacity grows over time.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three explained points, e.g. more flexible hiring increases the labour used; better allocation of labour raises productivity; more investment and expansion raise productive capacity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether the privatisation of a state-owned electricity company will improve its efficiency.
parts.answer: The profit motive and access to private finance may cut costs and improve service; but a private monopoly may raise prices, cut unprofitable rural supply and under-invest, so regulation and competition matter.
parts.working: Up to 5 marks for improvement: profit motive encourages cost cutting and less waste; private investment funds new power plants; less political interference; competition if market opened. Up to 5 marks for why not: may become a private monopoly – higher prices, less output; may cut supply to unprofitable remote areas; job losses; regulation needed; efficiency depends on management not ownership. Max 8; judgement needed for top band.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether supply-side policies are more effective than demand-side policies in reducing unemployment during a recession.
parts.answer: A balanced discussion. Demand-side (higher government spending, lower interest rates): acts quickly and directly raises demand and jobs when unemployment is cyclical; may cause inflation or debt. Supply-side (training, reducing regulation): tackles structural and frictional unemployment and raises long-run growth; works slowly and does little if firms lack demand for their output. The conclusion depends on the cause and length of unemployment; a combination is often best.
parts.working: 5–6 marks: developed arguments on both sides and a justified conclusion. 3–4 marks: one side well developed. 1–2 marks: unsupported statements.

practice.stem: A country's education spending was 4.0% of GDP in Year 1 and 4.6% of GDP in Year 2. GDP was $150 billion in Year 1 and $165 billion in Year 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate education spending in Year 1, in $ billion.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the increase in education spending between Year 1 and Year 2, in $ billion, to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark for education spending of $7.59 billion in Year 2; 1 mark for the increase of $1.59 billion.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one way in which higher education spending can increase the productive capacity of an economy.
parts.answer: A better-educated workforce has higher productivity, so more output is produced per worker. Skills also make it easier to adopt new technology and to innovate.
parts.working: 1 mark for the link between skills and productivity; 1 mark for the effect on output or productive capacity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why cutting income tax may not increase the supply of labour as much as expected.
parts.answer: Higher take-home pay may let workers reach their target income with fewer hours, so they choose more leisure (income effect). A small tax cut may not change incentives enough. Other constraints, such as childcare or transport, may limit how many hours people can work.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three explained points.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways in which a reduction in tariffs on imported machinery and raw materials could act as a supply-side policy.
parts.answer: Any two, each explained: cheaper imported machinery and inputs lower firms' costs, so they can produce more; competition from imports pushes domestic firms to become more efficient; firms gain access to better technology that raises productivity; access to a larger market allows economies of scale.
parts.working: 2 marks for each way fully explained.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following is NOT usually a macroeconomic aim of a government?
A maximising the profits of private firms
B low and stable inflation
C economic growth
D low unemployment
parts.answer: A maximising the profits of private firms
parts.working: The usual macroeconomic aims are economic growth, low unemployment, stable prices, balance of payments stability and redistribution of income. Profit maximisation is an objective of individual firms.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following best describes the macroeconomic aim of balance of payments equilibrium?
A government spending equals tax revenue in each year
B the value of exports of goods and services is roughly equal to the value of imports over a period
C the exchange rate is fixed against all other currencies
D household savings are at least 10% of income
parts.answer: B the value of exports of goods and services is roughly equal to the value of imports over a period
parts.working: Balance of payments equilibrium means that receipts from abroad and payments abroad roughly balance over time. A is a fiscal balance. C describes a fixed exchange rate system. D is not a macroeconomic aim.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define full employment.
parts.answer: A situation in which everyone who is willing and able to work at the current wage rate can find a job. Some frictional and structural unemployment may still exist.
parts.working: 1 mark: everyone willing and able to work can find a job; 1 mark: at the prevailing wage rate, with some frictional or structural unemployment still possible.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one conflict between the aims of low unemployment and low inflation.
parts.answer: Policies that raise demand to cut unemployment can push up prices as the economy nears full capacity, while policies to cut inflation, such as higher interest rates, reduce demand and can increase unemployment.
parts.working: 1 mark for the link between higher demand and higher prices (or vice versa); 1 mark for the policy needed for each aim and its effect on the other.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the balance of payments.
parts.answer: A record of all financial transactions between the residents of a country and the rest of the world over a period of time, including trade in goods and services and capital flows.
parts.working: 1 mark: record of transactions with the rest of the world; 1 mark: over a period of time.

practice.stem: In one year, a country's exports of goods and services are $48 billion and its imports of goods and services are $55 billion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the balance of trade and state whether it is a surplus or a deficit.
parts.answer: −$7 billion: a trade deficit of $7 billion (48 − 55 = −7)
parts.working: 1 mark for the calculation of −7; 1 mark for stating a deficit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one effect of this trade deficit on the exchange rate.
parts.answer: Importers sell the domestic currency to buy foreign currency to pay for the extra imports, so the supply of the domestic currency rises and its value tends to fall.
parts.working: 1 mark for the link to foreign currency demand or supply; 1 mark for depreciation of the currency.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways in which a government could reduce income inequality.
parts.answer: Any two, each explained: a progressive income tax takes a larger share of high incomes; welfare payments such as pensions and benefits target low-income households; free or subsidised education and health care help poorer families most; a minimum wage raises the lowest incomes.
parts.working: 2 marks for each way fully explained.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a government may want to achieve stable prices as a macroeconomic aim.
parts.answer: Any three, each explained: high inflation reduces the purchasing power of incomes, especially for people on fixed incomes; uncertainty about future prices discourages saving and investment; high inflation makes exports less competitive, worsening the trade balance; stable prices make planning easier for firms and households.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid point with an explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one macroeconomic aim, and explain how a rise in exports could help to achieve it.
parts.answer: Aim: for example economic growth, low unemployment or balance of payments equilibrium. Rising exports increase aggregate demand, so output and jobs rise; they also earn foreign currency and improve the trade balance.
parts.working: 1 mark for a correctly named aim; 1 mark for the rise in aggregate demand; 1 mark for the effect on jobs or the trade balance.

practice.stem:
Inflation and unemployment rates (%) for three countries in one year (hypothetical)
Country | Inflation rate | Unemployment rate
K | 3.4 | 6.9
L | 9.1 | 4.2
M | 2.1 | 8.7

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the sum of the inflation rate and the unemployment rate for each country.
parts.working: 1 mark for at least two correct sums; 1 mark for all three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the country with the lowest sum and explain one limitation of using this sum to judge economic performance.
parts.answer: Country K (10.3). The sum ignores economic growth, the balance of payments and how income is distributed, so it does not show overall performance.
parts.working: 1 mark for K; 1 mark for an explained limitation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two macroeconomic aims of a government, other than full employment and low inflation.
parts.answer: Economic growth; balance of payments stability
parts.working: 1 mark each, any two: economic growth; balance of payments stability; redistribution of income.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the aim of full employment may conflict with the aim of low inflation.
parts.answer: Policies that raise aggregate demand to cut unemployment push up demand for goods and labour; with fewer spare workers, wages and prices rise, causing demand-pull and cost-push inflation.
parts.working: 1 mark: policies to reduce unemployment raise aggregate demand; 1 mark: demand may exceed output capacity → demand-pull inflation; 1 mark: shortage of labour pushes up wages; 1 mark: firms pass on higher wage costs – cost-push inflation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether a government can achieve all of its main macroeconomic aims at the same time.
parts.answer: A balanced discussion. Conflicts: low unemployment and low inflation (the short-run trade-off); faster growth may raise imports and widen the trade deficit; growth may harm the environment; higher interest rates to cut inflation slow growth. Complementarity: supply-side policies such as training and competition can raise growth while lowering unemployment and inflation; sustained growth improves public finances. Conclusion: aims conflict in the short run, but a balanced policy mix can achieve several aims over time.
parts.working: 5–6 marks: developed arguments on both sides and a justified conclusion. 3–4 marks: one side well developed. 1–2 marks: unsupported statements.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a depreciation of the exchange rate can affect inflation and the balance of trade.
parts.answer: Imports become more expensive, so the prices of imported goods and inflation can rise; exports become cheaper for foreign buyers, so export demand can increase; the trade balance tends to improve over time; domestic producers face less competition from imports, which may let them raise prices.
parts.working: 1 mark each for four linked points, maximum 4.

practice.stem: A country's exports of goods are $120 billion and its imports of goods are $130 billion. Its exports of services are $40 billion and its imports of services are $35 billion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the balance of trade in goods.
parts.answer: −$10 billion (a deficit): 120 − 130 = −10
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the balance of trade in goods and services.
parts.answer: −$5 billion: exports of goods and services are $160 billion and imports are $165 billion (160 − 165 = −5)
parts.working: 1 mark for total exports of $160 billion and imports of $165 billion; 1 mark for −$5 billion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a government that uses higher interest rates to reduce inflation may face a trade-off with economic growth.
parts.answer: Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive, so households and firms spend and invest less; aggregate demand falls and output growth slows; firms may cut jobs, increasing unemployment; the effect takes time, so growth can slow before inflation falls.
parts.working: 1 mark each for four linked points, maximum 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three functions of government in a mixed economy.
parts.answer: Any three: provision of public goods; redistribution of income; regulation of firms and markets; stabilising the economy (inflation and unemployment); provision of merit goods such as education and health.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid function.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define a public good.
parts.answer: A good that is non-excludable and non-rivalrous: once provided, people cannot be prevented from using it, and one person's use does not reduce the amount available to others.
parts.working: 1 mark: non-excludable (no one can be excluded from using it); 1 mark: non-rivalrous (one person's use does not reduce the amount for others).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the public sector.
parts.answer: The part of the economy owned or controlled by government, including government services and state-owned enterprises.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two examples of merit goods that a government may provide.
parts.answer: Any two: education; health care; housing; school meals; vaccination programmes.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two reasons why a government may provide health services free at the point of use.
parts.answer: Any two: so that low-income households can access care; to create a healthier workforce; to encourage use of a service that benefits society as a whole (a merit good); to promote equality of access.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two government objectives when it spends money on education.
parts.answer: Any two: improving labour productivity; equality of opportunity; reducing poverty; promoting economic growth; social cohesion.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid objective.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two roles of a government in a national economy.
parts.answer: e.g. as a producer of goods and services such as education and roads; as a regulator protecting consumers and the environment
parts.working: 1 mark each for two roles + 1 mark each for explanation: producer (public and merit goods); employer (civil servants, teachers); regulator (laws on competition, pollution, safety); redistributor of income (taxes and benefits); manager of the economy (fiscal, monetary, supply-side policies).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one international role of a government.
parts.answer: e.g. negotiating trade agreements with other countries
parts.working: B1 any one: member of international organisations (e.g. WTO); negotiating trade agreements; setting tariffs; giving or receiving aid; cooperating on environmental issues.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why private firms may not provide enough public goods, such as street lighting or national defence, and how the government provides them.
parts.answer: Any four, each explained: public goods are non-excludable, so people who do not pay can still use them (the free-rider problem); firms cannot charge for consumption and so cannot make a profit; the government funds them through taxes; the government provides them free to all, so every citizen benefits.
parts.working: 1 mark per valid explained point, maximum 4.

practice.stem: A government's spending in one year is (in $ billion): education 60; health 45; defence 25; other services 70.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of total government spending that is spent on education.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of total government spending that is spent on health.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two advantages of government ownership of a natural monopoly, such as a national water supply network.
parts.answer: Any two, each explained: duplicating a network would waste resources, so one provider is more efficient; prices can be kept affordable rather than set to maximise profit; universal access, including remote areas, can be guaranteed; profits can be reinvested in the network or used for social objectives.
parts.working: 2 marks for each advantage fully explained.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a government may impose regulations on the pollution produced by factories.
parts.answer: Firms do not pay the full social cost of pollution, so they produce too much of it (negative externality); regulations such as emission limits force firms to take account of the damage to health and the environment; this protects the public and future generations.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three explained points.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a government can protect consumers from unsafe products.
parts.answer: Any three: setting and enforcing product safety standards; testing products before they are sold; requiring clear labels and warnings; banning dangerous goods; inspecting shops and factories and fining firms that break the rules.
parts.working: 1 mark for each described method.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether a government should own major industries such as electricity and rail.
parts.answer: A balanced discussion. For public ownership: natural monopolies would otherwise charge high prices; social objectives such as universal access can be pursued; profits do not have to be paid to private shareholders. Against: state firms may be inefficient, lack competition and face political interference; they add to the government's budget burden. Regulation or mixed ownership can address some concerns. The conclusion should weigh efficiency against social goals.
parts.working: 5–6 marks: developed arguments on both sides and a justified conclusion. 3–4 marks: one side well developed. 1–2 marks: unsupported statements.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a government may face a conflict between spending on defence and spending on health and education.
parts.answer: Any four, each explained: tax revenue is limited, so spending on one area reduces funds for others (opportunity cost); extra defence spending may need borrowing that adds to debt and interest payments; health and education raise productivity and growth in the long run; governments must balance security needs with social needs; political priorities decide the choice.
parts.working: 1 mark per valid explained point, maximum 4.

practice.stem: Government spending on education was 5.1% of GDP in Year 1, when GDP was $380 billion. In Year 2 it was 4.2% of GDP, when GDP was $400 billion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate education spending in Year 1 and in Year 2, in $ billion.
parts.working: 1 mark for each year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the change in education spending between the two years, in $ billion.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one reason why the government may need to keep education spending high even though its share of GDP has fallen.
parts.answer: Education builds skills that raise future productivity and growth, so cutting it can reduce long-run output and living standards.
parts.working: 1 mark for the reason (skills raise productivity or growth); 1 mark for the effect of a cut on future output or living standards.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a government can use a subsidy to support a domestic industry.
parts.answer: The government pays part of the firms' production costs, so they can lower prices or produce more; this helps domestic firms compete with imports and protects jobs.
parts.working: 1 mark: pays part of the costs; 1 mark: lower prices or higher output; 1 mark: domestic firms compete better and jobs are protected.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify one cost of this subsidy to society.
parts.answer: The subsidy is paid from taxes, adding to government spending; or inefficient firms may survive, using resources that could be used more productively.
parts.working: 1 mark for a valid cost.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A government wants to reduce the consumption of cigarettes, a demerit good. Which policy is most likely to achieve this?
A an indirect tax on cigarettes
B a subsidy to cigarette producers
C a reduction in the import duty on cigarettes
D removing the ban on smoking in public places
parts.answer: A an indirect tax on cigarettes
parts.working: An indirect tax raises producers' costs, shifts supply left and raises the price, so the quantity demanded falls. B, C and D would all raise consumption: B and C lower costs/prices (supply shifts right), and D removes a restriction on where people can smoke.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define a subsidy.
parts.answer: A payment made by the government to producers (or consumers) to lower the cost of producing or buying a product.
parts.working: 1 mark: payment/grant from the government; 1 mark: to producers to reduce costs/lower price or encourage output.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why a city government might subsidise public bus services in Lahore.
parts.answer: e.g. to reduce traffic congestion and pollution (external costs); to make travel affordable for low-income workers
parts.working: 1 mark for each reason + 1 mark for development, any two of: lower fares encourage people to switch from cars, reducing congestion and air pollution (external costs); public transport has external benefits so would be under-consumed in a free market; helps low-income households reach jobs and schools; keeps bus routes running that would be unprofitable; reduces fuel imports.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define a mixed economic system.
parts.answer: An economy in which resources are allocated partly by the market (private sector, using the price mechanism) and partly by the government (public sector).
parts.working: 1 mark: market / private sector decisions through prices; 1 mark: government (public sector) also allocates resources.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two ways in which a government intervenes in markets in a mixed economic system.
parts.answer: Any two of: indirect tax; subsidy; maximum or minimum price; regulation of standards; provision of public goods; nationalisation.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two correct methods.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which best describes a mixed economic system?
A an economy in which the state owns and allocates all resources
B an economy in which the government takes no part in any market
C an economy in which resources are allocated by both the market and the government
D an economy in which only producers set prices
parts.answer: C an economy in which resources are allocated by both the market and the government
parts.working: A describes a command economy and B a pure market economy; D describes a monopoly-type pricing decision, not an economic system. C combines market and government allocation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two features of a public sector organisation.
parts.answer: Any two of: owned and controlled by the government; objectives include social welfare, not only profit; may provide goods or services at low or zero cost to users; funded from taxation.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two correct features.

practice.stem:
The table shows the weekly market for wheat flour in a city.
Price (Rs per kg): 80, 90, 100, 110, 120
Quantity demanded (thousand kg): 700, 650, 600, 550, 500
Quantity supplied (thousand kg): 300, 400, 480, 550, 610

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the equilibrium price and the equilibrium quantity of wheat flour.
parts.answer: Rs 110 per kg; 550 thousand kg per week
parts.working: B1 price Rs 110; B1 quantity 550 thousand kg (where quantity demanded = quantity supplied).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The government sets a maximum price of Rs 90 per kg. Calculate the shortage that results.
parts.answer: 250 thousand kg per week
parts.working: M1 at Rs 90: quantity demanded 650, quantity supplied 400; A1 650 − 400 = 250 thousand kg.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two possible consequences of this maximum price.
parts.answer: e.g. queues/shortages leading to rationing; a black (illegal) market at higher prices
parts.working: 1 mark for each consequence identified + 1 mark for each explanation, any two of: shortage so queues form/some consumers go without; rationing or first-come-first-served allocation needed; black market develops where flour is sold above the legal price; producers earn less so may cut output or quality in the long run; poorer households can buy flour more cheaply (if they can obtain it).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Public healthcare in Pakistan is partly funded and provided by the government. Explain two reasons why the government provides healthcare rather than leaving it entirely to private hospitals.
parts.answer: Any two developed reasons, e.g. private hospitals may not serve low-income households (they cannot pay), so the market underprovides; healthcare is a merit good with positive externalities (a healthier workforce benefits everyone); information gaps mean patients cannot judge treatment quality; equity - access should not depend on income.
parts.working: 2 marks per reason: 1 mark for the point, 1 mark for the explanation of why the market fails to provide enough.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A government sets a maximum price of Rs 150 per kg for sugar, below the market price of Rs 190 per kg. Explain one likely benefit and one likely problem of this price control.
parts.answer: Benefit: sugar becomes more affordable for low-income households. Problem: at Rs 150 quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied (excess demand), so shortages, queues, rationing or a black market appear, and producers may cut supply.
parts.working: 2 marks for the benefit with explanation; 2 marks for the problem with explanation of excess demand.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A government sets a maximum price of Rs 120 per 5 kg bag of flour. At this price the quantity demanded is 800 bags and the quantity supplied is 500 bags per week. Calculate the excess demand per week.
parts.answer: 300 bags per week
parts.working: Excess demand = quantity demanded - quantity supplied = 800 - 500 = 300 bags. 1 mark for the method, 1 mark for the answer.

practice.stem: A government sets a minimum price for cotton of $1.60 per kg. The free-market equilibrium price is $1.40 per kg. At the minimum price, farmers supply 900 tonnes and buyers demand 650 tonnes (1 tonne = 1000 kg).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the surplus of cotton at the minimum price.
parts.answer: 250 tonnes

parts.label: b
parts.text: The government buys the whole surplus at the minimum price. Calculate the cost to the government.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Discuss whether a minimum price is the best way for the government to help cotton farmers.
parts.answer: Balanced answer: guarantees farmers a higher, stable income, but creates a surplus, costs the government money, raises prices for textile firms and may encourage over-production; alternatives such as subsidies for better seeds or direct income support may be better.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for why it may help: higher and more certain income for farmers; reduces risk so farmers keep growing cotton; protects rural jobs. Up to 3 marks for why it may not: surplus must be bought and stored at a cost ($400 000) – opportunity cost of government spending; higher input price for textile mills reduces their competitiveness; encourages inefficient farmers to stay; alternatives (subsidy on inputs, training, direct cash support) may be cheaper. Max 5; a conclusion is needed for full marks.

practice.stem: A government places a specific (per-unit) tax of 30 cents on each can of sugary drink. Before the tax, the price was $1.00 and 2.0 million cans were sold each week. After the tax, the price is $1.20 and 1.7 million cans are sold each week.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the government's weekly revenue from the tax.
parts.working: M1 tax per can × cans sold after tax = $0.30 × 1.7 million; A1 $510 000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the tax per can that is paid by consumers.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the tax might not reduce the consumption of sugary drinks very much.
parts.answer: Demand for sugary drinks is price inelastic (e.g. they are habit-forming, a can takes a small share of income and consumers see few satisfactory substitutes), so the price rise causes a smaller percentage fall in quantity demanded.
parts.working: 1 mark: demand is price inelastic; up to 3 more marks for development: drinks are habit-forming; spending on a can is a small share of income; few substitutes that consumers see as close; tax only partly passed on to consumers (price rose by 20 cents, not 30); consumers may switch to other untaxed sugary foods, so total sugar intake changes little; here a 20 % price rise cut quantity by only 15 % (PED −0.75).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether a government should set a maximum price on essential food items during a food shortage.
parts.answer: Discussion. For: keeps essentials affordable for low-income households; protects against profiteering. Against: a maximum price below equilibrium creates excess demand, reduces supply, leads to queues, rationing and black markets, and lowers quality; a subsidy or cash transfer may target the poor without these side effects. Reasoned conclusion needed.
parts.working: Up to 8 marks (levels). Two developed sides with economic reasoning (shortage, supply response, affordability) and a supported conclusion, e.g. a maximum price only for a short period, or targeted support, earns the top band.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The government introduces a subsidy of Rs 20 per litre on cooking oil. Analyse two effects of this subsidy: one on the market for cooking oil and one on government spending.
parts.answer: Market: the subsidy lowers the cost of supply, so supply increases (shifts right); the price paid by consumers falls and quantity demanded rises. Government spending: the subsidy is paid per litre, so spending rises; funds may be diverted from other public services (opportunity cost), and over-consumption risk may follow.
parts.working: 3 marks for each fully developed effect (cause, chain of reasoning, effect on the market or budget). Accept the price and quantity changes shown on a diagram described in words.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a subsidy on public transport fares could reduce traffic congestion in a large city.
parts.answer: Lower fares make public transport cheaper than private cars, so more people switch from cars to buses or trains; fewer cars on the roads reduce congestion; the external costs of congestion and pollution also fall.
parts.working: 2 marks for the switch from private to public transport with a reason; 2 marks for the reduction in road traffic and congestion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The price of chicken feed falls. State what happens to the supply curve of chicken meat.
parts.answer: It shifts to the right (supply increases).
parts.working: B1 shifts right/outwards.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain, describing a demand and supply diagram, the effect of this change on the equilibrium price and quantity of chicken meat.
parts.answer: Supply curve shifts right; at the old price there is excess supply; price falls and quantity rises to a new equilibrium.
parts.working: 1 mark: lower costs of production so supply curve shifts from S1 to S2 (right); 1 mark: excess supply at original price; 1 mark: equilibrium price falls (P1 to P2); 1 mark: equilibrium quantity rises (Q1 to Q2), a movement along the demand curve.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define complementary goods.
parts.answer: Goods that are used together, so a change in the price of one changes the demand for the other in the opposite direction (joint demand).
parts.working: 1 mark: goods used together/joint demand; 1 mark: e.g. cars and petrol, or the inverse price–demand relationship.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the effect of a fall in the price of petrol on the demand for cars.
parts.answer: Running a car becomes cheaper, so demand for cars rises (curve shifts right).
parts.working: 1 mark: cars cheaper to run/more attractive; 1 mark: demand for cars increases, curve shifts right.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one other cause of an increase in the demand for cars.
parts.answer: e.g. a rise in incomes
parts.working: Any one: higher incomes; cheaper car loans (lower interest rates); population growth; rise in price of public transport (substitute); advertising.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define a normal good.
parts.answer: A good for which demand rises when consumers' incomes rise (and falls when incomes fall).
parts.working: 1 mark: linked to income / demand rises with income; 1 mark: direction stated (positive relationship).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The price of tea rises. Coffee is a substitute for tea. State the effect on the demand for coffee and give the reason.
parts.answer: Demand for coffee rises (increases), because consumers switch from the more expensive tea to coffee.
parts.working: 1 mark: demand for coffee rises; 1 mark: consumers switch to the substitute because tea is now dearer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The price of bananas falls from $2.00 to $1.50 per kg. Describe the effect on the quantity of bananas demanded, and name the type of change this is.
parts.answer: The quantity of bananas demanded rises (extends) along the same demand curve; this is a movement along the demand curve caused by a change in price.
parts.working: 1 mark: quantity demanded increases as price falls (law of demand); 1 mark: it is a movement along the curve, not a shift.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Floods in Sindh destroy part of the mango crop. Explain the effect on the market for mangoes.
parts.answer: Supply falls (curve shifts left), creating excess demand at the old price, so price rises and quantity bought and sold falls.
parts.working: 1 mark: supply decreases/curve shifts left; 1 mark: fewer mangoes available at each price; 1 mark: price rises; 1 mark: equilibrium quantity falls (contraction along demand curve).

parts.label: b
parts.text: At the same time, incomes in the country rise so the demand for mangoes increases. Explain why the equilibrium price of mangoes will definitely rise but the change in equilibrium quantity is uncertain.
parts.answer: Both a fall in supply and a rise in demand push price up; the fall in supply lowers quantity while the rise in demand raises it, so the net effect depends on which shift is larger.
parts.working: 1 mark: both shifts raise price; 1 mark: supply shift reduces quantity, demand shift increases it; 1 mark: final quantity depends on relative size of the two shifts.

practice.stem:
The table shows the market for smartphones in a country.
Year 1: average price $250, quantity sold 4.0 million
Year 2: average price $220, quantity sold 4.8 million

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in the average price of smartphones between the two years.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify whether a shift in demand or a shift in supply best explains the change in price and quantity, and give one possible cause.
parts.answer: An increase (rightward shift) in supply, e.g. cheaper components or new technology lowering production costs.
parts.working: 1 mark: supply increased/shifted right; 1 mark: because price fell while quantity rose (a demand increase would raise price); 1 mark for a valid cause: lower cost of components, new technology, more firms entering, subsidy, lower import duty.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a rise in the price of petrol causes a movement along the demand curve for petrol rather than a shift of the demand curve.
parts.answer: Price is shown on the vertical axis, so a change in price moves the buyer along the existing demand curve: quantity demanded falls as price rises (ceteris paribus). A shift only happens when a non-price factor changes, such as income, tastes, the price of substitutes or complements, or population.
parts.working: 2 marks: a change in price moves buyers along the same curve, with the fall in quantity demanded. 2 marks: a shift needs a non-price factor to change, which did not happen here.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The price of a rival brand of smartphone falls. The two brands are close substitutes. Explain the likely effect on the demand for the first brand.
parts.answer: Demand for the first brand falls, because consumers switch to the cheaper rival. The demand curve for the first brand shifts to the left (a decrease in demand), since the change is in the price of a substitute, which is a non-price factor.
parts.working: 2 marks: demand for the first brand falls as buyers switch to the cheaper substitute; 2 marks: the curve shifts left because the change is a non-price factor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The price of a 5 kg bag of rice rises from Rs 180 to Rs 225. Calculate the percentage change in the price.
parts.answer: 25.0 %  (an increase of 25.0 %)
parts.working: Percentage change = (225 - 180) / 180 x 100 = 25.0 %. 1 mark for the method, 1 mark for the answer with the % sign.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The price of cars rises sharply. Car fuel is a complement of cars. Explain the effect of this rise on the demand for car fuel.
parts.answer: Demand for car fuel also falls (shifts left), because fuel is a complement of cars: when fewer cars are bought, less fuel is needed. The demands for the two complements move in the same direction.
parts.working: 2 marks: higher car price reduces demand for cars; 2 marks: demand for the complementary fuel falls as well, shown as a leftward shift.

practice.stem: A medical report says that a high intake of sugar harms health. At the same time, the price of honey, a substitute for sugar, rises.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the effect of each event on the demand for sugar.
parts.answer: Health report: tastes change, demand falls (shifts left). Rise in honey price: honey is a substitute so consumers switch to sugar, demand rises (shifts right).
parts.working: Health report: 1 mark demand curve shifts left, 1 mark consumers see sugar as harmful/tastes change. Honey: 1 mark demand for sugar shifts right, 1 mark sugar now relatively cheaper substitute.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether the equilibrium price of sugar will rise or fall.
parts.answer: It depends on which shift is larger: if the health effect is stronger, demand falls overall and price falls; if the substitution effect is stronger, price rises; if equal, price unchanged. Honey may be a weak substitute, so the health effect may dominate.
parts.working: 1 mark: net effect depends on relative size of shifts; 1 mark: larger fall → price falls; 1 mark: larger rise → price rises; 1 mark: judgement, e.g. honey is much more expensive/used differently so is a weak substitute; or supply unchanged so price follows net demand.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify and explain two non-price factors, other than income, that could increase the demand for fresh milk in a city.
parts.answer: Any two, each developed: population growth (more consumers); advertising or health campaigns changing tastes; a rise in the price of a substitute such as soft drinks; a fall in the price of a complement such as breakfast cereal; expectations that milk prices will rise (buying now).
parts.working: 3 marks per factor: 1 mark for naming the factor, 2 marks for the explanation of why demand increases (shift to the right).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether a rise in the price of sugar will always lead to a fall in the total demand for sugar.
parts.answer: Discussion. For a fall: the law of demand; buyers may switch to honey or artificial sweeteners; people may reduce sweets and fizzy drinks. Against or limits: sugar has few close substitutes and is a small but necessary ingredient, so demand may fall only slightly; population growth or rising incomes may offset the fall; a rise in price is a movement along the curve, so the total may still rise in some markets. Reasoned conclusion needed.
parts.working: Up to 8 marks (levels): two developed sides, each with economic reasoning (substitutes, the size of the price effect, population), and a supported conclusion that the fall in quantity is not certain to reduce total demand.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the demand for an inferior good, such as low-quality bread, is likely to fall when consumers' incomes rise. State what type of change this is.
parts.answer: As income rises, consumers can afford better-quality goods (e.g. more expensive bread or other foods), so they buy less of the inferior good; this is a fall in demand (a shift to the left), caused by a change in income, a non-price factor.
parts.working: 2 marks: higher income leads consumers to switch to better goods; 1 mark: demand falls; 1 mark: this is a leftward shift, not a movement along the curve.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define price elasticity of demand.
parts.answer: The responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in the product's price.
parts.working: 1 mark: responsiveness/sensitivity of quantity demanded; 1 mark: to a change in its own price (or the formula % change in Qd ÷ % change in price).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the demand for salt is price inelastic.
parts.answer: Few close substitutes; it takes a very small share of income; it is a necessity.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two reasons + 1 mark each for explanation: no close substitutes so consumers keep buying; small proportion of income so a price rise is hardly noticed; necessity used in cooking every day; bought in small amounts infrequently.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The price of a cinema ticket rises from $5 to $6. The quantity of tickets demanded falls from 1,000 to 900 per week. Calculate the price elasticity of demand (ignore the minus sign).
parts.working: %change in quantity = (900 - 1000) / 1000 x 100 = -10 %; %change in price = (6 - 5) / 5 x 100 = 20 %; PED = 10 / 20 = 0.5. 1 mark for the method, 1 mark for the answer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the formula for price elasticity of demand.
parts.answer: PED = percentage change in quantity demanded / percentage change in price.
parts.working: 1 mark: quantity demanded change divided by price change; 1 mark: both expressed as percentage changes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The price of mangoes rises by 10 %. The quantity of mangoes demanded falls by 25 %. Calculate the price elasticity of demand and state whether demand is elastic or inelastic.
parts.answer: PED = 25 / 10 = 2.5; demand is elastic (greater than 1).
parts.working: 1 mark: correct calculation of PED = 2.5; 1 mark: elastic because the value is greater than 1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the demand for rice is likely to be price inelastic in a country where rice is the main staple food.
parts.answer: Any two, developed: rice is a basic staple that households need every day, so they keep buying when the price rises; there are few close substitutes in the local diet, so quantity demanded changes little; buying rice is a habit, so consumers do not switch quickly.
parts.working: 2 marks per reason: 1 mark for the reason, 1 mark for the explanation of why quantity demanded changes little.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The price of a product rises from $8 to $10. The quantity demanded falls from 500 units to 450 units. What is the price elasticity of demand?
A −0.4
B −2.5
C −0.1
D −4.0
parts.working: % change in quantity demanded = −50/500 = −10 %; % change in price = 2/8 = +25 %; PED = −10 ÷ 25 = −0.4. B inverts the formula (price change ÷ quantity change).

practice.stem: A bus company in Karachi raises its fare from Rs 50 to Rs 60. The number of passengers falls from 12 000 to 9 000 per day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the price elasticity of demand for bus travel.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the change in the company's daily total revenue.
parts.answer: Falls by Rs 60 000 (from Rs 600 000 to Rs 540 000)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why your answer to (b) is consistent with your answer to (a).
parts.answer: Demand is price elastic (PED > 1 in size), so the percentage fall in passengers is greater than the percentage rise in fare and revenue falls.
parts.working: 1 mark: demand is elastic; 1 mark: %ΔQd larger than %ΔP so total revenue falls when price rises.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two factors that make the demand for a product price elastic.
parts.answer: Any two, developed: many close substitutes available (consumers can switch easily); a luxury or non-essential good; a large share of household income; a long time period to adjust.
parts.working: 2 marks per factor: 1 mark for the factor, 1 mark for explaining why a price rise causes a large fall in quantity demanded.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A cafe cuts the price of a cup of tea from Rs 80 to Rs 72. Daily cups sold rise from 250 to 300. What is the price elasticity of demand (ignoring the sign)?
A 0.25
B 0.5
C 2.0
D 5.0
parts.working: Percentage change in quantity = 50 / 250 = 20 %; percentage change in price = 8 / 80 = 10 %; PED = 20 / 10 = 2.0 (elastic). B uses the inverted ratio (10 / 20 = 0.5), so it is wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A bus company raises its fare from Rs 40 to Rs 50. Daily passengers fall from 2,500 to 2,250. (a) Calculate the price elasticity of demand (ignore the sign) and state whether demand is elastic or inelastic. (b) State whether the company's total revenue rises or falls.
parts.answer: (a) PED = 10 / 25 = 0.4; inelastic. (b) Total revenue rises from Rs 100,000 to Rs 112,500.
parts.working: (a) %change in quantity = -10 %, %change in price = +25 %, PED = 0.4 (inelastic, below 1). 1 mark for the value, 1 mark for inelastic. (b) Before: 40 x 2,500 = 100,000; after: 50 x 2,250 = 112,500, so revenue rises. 1 mark for direction, 1 mark for the figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The price elasticity of demand for a product is -1.4. The price rises by 12 %. Calculate the percentage change in the quantity demanded.
parts.answer: -16.8 %  (quantity demanded falls by 16.8 %)
parts.working: Percentage change in quantity = PED x percentage change in price = -1.4 x 12 = -16.8 %. 1 mark for the method, 1 mark for the answer with the minus sign or the word "falls".

practice.stem: A cinema estimates that the price elasticity of demand is −0.6 for weekend tickets and −1.8 for weekday tickets.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in the quantity demanded of weekday tickets if the cinema cuts the weekday price by 10 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether the cinema should cut the price of both weekday and weekend tickets.
parts.answer: Cut weekday prices (elastic: revenue rises) but not weekend prices (inelastic: revenue falls); consider costs, capacity, competitors and accuracy of estimates.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for analysis: weekday demand elastic, 10 % cut raises Qd by 18 % so total revenue rises; weekend demand inelastic, cut raises Qd by only 6 % so revenue falls; may consider raising weekend prices instead. Up to 2 marks for evaluation: extra viewers raise snack sales; limited seats at weekends; estimates may be wrong or change; rivals may react; costs per extra viewer. Max 6.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Brand X and Brand Y sell two different products. Brand X raises its price from $4.00 to $4.60 and its daily quantity demanded falls from 900 to 810. Brand Y raises its price from $10 to $11 and its daily quantity demanded falls from 500 to 440. (a) Calculate the price elasticity of demand for each brand (ignore the sign), giving each answer to 2 decimal places. (b) Identify which brand has the more elastic demand and explain what this means for total revenue.
parts.answer: (a) Brand X: PED = 0.67; Brand Y: PED = 1.20. (b) Brand Y is more elastic. Its price rise lowers total revenue (from $5,000 to $4,840), because the fall in quantity outweighs the higher price; Brand X (inelastic) gains revenue from its price rise (from $3,600 to about $3,726).
parts.working: (a) 1 mark each for correct calculation (X: 10 / 15 = 0.67; Y: 12 / 10 = 1.2). (b) 1 mark for identifying Y as more elastic (value above 1 vs below 1); 1 mark for the consequence for total revenue (price rise lowers revenue for an elastic good).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A firm sells a product with a price elasticity of demand of -2.5 at its current price of $30. The firm wants to increase its total revenue. Discuss whether it should raise or lower its price.
parts.answer: Discussion. Demand is elastic (2.5 is above 1), so quantity demanded changes proportionally more than price. A price cut raises quantity demanded by more than the fall in price, so total revenue rises, so the firm should lower the price. Limits: lower prices reduce the margin per unit and may cause price wars with rivals; extra output may need extra capacity or cost; rival firms may respond; demand may not be elastic at all prices; a reasoned conclusion is needed.
parts.working: Up to 8 marks (levels): correct link between elasticity and revenue (elastic demand: price cut increases revenue); two developed points about costs, competitors or capacity; a supported conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the demand for petrol is likely to be price inelastic in the short run but more elastic in the long run.
parts.answer: Short run: few substitutes available quickly, petrol is needed for daily travel, and habits and car ownership cannot change quickly, so quantity demanded changes little. Long run: consumers can buy more fuel-efficient or electric cars, use public transport, or move closer to work, so quantity demanded falls more when price rises.
parts.working: 3 marks for the short-run explanation (two developed points); 3 marks for the long-run explanation (time allows substitution, behaviour change or new purchases).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define demand.
parts.answer: The willingness and ability to buy a product at a given price over a period of time.
parts.working: 1 mark: willingness and ability (effective demand); 1 mark: at a given price/in a given time period.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference between a movement along a demand curve and a shift of a demand curve.
parts.answer: A movement (extension/contraction) is caused only by a change in the product's own price; a shift is caused by a change in a non-price factor such as income, tastes or the price of related goods.
parts.working: 1 mark: movement caused by change in own price; 1 mark: extension when price falls/contraction when price rises; 1 mark: shift caused by change in other (non-price) factors; 1 mark: example, e.g. rise in income shifts demand right.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the law of demand.
parts.answer: As the price of a good rises, the quantity demanded falls (and as price falls, quantity demanded rises), ceteris paribus.
parts.working: 1 mark: inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded; 1 mark: other factors held constant (ceteris paribus).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two determinants of demand other than price.
parts.answer: Any two of: consumers' income; tastes and preferences; prices of substitutes or complements; population size; advertising; expectations of future prices.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two correct determinants.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what happens to the demand for a normal good when consumers' incomes rise.
parts.answer: Demand increases; the demand curve shifts to the right.
parts.working: 1 mark: demand rises (curve shifts right) because income is a non-price factor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the shape of a demand curve for a normal good, and explain its slope in words.
parts.answer: The demand curve slopes downwards from left to right, showing an inverse relationship: as price falls, quantity demanded rises.
parts.working: 1 mark: downward-sloping (negative gradient) from left to right; 1 mark: inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded (law of demand).

practice.stem:
Three consumers make up the market for a snack bar. Their weekly demand is:
Price $2: Ali 10, Bina 6, Chen 8
Price $3: Ali 7, Bina 5, Chen 6
Price $4: Ali 5, Bina 3, Chen 2

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the market quantity demanded at a price of $3.
parts.answer: 18 units

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in the market quantity demanded when the price rises from $2 to $4. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two factors, other than price, that could shift the market demand curve for this snack to the right.
parts.answer: e.g. a rise in consumers' incomes; a successful advertising campaign
parts.working: 1 mark each for two factors + 1 mark each for explanation, any two of: higher incomes (normal good); advertising/change in tastes; rise in price of a substitute; fall in price of a complement; more consumers (population growth).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Two consumers, A and B, have the demand schedules below (quantity in units per week).
Price ($): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
Consumer A: 10, 8, 6, 4, 2
Consumer B: 7, 5, 3, 1, 0
Calculate the market demand (total quantity demanded) at a price of $2 and at a price of $4.
parts.answer: At $2: 13 units; at $4: 5 units.
parts.working: Market demand = sum of individual demands. At $2: 8 + 5 = 13; at $4: 4 + 1 = 5. 2 marks for each correct total.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A popular social media trend increases demand for a particular brand of trainers at every price. Explain whether this is a movement along or a shift of the demand curve.
parts.answer: A shift of the demand curve to the right (an increase in demand), because the change is in tastes or advertising, which are non-price factors.
parts.working: 1 mark: a shift (not a movement); 1 mark: the cause is a non-price factor (tastes or advertising).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the market demand for electric cars might increase in Pakistan over the next five years.
parts.answer: Any two, developed: rising petrol prices make electric cars relatively cheaper to run (fuel is a substitute); government tax incentives lower the price to consumers; growing awareness of environmental issues changes tastes; better battery technology and a wider charging network improve the product.
parts.working: 2 marks per reason: 1 mark for the reason, 1 mark for how it increases demand at each price (shift to the right).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how advertising by a company can shift the market demand for its product.
parts.answer: Advertising informs consumers about the product or changes their tastes and preferences, so they want more of it at each price. The demand curve shifts to the right, so a higher quantity is demanded at every price.
parts.working: 2 marks: advertising changes awareness, tastes or preferences (non-price factor); 2 marks: demand curve shifts right, so more is demanded at each price.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between an increase in demand and an increase in quantity demanded.
parts.answer: An increase in quantity demanded is a movement along the demand curve caused by a fall in the price of the good itself. An increase in demand is a shift of the whole curve to the right caused by a non-price factor, such as higher income, so more is demanded at every price.
parts.working: 2 marks: an increase in quantity demanded is a movement along the curve caused by a price change; 2 marks: an increase in demand is a shift of the curve caused by a non-price factor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two products for which demand is likely to rise as the population ages.
parts.answer: e.g. health care/medicines and retirement homes
parts.working: 1 mark each for two: medical services, medicines, care homes, mobility aids, pensions/financial advice, leisure travel for retired people.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse how an ageing population could change the pattern of demand in an economy such as Japan.
parts.answer: Demand shifts towards health care, care services and products for older people and away from goods for the young (schools, baby products); total spending may fall as more people live on pensions; firms and labour move between markets.
parts.working: Up to 6 marks: demand curves for health/care products shift right raising price and output (2); demand for products for young people (toys, schooling, starter homes) shifts left (2); lower average incomes of retired people reduce demand for some luxury goods/raise saving behaviour (1); resources reallocated through the price mechanism, e.g. more workers become carers (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The population of a town is 250,000 and grows by 2 % each year. Each person buys 4 kg of rice per year, and this does not change. Calculate the total market demand for rice, in tonnes, after three years.
parts.answer: 1061.2 tonnes (about 1,061,208 kg)
parts.working: Population after 3 years = 250,000 x 1.02^3 = 265,302; demand = 265,302 x 4 = 1,061,208 kg = 1061.2 tonnes. 2 marks for the population, 2 marks for the demand in kg, 2 marks for converting to tonnes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether a government can reduce the market demand for cigarettes by using advertising campaigns alone.
parts.answer: Discussion. For: campaigns that highlight health harms can change tastes and expectations, shifting demand to the left; they can reach young people and inform smokers who underestimate risks. Against: addictive goods have inelastic demand, so consumers may keep buying; advertising by tobacco firms may offset campaigns; campaigns cost money and work slowly; higher taxes, age limits and bans may be more effective. Reasoned conclusion.
parts.working: Up to 8 marks (levels): two developed sides, each linking the policy to demand (shift left or inelastic demand), plus evaluation of how effective advertising is compared with other measures, and a supported conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The market demand for a good is Qd = 120 - 4P for the existing consumers. At a price of $10, calculate the market quantity demanded before and after a new group of consumers enters the market with demand Qd = 40 - 2P. State whether this change is a shift or a movement.
