parts.answer: Before: 80 units; after: 100 units. The change is a shift of the market demand curve to the right (an increase in demand) caused by more consumers.
parts.working: Before: 120 - 4 x 10 = 80 (2 marks). After: 80 + (40 - 2 x 10 = 20) = 100 (2 marks). Shift, because the number of buyers (non-price factor) changes (2 marks).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define external cost.
parts.answer: A cost of an economic activity that falls on third parties who are not involved in it and is not paid by the producer or consumer.
parts.working: 1 mark: cost to a third party; 1 mark: not paid for/not included in the price.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two external costs that a new cement factory could create for a nearby village in Punjab.
parts.answer: e.g. dust pollution causing breathing illnesses; heavy lorries causing noise and damaging roads
parts.working: 1 mark each for two costs + 1 mark each for explanation: air/dust pollution harming health and raising medical bills; noise; damage to crops from dust reducing farm income; congestion and road damage from lorries; water use lowering wells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define market failure.
parts.answer: A situation in which the free market does not allocate resources efficiently, so too much or too little of a good is produced or consumed and welfare is lost.
parts.working: 1 mark: free market fails to allocate resources efficiently; 1 mark: leads to over- or under-production/consumption (a welfare loss).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define a merit good.
parts.answer: A good that the free market under-consumes, which the government believes would benefit society more than individuals realise, so it is provided or subsidised.
parts.working: 1 mark: under-consumed by the free market; 1 mark: government judges it beneficial to society (has positive externalities or is underestimated by consumers).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two examples of demerit goods.
parts.answer: Any two of: cigarettes/tobacco; alcohol; sugary fizzy drinks; gambling.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two correct examples.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define a positive externality of consumption.
parts.answer: A benefit received by third parties (people not involved in the transaction) from the consumption of a good.
parts.working: 1 mark: benefit to third parties; 1 mark: arises from consumption, not from the buyer's own private benefit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two characteristics of a public good.
parts.answer: Non-excludable: people who do not pay cannot be stopped from benefiting. Non-rival: one person's use does not reduce the amount available to others.
parts.working: 1 mark: non-excludable + 1 mark explanation; 1 mark: non-rival + 1 mark explanation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a market system might not provide street lighting.
parts.answer: Because of the free-rider problem, consumers would not pay, so private firms could not make a profit.
parts.working: 1 mark: free-rider problem/people can benefit without paying; 1 mark: firms cannot charge so no profit, so it is not provided (missing market).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a free market may underprovide street lighting.
parts.answer: Street lighting is a public good: it is non-excludable, so people can enjoy it without paying (free riders), and it is non-rival, so one person's use does not reduce others'. Private firms therefore cannot charge enough to cover costs, so the market provides too little.
parts.working: 2 marks: non-excludable and free riders; 2 marks: private firms cannot earn enough revenue, so they under-supply or do not supply it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why information gaps can lead to market failure in the market for second-hand cars.
parts.answer: Any two developed: buyers cannot judge the true quality of a used car, so they will not pay a fair price for a good car (adverse selection, good sellers withdraw); buyers may purchase a faulty car that costs them more later, so resources are wasted and the market allocates inefficiently.
parts.working: 2 marks per reason: 1 mark for the reason, 1 mark for the explanation of the inefficient outcome.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A chemical factory produces 5,000 tonnes of output per year. Its private cost is $40 per tonne. It also causes an external cost (pollution) of $12 per tonne. (a) Calculate the total external cost per year. (b) Calculate the total social cost per year.
parts.answer: (a) $60,000 per year. (b) $260,000 per year.
parts.working: (a) 5,000 x 12 = 60,000 (2 marks). (b) Private cost 5,000 x 40 = 200,000; social cost = private + external = 200,000 + 60,000 = 260,000 (2 marks).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways in which a government could correct a negative externality from a factory's pollution.
parts.answer: Any two developed: an indirect tax (pollution tax) raises the firm's private cost towards the social cost, so output falls; regulation or emission limits forbid output above a set level; tradable pollution permits create a market price for pollution; a subsidy for cleaner production lowers the cost of cutting pollution.
parts.working: 2 marks per method: 1 mark for the method, 1 mark for how it reduces the external cost or output.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how market power held by a single dominant firm can lead to market failure.
parts.answer: A dominant firm can restrict output and charge a higher price than would exist in a competitive market, so quantity is lower than the efficient level (allocative inefficiency). Consumers lose surplus and have less choice, and the firm may have less incentive to innovate or cut costs.
parts.working: 2 marks: restricted output and higher price (inefficiency); 2 marks: welfare loss to consumers or less innovation.

practice.stem: A chemical plant has private costs of $12 million a year and causes external costs of $5 million a year. Its private benefits are $15 million a year and it creates external benefits of $1 million a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the social cost and the social benefit of the plant.
parts.answer: Social cost $17 million; social benefit $16 million
parts.working: B1 social cost = private cost + external cost = 12 + 5 = $17m; B1 social benefit = 15 + 1 = $16m.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the plant would operate in a free market even though this may be a market failure.
parts.answer: The owner compares only private benefit ($15m) with private cost ($12m) and makes a profit; but social cost ($17m) exceeds social benefit ($16m), so society is worse off and resources are misallocated.
parts.working: 1 mark: private benefit > private cost so profitable; 1 mark: external costs ignored by the firm; 1 mark: social cost > social benefit so over-production/inefficient allocation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest and explain one government policy that could correct this market failure.
parts.answer: e.g. a tax on pollution equal to the external cost
parts.working: 1 mark: policy (pollution tax, regulation/emission limits, tradable permits, fines); up to 2 marks explaining how it makes the firm pay for or reduce the external cost.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A vaccination programme has a social benefit of $1.5 million a year, but its private benefit to vaccinated people is only $0.9 million a year. (a) Calculate the external benefit per year. (b) Explain why the free market would underprovide vaccines.
parts.answer: (a) $600,000 per year. (b) Because the external benefit is not paid for by anyone, buyers do not pay for benefits to others (free riders), so demand is too low and firms supply less than the socially optimal quantity.
parts.working: (a) 1,500,000 - 900,000 = 600,000 (2 marks). (b) 2 marks: buyers only consider private benefit, so demand is below the social optimum; 2 marks: firms supply less, so underprovision and a welfare loss.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether the government should provide healthcare directly, or rely on private firms to provide it.
parts.answer: Discussion. Government provision: ensures access for low-income households; healthcare is a merit good with positive externalities; avoids private profit-driven neglect of remote areas. Private provision: competition may improve efficiency and choice; government may waste money or have long waiting lists; a mix of public and private can be used (e.g. subsidised private care). Reasoned conclusion.
parts.working: Up to 8 marks (levels): two developed sides with economic reasoning (merit good, equity, efficiency, funding), plus a supported conclusion, e.g. a mixed approach with government funding for equity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse how a government subsidy on school education could help correct market failure, and state one problem with using subsidies to do this.
parts.answer: Subsidies lower the price paid by families, so more children attend school; this increases consumption of a merit good that the free market under-provides, and it captures positive externalities such as a better-educated workforce. A problem: subsidies cost taxpayers money (opportunity cost) and may not reach the poorest, or may be wasted if quality does not improve.
parts.working: 3 marks: the subsidy raises consumption and the positive externality is captured (developed chain); 3 marks: a developed problem (cost to government, targeting, or waste).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In a market economic system, what mainly decides which goods are produced?
A consumer demand working through the price mechanism
B government planning officials
C trade unions
D the central bank
parts.answer: A consumer demand working through the price mechanism
parts.working: In a market system resources are allocated by the price mechanism: firms produce what consumers are willing and able to buy at a profit. B describes a planned economy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two features of a market economic system.
parts.answer: Any two of: resources are mainly privately owned; decisions are made by individuals and firms; prices are set by supply and demand; the profit motive drives production; little or no government intervention.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two correct features.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define consumer sovereignty.
parts.answer: The power of consumers to decide what is produced through their spending choices in the market.
parts.working: 1 mark: consumers' spending decides what is produced; 1 mark: their choices send signals to producers through prices and sales.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two advantages of a market economic system to consumers.
parts.answer: Any two of: a wide choice of goods and services; competition tends to lower prices; quality and innovation improve; production is efficient.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two correct advantages.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following is NOT a feature of a market economic system?
A private ownership of firms
B prices set by supply and demand
C the state decides which goods are produced
D the profit motive encourages firms to innovate
parts.answer: C the state decides which goods are produced
parts.working: A, B and D are all features of a market economy. C describes a command (planned) economy, where the state decides output.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two disadvantages of a market economic system for low-income households.
parts.answer: Any two developed: goods and services that are essential (such as health care) may be unaffordable because the market only supplies to those who can pay; large inequalities of income widen; public goods such as clean water or street lighting may not be provided; local or remote areas may be unserved.
parts.working: 2 marks per disadvantage: 1 mark for the point, 1 mark for explaining why low-income households lose out.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the price mechanism signals a shortage of a good in a market economy and how this leads to a reallocation of resources.
parts.answer: A shortage means demand exceeds supply at the current price, so the price rises. The higher price signals to producers that the good is profitable, so more resources (labour, land, capital) move into producing it and supply expands, while consumers reduce their demand.
parts.working: 2 marks: a shortage raises the price, which acts as a signal; 2 marks: higher profit attracts resources and supply rises until the shortage is removed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the role of the profit motive in encouraging firms to develop new products in a market economy.
parts.answer: Firms want higher profit, so they develop new products to gain a competitive advantage and extra sales; competition forces firms to innovate or lose customers, so better products are produced over time.
parts.working: 2 marks: the profit motive encourages firms to develop new products; 2 marks: competition forces innovation, so better and cheaper products result.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why firms in a market economy may not supply some basic services, such as clean water in remote villages.
parts.answer: Any three developed reasons: supplying remote, low-income areas is costly and earns little profit; firms have no profit motive to serve areas where people cannot pay; water is non-excludable, so free riders may use it without paying; firms cannot profit from it and so will under-supply it, requiring government intervention.
parts.working: 2 marks per developed reason (1 mark for the point, 1 mark for the explanation of why the market fails to supply it).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify one reason why a market economy might produce too many demerit goods, such as cigarettes.
parts.answer: Consumers may underestimate the harm (an information gap) and demand is driven by addiction or preference, so firms profitably supply them; the market does not take account of the external costs to others.
parts.working: 1 mark for the reason; 1 mark for the explanation (information gap, addiction, or external costs ignored).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why incomes in a market economy may be unequal.
parts.answer: Any two developed: differences in skills, education and training lead to different earnings; some people inherit wealth, property or land; some own capital that earns profit; discrimination or luck (e.g. ill health) affects earnings.
parts.working: 2 marks per reason: 1 mark for the reason, 1 mark for explaining why it leads to unequal income.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether a market economic system is better than a mixed economic system for a developing economy.
parts.answer: Balanced: market system gives incentives, choice and efficiency; but may under-provide public and merit goods, ignore external costs and create inequality, which a mixed system can address – though government failure is possible.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for the market system: profit motive encourages efficiency and innovation; wide consumer choice; resources respond quickly to price signals; no costly bureaucracy. Up to 4 marks for the mixed system: government provides public goods (roads, street lights) and merit goods (education, health); corrects external costs; reduces inequality through taxes and benefits; protects consumers from monopolies. Evaluation (needed for top marks): depends on government efficiency/corruption, level of development, size of markets. Max 8.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether the price mechanism alone can ensure that healthcare is distributed fairly.
parts.answer: Discussion. The price mechanism allocates healthcare to those who can pay, so low-income groups may go without, and remote areas may be neglected. It can provide efficiency, choice and competition. Fairness, a merit good and positive externalities justify government provision or subsidies. Reasoned conclusion, e.g. the price mechanism alone cannot ensure fairness.
parts.working: Up to 8 marks (levels): two developed sides with economic reasoning about affordability, equity and efficiency, and a supported conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse how a sudden rise in the world price of petrol would lead to resources moving between sectors in a market economy, and how this affects a commuter's spending.
parts.answer: Higher petrol prices make transport more costly, so demand for other transport (e.g. buses or bicycles) and for fuel-efficient vehicles rises; firms in these sectors expand and attract labour and capital, while sectors using lots of fuel contract. The commuter spends a larger share of income on petrol, so less is left for other goods.
parts.working: 3 marks: resources move towards transport alternatives through price signals; 3 marks: effect on the commuter's spending (larger share on petrol, lower spending elsewhere).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a change in consumer tastes towards organic vegetables would lead to a reallocation of land and labour in a market economy.
parts.answer: Rising demand for organic vegetables raises their price and profit, so farmers switch land to organic production; demand for labour rises in organic farms, drawing workers from other farming work; the price mechanism signals and rewards the change without any government direction.
parts.working: 2 marks: higher demand raises price and profit; 2 marks: farmers switch land to organic crops; 2 marks: labour moves to the expanding sector through wage signals.

practice.stem:
The table shows the daily market for notebooks in a town.
Price (Rs): 40, 50, 60, 70, 80
Quantity demanded: 900, 800, 700, 600, 500
Quantity supplied: 300, 500, 700, 900, 1100

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the equilibrium price.
parts.answer: Rs 60
parts.working: B1 Rs 60 (quantity demanded = quantity supplied = 700).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the excess demand at a price of Rs 50.
parts.answer: 300 units

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the market would move to equilibrium if the price were Rs 50.
parts.answer: Shortage → consumers compete/sellers raise price → quantity supplied extends, quantity demanded contracts until Rs 60.
parts.working: 1 mark: shortage/excess demand at Rs 50; 1 mark: price is bid up; 1 mark: Qs rises and Qd falls until they are equal at Rs 60 (700 units).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define market equilibrium.
parts.answer: The price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied, so there is neither a shortage nor a surplus and no pressure for price to change.
parts.working: 1 mark: quantity demanded equals quantity supplied; 1 mark: no shortage or surplus, so price is stable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what happens in a market when the price is above the equilibrium price.
parts.answer: Quantity supplied is greater than quantity demanded, so there is a surplus; sellers reduce their prices to sell the excess, and the price falls back towards equilibrium.
parts.working: 1 mark: surplus (supply exceeds demand); 1 mark: price falls as sellers compete, moving back to equilibrium.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The table shows market demand and supply at each price.
Price ($): 1, 2, 3, 4
Quantity demanded: 100, 80, 70, 40
Quantity supplied: 40, 60, 70, 100
State the equilibrium price and the equilibrium quantity.
parts.answer: Equilibrium price = $3; equilibrium quantity = 70 units.
parts.working: At $3, quantity demanded = quantity supplied = 70. 1 mark for the price, 1 mark for the quantity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the effect on the equilibrium price of a rise in demand when supply is fixed.
parts.answer: The equilibrium price rises, because demand exceeds supply at the old price (a shortage) and buyers bid the price up until quantity demanded equals the fixed quantity supplied.
parts.working: 1 mark: price rises; 1 mark: demand exceeds supply at the old price so the price rises to restore equilibrium.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
At a price of $6, the quantity demanded of a product is 300 units and the quantity supplied is 500 units. What is the situation in this market?
A excess supply of 200 units; the price will tend to fall
B excess demand of 200 units; the price will tend to rise
C excess supply of 200 units; the price will tend to rise
D the market is in equilibrium
parts.answer: A excess supply of 200 units; the price will tend to fall
parts.working: Quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded by 500 − 300 = 200, so there is a surplus; sellers cut prices to clear stocks. B confuses surplus with shortage.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State and explain the effect on the equilibrium price and quantity of an increase in supply, with demand unchanged.
parts.answer: The equilibrium price falls and the equilibrium quantity rises, because the extra supply at each price creates a surplus at the old price; sellers cut prices to sell it, which lets consumers buy more.
parts.working: 1 mark: price falls; 1 mark: quantity rises; 2 marks: explanation of the surplus at the old price leading to a fall in price.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The demand for a product is Qd = 180 - 4P and the supply is Qs = 60 + 2P, where P is the price in dollars. (a) Calculate the equilibrium price and quantity. (b) Calculate the excess demand at a price of $15.
parts.answer: (a) Equilibrium price = $20; equilibrium quantity = 100 units. (b) Excess demand = 120 - 90 = 30 units.
parts.working: (a) 180 - 4P = 60 + 2P, so 120 = 6P, P = 20; Q = 180 - 80 = 100 (2 marks). (b) At P = 15: Qd = 120 and Qs = 90, so excess demand = 30 (2 marks).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, using the price mechanism, why a price above the equilibrium cannot last in a free market.
parts.answer: At a price above equilibrium there is a surplus: firms cannot sell all their output, stocks build up, and sellers compete by cutting prices. As the price falls, quantity demanded rises and quantity supplied falls until the surplus disappears at equilibrium.
parts.working: 2 marks: surplus leads to unsold stock and competition between sellers who cut price; 2 marks: falling price raises demand and reduces supply until equilibrium is restored.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The demand for a product is Qd = 240 - 3P and the supply is Qs = 40 + 5P, where P is the price in dollars. Calculate the equilibrium price and the equilibrium quantity.
parts.answer: Equilibrium price = $25; equilibrium quantity = 165 units.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The demand for a good is Qd = 90 - 2P and the supply is Qs = 30 + 4P, where P is the price in dollars. What is the equilibrium price?
A $5
B $10
C $15
D $20
parts.working: At equilibrium 90 - 2P = 30 + 4P, so 60 = 6P and P = 10 (quantity 70). A, C and D do not make quantity demanded equal to quantity supplied: at $20 supply (110) exceeds demand (50).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The demand for a good is Qd = 240 - 3P and the supply is Qs = 40 + 5P, where P is in dollars. An indirect tax of $4 per unit is imposed on producers, so their new supply is Qs = 40 + 5(P - 4). (a) Calculate the new equilibrium price paid by consumers. (b) Calculate the new equilibrium quantity.
parts.working: 240 - 3P = 40 + 5(P - 4) = 20 + 5P, so 220 = 8P, P = 27.5 (3 marks). Q = 240 - 3 x 27.5 = 157.5 (3 marks). Quantity falls, and consumers pay more than before ($25).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The demand for a good is Qd = 260 - 3P (demand has risen by 20 units at each price) and the supply is Qs = 40 + 5P. Compare the new equilibrium price and quantity with the original equilibrium of $25 and 165 units. Analyse the changes.
parts.answer: New equilibrium: P = $27.50 and Q = 177.5 units. Compared with the original, the price rises by $2.50 and the quantity traded rises by 12.5 units.
parts.working: 260 - 3P = 40 + 5P gives P = 27.5 and Q = 177.5 (3 marks). Analysis (3 marks): higher demand creates a shortage at the old price; price rises and this raises quantity supplied along the supply curve, so the market clears at a higher quantity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether the market equilibrium price will always remain stable over time.
parts.answer: Discussion. Equilibrium shifts whenever demand or supply changes (e.g. incomes, technology, weather, expectations), so price is not stable; producers respond with delays (e.g. farmers planting), causing cycles; government policy and speculation also change prices. However, in some markets prices are relatively stable for long periods when both curves change little. Reasoned conclusion.
parts.working: Up to 8 marks (levels): two developed points about shifts of the curves and time lags or external shocks, plus evaluation of when stability is likely, and a supported conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The demand for a good is Qd = 150 - 2P and the supply is Qs = 30 + 3P, where P is the price in dollars. The government sets a maximum price of $20. Calculate the quantity demanded, the quantity supplied and the excess demand, and state the likely effect.
parts.answer: Qd = 110 units; Qs = 90 units; excess demand = 20 units. Likely effect: shortages, queues, rationing or a black market.
parts.working: 150 - 2 x 20 = 110 (1 mark); 30 + 3 x 20 = 90 (1 mark); excess demand = 110 - 90 = 20 (1 mark); likely effect of the shortage (1 mark). (The original equilibrium is P = $24, Q = 102.)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following is a macroeconomic issue?
A the national unemployment rate
B the price of rice in one city market
C the wages of nurses at one hospital
D the output of a single car manufacturer
parts.answer: A the national unemployment rate
parts.working: Macroeconomics studies the whole economy, e.g. national unemployment, inflation, growth. B, C and D concern individual markets or decision makers, which is microeconomics.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two macroeconomic objectives of a government.
parts.answer: Any two of: low and stable inflation; low unemployment; economic growth; balance of payments equilibrium; a fairer distribution of income.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two correct objectives.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give one example of a microeconomic issue and one example of a macroeconomic issue.
parts.answer: Microeconomic: the price of bread in one shop, or the wage of a bus driver. Macroeconomic: the national inflation rate, the national unemployment rate, or the growth of GDP.
parts.working: 1 mark for a correct micro example (individual market, firm or household); 1 mark for a correct macro example (whole economy).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following is a microeconomic decision?
A the government chooses the national interest rate
B a bakery decides how many loaves to bake this week
C the central bank changes the money supply
D the government sets the size of the budget deficit
parts.answer: B a bakery decides how many loaves to bake this week
parts.working: A, C and D are national decisions about the whole economy (macroeconomic). B is one firm deciding its own output in one market, which is microeconomic.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define inflation.
parts.answer: A sustained increase in the general price level (average prices) of goods and services over time.
parts.working: 1 mark: general price level rises; 1 mark: sustained over time, not a one-off increase.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between microeconomics and macroeconomics.
parts.answer: Microeconomics studies individual markets and decision makers; macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole.
parts.working: 1 mark: micro – individual consumers, workers, firms or markets; 1 mark: macro – whole economy, e.g. inflation, unemployment, economic growth.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify three decision makers studied in microeconomics and give an example of a decision each makes.
parts.answer: e.g. households/consumers – what to buy; workers – which job to take; firms – what and how much to produce
parts.working: 1 mark each for three decision makers with a matching decision: consumers/households (spending, saving), workers (occupation, hours), firms/producers (output, prices, methods), government (as a decision maker in a market, e.g. setting a tax on one product).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The consumer price index rises from 120 to 126 in one year. Calculate the percentage increase in the price level.
parts.working: (126 - 120) / 120 x 100 = 5.0 %. 1 mark for the method, 1 mark for the answer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a rise in the national unemployment rate is considered a macroeconomic issue, even though it affects individual workers.
parts.answer: Unemployment affects the whole economy: unemployed people spend less, so aggregate demand and national output (GDP) fall; government tax revenue falls while welfare spending rises; the problem is a national one that needs national policies.
parts.working: 2 marks: lower aggregate spending and national output (aggregate effect); 2 marks: lower tax revenue and higher welfare spending, so it is a national problem.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways in which a rise in the national interest rate can affect a household's spending decisions.
parts.answer: Any two developed: borrowing becomes more expensive (higher mortgage or loan repayments), so the household borrows and spends less; saving pays a higher return, so the household saves more and spends less; the cost of credit cards and hire purchase rises.
parts.working: 2 marks per way: 1 mark for the point, 1 mark for the explanation of the reduction in spending.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse how a rise in the world price of wheat affects a bakery (a microeconomic decision-maker) and the national inflation rate (a macroeconomic issue) in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Bakery: wheat is a major cost, so profit falls unless the bakery raises bread prices or cuts costs or output. National: higher food prices feed into the general price level, so the inflation rate rises; households' real incomes fall, and the central bank may respond with higher interest rates.
parts.working: 3 marks for a developed micro analysis (cost, profit, price or output decision); 3 marks for a developed macro analysis (general price level, inflation, real income).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Real GDP rises from 4,500 billion to 4,635 billion in one year. Calculate the percentage growth in real GDP.
parts.working: (4,635 - 4,500) / 4,500 x 100 = 3.0 %. 1 mark for the method, 1 mark for the answer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a government may use tax policy to influence the whole economy, rather than to change the price in one market.
parts.answer: Tax policy (e.g. changing income tax or VAT) changes the spending power of all households and firms, so it affects total demand, inflation and growth across the whole economy. One market-level tax would only change prices in that market.
parts.working: 2 marks: tax changes aggregate spending across all households and firms; 2 marks: the effect is on inflation, employment or growth, not one market.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse the link between a high national unemployment rate, a fall in government tax revenue and an increase in government spending.
parts.answer: Unemployed workers do not pay income tax, and their spending pays less sales tax, so tax revenue falls; at the same time unemployment benefits and welfare spending rise, so the budget deficit grows. The government may need to borrow or cut other services.
parts.working: 3 marks: link between unemployment and falling tax revenue; 3 marks: link between unemployment and rising welfare spending, with the budget effect.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether a government should give priority to macroeconomic objectives (such as growth, low inflation and employment) over microeconomic issues (such as the price of rice in one market).
parts.answer: Discussion. Macro: affects all households and firms, so a stable economy is needed for growth and jobs; micro issues can be left to markets or targeted support. Micro: a rise in the price of a basic food can harm poor households even if inflation is low; markets are linked, so micro problems can become macro. Reasoned conclusion, e.g. both are linked and need appropriate, targeted policy.
parts.working: Up to 8 marks (levels): two developed sides showing how micro and macro issues interact, plus evaluation of the priority given, and a supported conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a macroeconomic decision by the central bank to raise the interest rate would affect a household's decision to buy a new home, and how it links to inflation.
parts.answer: Higher interest rates raise mortgage repayments, so the household is less able to borrow and may delay buying a home; higher rates reduce total spending, which slows the rise in the general price level (inflation) by reducing demand across the economy.
parts.working: 3 marks: effect on the household (higher mortgage cost, delay of purchase); 3 marks: link to aggregate demand and lower inflation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define supply.
parts.answer: The quantity of a good that producers are willing and able to offer for sale at a given price in a given period.
parts.working: 1 mark: quantity producers are willing and able to offer; 1 mark: at a given price in a given time period.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the law of supply.
parts.answer: As the price of a good rises, the quantity supplied rises (and as price falls, quantity supplied falls), ceteris paribus.
parts.working: 1 mark: positive relationship between price and quantity supplied; 1 mark: other factors held constant.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two determinants of supply other than price.
parts.answer: Any two of: costs of production (wages, raw materials, energy); technology; taxes and subsidies; number of producers; weather or natural conditions; expectations of future prices.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two correct determinants.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the shape of a supply curve, and state the direction in which the curve moves when the price of inputs falls.
parts.answer: The supply curve slopes upwards from left to right. When input prices fall, the supply curve shifts to the right (an increase in supply).
parts.working: 1 mark: upward-sloping from left to right; 1 mark: lower input costs shift the curve right.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following would cause a movement along the supply curve of wheat rather than a shift of the curve?
A a rise in the price of wheat
B a subsidy paid to wheat farmers
C the introduction of higher-yield seeds
D a drought
parts.answer: A a rise in the price of wheat
parts.working: Only a change in the product's own price causes a movement (extension or contraction) along the supply curve. B, C and D change conditions of supply and shift the curve.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a fall in the price of fertiliser increases the supply of wheat.
parts.answer: Fertiliser is an input, so a lower price lowers the cost of producing wheat; farmers can make more profit at each market price, so they are willing to supply more at every price. The supply curve shifts to the right.
parts.working: 2 marks: fertiliser is a cost of production, so lower costs; 2 marks: at each price farmers supply more, so the supply curve shifts right.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between an increase in supply and an increase in quantity supplied.
parts.answer: An increase in quantity supplied is a movement up along the supply curve, caused by a rise in the price of the good itself. An increase in supply is a shift of the whole supply curve to the right, caused by a non-price factor such as lower costs, better technology or a subsidy.
parts.working: 2 marks: increase in quantity supplied is a movement along the curve caused by a price rise; 2 marks: increase in supply is a rightward shift caused by a non-price factor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Four farms supply sugar cane at a price of $50 per tonne. Farm A supplies 12 tonnes, Farm B 20 tonnes, Farm C 8 tonnes and Farm D 15 tonnes. Calculate the market supply at $50.
parts.answer: 55 tonnes
parts.working: Market supply = sum of individual supplies = 12 + 20 + 8 + 15 = 55 tonnes. 1 mark for adding the four farms, 1 mark for the answer with units.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how new technology, such as automated milking machines, can increase the supply of milk.
parts.answer: Automated machines raise output per worker and lower the cost per litre, so farms can produce more profitably at each price. The supply curve for milk shifts to the right, so more milk is supplied at every price.
parts.working: 2 marks: lower costs or higher productivity per worker; 2 marks: at each price more is supplied, so the supply curve shifts right.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following would shift the supply curve for bread to the left?
A a rise in the price of bread
B a fall in the price of wheat flour
C an increase in the wages of bakers
D an increase in the number of bakeries
parts.answer: C an increase in the wages of bakers
parts.working: A is a movement along the curve, not a shift. B and D raise supply (shift right). C raises production costs, so supply falls and the curve shifts left.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the effect on the supply of wheat of a rise in the price of a competing crop, such as sugar cane, which farmers could grow on the same land.
parts.answer: Sugar cane becomes more profitable, so farmers switch land and resources away from wheat to sugar cane; the supply of wheat falls and its supply curve shifts to the left at every price.
parts.working: 2 marks: rise in the price of the competing crop makes it more profitable to grow; 2 marks: farmers switch land away from wheat, so supply of wheat falls (left shift).

practice.stem: A farm's weekly supply of dates is 100 tonnes at $10 per kg, 200 tonnes at $20 per kg and 300 tonnes at $30 per kg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: New technology increases the quantity supplied by 25 % at every price. Calculate the new quantity supplied at $20 per kg.
parts.answer: 250 tonnes

parts.label: b
parts.text: Farm workers' wages rise at the same time as the government introduces a subsidy for date farmers. Analyse the possible effect on the supply of dates.
parts.answer: Higher wages raise costs and shift supply left; the subsidy lowers costs and shifts supply right; the overall effect depends on the relative size of the two changes.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks: higher wages raise costs of production, supply shifts left/less supplied at each price. Up to 2 marks: subsidy reduces costs/is extra revenue, supply shifts right. Up to 2 marks: net effect depends on which is larger; with demand unchanged, price falls if supply rises overall and rises if supply falls.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The supply of a product is Qs = 30 + 4P, where P is the price (in dollars) that producers receive per unit. Before any subsidy, buyers pay $20 per unit and producers receive $20. (a) Calculate the quantity supplied before a subsidy. (b) A subsidy of $5 per unit is paid to producers, so they now receive P + 5 for each unit. Calculate the new quantity supplied at the same market price of $20. (c) Explain the effect of the subsidy on the supply curve.
parts.answer: (a) 110 units. (b) 130 units. (c) The subsidy lowers the cost of supply, so the supply curve shifts to the right; at every price more is supplied.
parts.working: (a) 30 + 4 x 20 = 110 (2 marks). (b) Producers now receive 25, so 30 + 4 x 25 = 130 (2 marks). (c) Lower costs shift supply right, so more is supplied at each price (2 marks).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether a government should subsidise farmers to increase the food supply of the country.
parts.answer: Discussion. For: a subsidy lowers costs and shifts supply right, which can increase food security, reduce imports and stabilise prices for consumers; it supports rural incomes. Against: subsidies are costly to taxpayers (opportunity cost); they may encourage inefficiency or over-production; benefits may go to large landowners rather than the poor; alternatives such as investment in irrigation or research may be more effective. Reasoned conclusion.
parts.working: Up to 8 marks (levels): two developed sides with reasoning on supply response, cost and equity, and a supported conclusion that weighs the alternatives.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A drought destroys half of a country's onion harvest. Analyse the effect on the supply curve, the market price and the market quantity of onions.
parts.answer: The supply curve shifts to the left, because the drought reduces the quantity producers can supply at each price. The equilibrium price rises because there is a shortage at the old price; the equilibrium quantity falls, because less is produced and sold.
parts.working: 2 marks: supply curve shifts left (non-price factor, weather); 2 marks: price rises as demand exceeds supply; 2 marks: market quantity falls, though the price rise partly offsets it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define price elasticity of supply.
parts.answer: The responsiveness of quantity supplied to a change in price, measured as the percentage change in quantity supplied divided by the percentage change in price.
parts.working: 1 mark: responsiveness of quantity supplied to price; 1 mark: percentage change in quantity supplied divided by percentage change in price.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two factors that determine the price elasticity of supply.
parts.answer: Any two of: the time period (how long producers have to adjust); spare capacity; the level of stocks; how easily resources can be moved to or from production; storage costs.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two correct factors.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The price of a litre of milk rises from $0.80 to $1.00 and the quantity supplied rises from 6,000 to 6,900 litres per week. Calculate the price elasticity of supply.
parts.answer: PES = 0.6
parts.working: %change in quantity supplied = 900 / 6,000 x 100 = 15 %; %change in price = 0.20 / 0.80 x 100 = 25 %; PES = 15 / 25 = 0.6. 1 mark for the method, 1 mark for the answer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what a price elasticity of supply value of 0 means.
parts.answer: Supply is perfectly inelastic: quantity supplied does not change at all, however much the price changes.
parts.working: 1 mark: quantity supplied does not respond to a price change; 1 mark: this is perfectly inelastic supply.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The price of a product rises from $20 to $25 and the quantity supplied rises from 400 to 460 units. What is the price elasticity of supply?
A 0.6
B 1.67
C 0.15
D 6.0
parts.working: % change in Qs = 60/400 = 15 %; % change in price = 5/20 = 25 %; PES = 15 ÷ 25 = 0.6 (inelastic). B inverts the formula.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the supply of new office space is likely to be price inelastic in the short run.
parts.answer: Constructing buildings takes years, so producers cannot increase supply quickly when the price rises; there is little spare capacity, and suitable land and planning permission are limited, so quantity supplied changes very little.
parts.working: 2 marks: long construction time means supply cannot respond quickly; 2 marks: limited land, capacity or planning permission keeps quantity fixed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the price elasticity of supply is usually greater in the long run than in the short run.
parts.answer: In the long run firms have time to build new capacity, hire and train workers, and buy new machinery; new firms can enter the market. So quantity supplied can respond much more to a price rise.
parts.working: 2 marks: firms can adjust capacity, labour and equipment over time; 2 marks: new firms can enter, so supply responds more.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The price of a tonne of cotton rises from Rs 45,000 to Rs 50,000. The quantity supplied rises from 3,000 tonnes to 3,450 tonnes. Calculate the price elasticity of supply and state whether supply is elastic or inelastic.
parts.answer: PES = 1.35; supply is elastic (greater than 1).
parts.working: %change in quantity supplied = 450 / 3,000 = 15 %; %change in price = 5,000 / 45,000 = 11.1 %; PES = 15 / 11.1 = 1.35 (2 marks). Elastic because it is greater than 1 (2 marks).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The price elasticity of supply of a product is 0.6. The price rises by 25 %. Calculate the percentage change in the quantity supplied.
parts.answer: 15 %  (quantity supplied rises by 15 %)
parts.working: 0.6 x 25 = 15 %. 1 mark for the method, 1 mark for the answer.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A firm's quantity supplied rises from 500 to 600 units when its price rises from $20 to $25. What is its price elasticity of supply?
A 0.8
B 1.25
C 0.2
D 5.0
parts.working: %change in quantity = 100 / 500 = 20 %; %change in price = 5 / 20 = 25 %; PES = 20 / 25 = 0.8. B inverts the ratio, and C and D use the wrong base.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how holding stocks of finished goods affects the price elasticity of supply of a manufacturer.
parts.answer: Stocks let a firm sell extra units straight away when the price rises, so quantity supplied responds quickly; with stocks, supply is more elastic. Without stocks the firm must produce more first, so supply responds slowly and PES is lower.
parts.working: 2 marks: stocks allow an immediate increase in quantity supplied; 2 marks: without stock, production must be increased first, so supply is less elastic.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the supply of fresh tomatoes is price inelastic in the short run.
parts.answer: Tomatoes take months to grow so output cannot be increased quickly; they are perishable so stocks cannot be stored and released when the price rises.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two reasons + 1 mark each for explanation: time needed to grow crops; perishable – no stocks; land and other resources already committed; farmers may lack spare capacity/greenhouses.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the building of cold-storage warehouses could change the price elasticity of supply of tomatoes.
parts.answer: PES becomes more elastic because tomatoes can be stored and supplied to the market when prices rise.
parts.working: 1 mark: supply more elastic; 1 mark: stocks can be held and released quickly in response to price changes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Three products have the following price and quantity supplied changes. Product P: price $8 to $10, quantity supplied 400 to 440. Product Q: price $15 to $18, quantity supplied 300 to 345. Product R: price $20 to $22, quantity supplied 500 to 530. (a) Calculate the price elasticity of supply for each product. (b) Rank the products from the most to the least elastic supply and explain one reason why the ranking might be explained by the production process.
parts.answer: (a) P = 0.4; Q = 0.75; R = 0.6. (b) Ranking: Q, then R, then P (most to least elastic). Explanation: a product with spare capacity or stock, or one that can be produced quickly, has more elastic supply.
parts.working: (a) 1 mark each for correct PES (P: 10 / 25 = 0.4; Q: 15 / 20 = 0.75; R: 6 / 10 = 0.6), 3 marks in total. (b) 1 mark for the correct ranking; 2 marks for a developed explanation of why production conditions differ (spare capacity, stocks, time to adjust).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether a government can rely on high market prices alone to increase the supply of a crop in the short run.
parts.answer: Discussion. High prices raise profit and encourage farmers to plant more, but in the short run supply is inelastic because crops take time to grow, land and labour cannot be expanded quickly, and there are few inputs such as seeds and fertiliser. Weather can also destroy the crop. Prices may need to stay high for several seasons. Government measures such as irrigation, credit and seed supply can speed the response. Reasoned conclusion.
parts.working: Up to 8 marks (levels): two developed sides on how inelastic short-run supply limits the response to price, plus evaluation of alternatives or time lags, and a supported conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A firm's quantity supplied is 2,000 units at a price of $50. Its price elasticity of supply is 2.0. The price rises to $52.50, a rise of 5 %. (a) Calculate the percentage change in quantity supplied. (b) Calculate the new quantity supplied.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following is a protectionist measure?
A an import quota
B a free trade agreement
C the removal of a tariff
D a fall in international shipping costs
parts.answer: A an import quota
parts.working: A quota is a physical limit on the quantity of imports, so it protects domestic producers. B and C reduce trade barriers; D is a cause of globalisation, not a policy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define globalisation.
parts.answer: The process by which the world's economies become more closely connected through trade, investment, movement of people and information.
parts.working: 1 mark: increasing integration/interdependence of economies; 1 mark: through trade, capital flows, MNCs, migration or technology.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two causes of globalisation.
parts.answer: Improvements in transport (containers, air freight) lowered costs of trade; the internet and mobile communications make it easier to do business across borders
parts.working: 1 mark each for two causes + 1 mark each for explanation: cheaper/faster transport; better communications/internet; reduced trade barriers and trade agreements; growth of MNCs; more freedom of capital movements.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why a government may protect its domestic industries.
parts.answer: To protect infant industries until they can compete; to protect jobs in domestic industries
parts.working: 1 mark each for two reasons + 1 mark each for explanation: infant industry argument; protect employment; prevent dumping; protect strategic industries (food, defence); reduce a current account deficit; raise tariff revenue.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one method of protection other than a tariff.
parts.answer: e.g. a quota
parts.working: B1 any one: quota; embargo; subsidy to domestic producers; strict product standards/regulations; exchange controls.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is a reason for a government to impose a tariff on imports?
A to lower the prices of imported goods for consumers
B to protect infant industries from foreign competition
C to encourage more imports
D to remove barriers to trade
parts.answer: B to protect infant industries from foreign competition
parts.working: A, C and D are not reasons for a tariff: a tariff raises import prices and reduces imports, and removing barriers is the opposite of a tariff.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define a tariff.
parts.answer: A tax (duty) on imported goods, which raises the price of the imports for domestic buyers.
parts.working: 1 mark: a tax or duty on imports; 1 mark: it raises the price of imports to domestic buyers (protection or revenue).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A country imposes an ad valorem tariff of 20 % on imported mobile phones. A phone has an import price of $150 before the tariff. If the whole tariff is passed on, what is the price after the tariff?
A $180
B $170
C $30
D $150
parts.working: 20 % of $150 = $30, so the price becomes $150 + $30 = $180. C is only the amount of the tariff.

practice.stem: Before a tariff, the world price of steel is $600 per tonne. A country demands 10 million tonnes a year and domestic firms supply 4 million tonnes, so 6 million tonnes are imported. The government imposes a tariff of $100 per tonne. Domestic supply rises to 5 million tonnes and domestic demand falls to 9 million tonnes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the quantity of steel imported after the tariff.
parts.answer: 4 million tonnes
parts.working: B1 9 − 5 = 4 million tonnes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the government's revenue from the tariff.
parts.answer: $400 million
parts.working: M1 4 million × $100; A1 $400 million.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two disadvantages of the tariff for the country.
parts.answer: Steel users pay higher prices, raising costs for construction and car firms; other countries may retaliate with tariffs on the country's exports
parts.working: 1 mark each for two disadvantages + 1 mark each for explanation: higher prices for consumers/firms using steel; less choice; protected domestic firms may become inefficient; retaliation reduces exports; resources move to less efficient domestic producers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define a multinational company (MNC).
parts.answer: A firm that has its headquarters in one country and production or operations in more than one country.
parts.working: 1 mark: firm operating/producing in more than one country; 1 mark: headquarters in one (home) country.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A foreign car manufacturer opens a factory in Pakistan. Explain two benefits to Pakistan.
parts.answer: Creates jobs and incomes; brings new technology and skills; may increase exports and tax revenue
parts.working: 1 mark each for two benefits + 1 mark each for explanation: employment and higher incomes; training and transfer of technology/management skills; tax revenue (corporation tax); exports improve the current account; more choice for consumers; local suppliers (parts makers) gain orders.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define dumping.
parts.answer: Selling a product in a foreign market at a price below its cost of production (or below the price in the home market).
parts.working: 1 mark: selling exports abroad; 1 mark: at below cost/below home-market price.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a government might respond to dumping by imposing a tariff.
parts.answer: Dumped imports undercut domestic firms, threatening output and jobs; a tariff raises the import price to a fair level so domestic firms can compete.
parts.working: 1 mark: dumped goods unfairly cheap; 1 mark: domestic firms lose sales/close, jobs lost; 1 mark: tariff raises price of imports and restores competition (anti-dumping duty).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A specific tariff of $6 per unit is placed on imported bicycles that cost $85 each before the tariff. If the whole tariff is passed on to buyers, what is the price of one bicycle after the tariff?
A $79
B $85
C $91
D $97
parts.working: Price after tariff = 85 + 6 = $91. A subtracts the tariff; D doubles it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two disadvantages to consumers of protectionism, such as tariffs and quotas.
parts.answer: Any two developed: higher prices for imported goods and less choice, since fewer foreign goods are available; domestic firms face less competition, so they may be less efficient and quality may not improve; consumers pay more for goods because the protected industry faces less pressure to cut costs.
parts.working: 2 marks per disadvantage: 1 mark for the point, 1 mark for explaining the effect on consumers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether a country should remove all its barriers to trade.
parts.answer: Free trade gives lower prices, more choice, competition and export opportunities through specialisation; but infant and strategic industries may need protection, jobs may be lost, dumping may occur and the country may become over-dependent on imports.
parts.working: Up to 5 marks for removing barriers: lower prices/more choice for consumers; cheaper imported raw materials for firms; competition improves efficiency; specialisation raises world output; other countries more likely to lower their barriers. Up to 5 marks against: infant industries cannot compete; structural unemployment in declining industries; dumping; loss of tariff revenue; strategic industries (food, energy) at risk; current account deficit. Max 8; judgement needed for top band.

practice.stem: After joining a regional free trade area, a country's exports rose from $25 billion to $31 billion a year and its imports rose from $30 billion to $39 billion a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in the country's exports.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in the country's imports.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Analyse why joining the free trade area might increase the country's imports by more than its exports.
parts.answer: Removing its own tariffs makes imports cheaper so demand rises; partner countries' firms may be more efficient; domestic firms may lack the capacity or quality to expand exports quickly; higher incomes also raise demand for imports.
parts.working: 1 mark: tariffs on imports removed, lowering import prices; 1 mark: consumers/firms switch from domestic goods to cheaper imports; 1 mark: domestic exporters face strong competition/slow to raise capacity or quality; 1 mark: other reason, e.g. imported capital goods needed by exporters, rising incomes, partners already had low tariffs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a quota and an embargo.
parts.answer: A quota limits the quantity of a product that can be imported; an embargo is a complete ban on trade in a product or with a country.
parts.working: 1 mark: quota – limit on quantity; 1 mark: embargo – total ban.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether a quota on imported cars will protect jobs in a country's car industry.
parts.answer: Restricting imports shifts demand to domestic producers, protecting jobs in the short run; but higher car prices reduce total sales, protected firms may stay inefficient, retaliation can cut exports and jobs, and car-dealing and service jobs linked to imports may be lost.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for protection: fewer imports, consumers buy domestic cars; domestic output and employment rise/are maintained; time for industry to become competitive. Up to 4 marks against: car prices rise so fewer cars sold overall; lack of competition → inefficiency, jobs at risk later; retaliation hurts exporters; jobs lost in import/sales businesses; domestic firms may use imported parts or automate. Max 6; judgement needed for top marks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether globalisation has increased inequality within developing countries.
parts.answer: Discussion. For: skilled workers and owners of export firms gain high wages and profits; workers in traditional sectors may lose jobs to imports or automation; rural areas may fall behind. Against: globalisation creates jobs, lifts incomes, lowers prices and brings technology and investment; inequality may reflect domestic policies such as education and tax. Reasoned conclusion.
parts.working: Up to 8 marks (levels): two developed sides showing the effect on different groups of workers and regions, plus evaluation of other causes, and a supported conclusion.

practice.subtopic: Current account of the balance of payments

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following is recorded as a credit (inflow) in the trade in services section of a country's current account?
A spending by foreign tourists visiting the country
B imports of machinery
C interest paid to foreign banks
D spending by the country's residents on holidays abroad
parts.answer: A spending by foreign tourists visiting the country
parts.working: Foreign tourists' spending is an export of services, so it is a credit. B is a debit in trade in goods; C is a primary income debit; D is an import of services (debit).

practice.subtopic: Current account of the balance of payments

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the four components of the current account of the balance of payments.
parts.answer: Trade in goods; trade in services; primary income; secondary income
parts.working: 1 mark for any two; 2 marks for all four.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a current account deficit.
parts.answer: When the value of money flowing out of the country on the current account (imports of goods and services, income paid abroad) is greater than the value flowing in.
parts.working: 1 mark: debits/outflows exceed credits/inflows; 1 mark: on trade in goods and services plus primary and secondary income.

practice.subtopic: Current account of the balance of payments

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each item, state whether it is recorded in primary income or secondary income, and whether it is a credit or a debit for Pakistan:
(i) profits sent home by a foreign-owned company operating in Pakistan
(ii) money sent home by Pakistani workers in the Gulf
(iii) aid given by Pakistan's government to a country hit by an earthquake
(iv) interest received by Pakistani residents on savings held abroad
parts.answer: (i) primary income, debit; (ii) secondary income, credit; (iii) secondary income, debit; (iv) primary income, credit
parts.working: 1 mark for each item correctly classified (both section and credit/debit).

practice.subtopic: Current account of the balance of payments

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following is recorded as a debit (outflow) in the secondary income account of Pakistan?
A remittances sent home to Pakistan by Pakistani workers abroad
B foreign aid given by the government of Pakistan to another country
C spending by foreign tourists visiting Pakistan
D interest paid to foreign lenders
parts.answer: B foreign aid given by the government of Pakistan to another country
parts.working: Secondary income covers transfers with no payment in return. Aid given is an outflow (debit). A is an inflow (credit); C is a trade in services credit; D is primary income.

practice.subtopic: Current account of the balance of payments

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the current account of the balance of payments.
parts.answer: A record of a country's transactions with the rest of the world over a period, covering trade in goods and services and the flows of income and transfers.
parts.working: 1 mark: record of transactions with the rest of the world over a period; 1 mark: covers goods, services, income and transfers.

practice.subtopic: Current account of the balance of payments

parts.label: a
parts.text: In one year Pakistan's exports of services are $4.2 billion and its imports of services are $3.1 billion. Calculate the balance of trade in services.
parts.answer: $1.1 billion (a surplus)
parts.working: 4.2 - 3.1 = 1.1. 1 mark for the method, 1 mark for the answer; the positive figure is a surplus.

practice.subtopic: Current account of the balance of payments

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A country's current account shows (in $ billion): trade in goods −12, trade in services +4, primary income −3, secondary income +9. What is the current account balance?
A −$2 billion
B −$8 billion
C +$2 billion
D −$11 billion
parts.answer: A −$2 billion
parts.working: Current account = −12 + 4 − 3 + 9 = −$2 bn. B is only the balance of trade in goods and services (−12 + 4); D leaves out secondary income.

practice.subtopic: Current account of the balance of payments
practice.stem:
Current account data for a country in one year ($ billion):
exports of goods 28; imports of goods 45
exports of services 7; imports of services 6
primary income credits 1; primary income debits 5
secondary income (net, mainly workers' remittances) +30

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the balance of trade in goods.
parts.answer: −$17 billion

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the current account balance.
parts.answer: +$10 billion (surplus)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why workers' remittances are important for this country's current account.
parts.answer: Remittances (secondary income) of $30 bn more than offset the large deficit on trade in goods, turning the current account into a surplus and providing foreign currency to pay for imports.
parts.working: 1 mark: remittances recorded as secondary income credit; 1 mark: they cover the trade in goods deficit (30 > 17)/without them the current account would be in deficit (−$20 bn); 1 mark: provide foreign currency/support the exchange rate/raise household incomes.

practice.subtopic: Current account of the balance of payments

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two causes of a current account deficit.
parts.answer: High domestic incomes raise spending on imports; high inflation or an appreciated currency makes exports uncompetitive
parts.working: 1 mark each for two causes + 1 mark each for explanation: rising incomes → more imports; high relative inflation → exports dearer; exchange rate appreciation; low productivity/poor quality of exports; dependence on imported fuel or capital goods; large profit outflows to foreign firms (primary income).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one possible consequence of a long-term current account deficit.
parts.answer: e.g. pressure for the currency to depreciate, raising import prices and inflation
parts.working: 1 mark for consequence + 1 mark for explanation: currency depreciation/reserves fall; borrowing from abroad and growing foreign debt; loss of jobs in industries competing with imports; lower aggregate demand.

practice.subtopic: Current account of the balance of payments

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A country's current account shows (in $ billion): trade in goods -5, trade in services +7, primary income -9, secondary income +2. What is the current account balance?
A -$7 billion
B -$5 billion
C +$4 billion
D +$5 billion
parts.answer: B -$5 billion
parts.working: Current account = -5 + 7 + (-9) + 2 = -5. A (-7) leaves out secondary income; C (+4) leaves out primary income; D (+5) reverses the sign of the answer.

practice.subtopic: Current account of the balance of payments

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a rise in global demand for Pakistan's textiles would affect the current account of its balance of payments.
parts.answer: Exports of textiles rise, so there is a larger credit (inflow) in the trade in goods section; the trade balance improves, so the current account deficit falls or the surplus rises.
parts.working: 2 marks: higher exports are a credit in trade in goods; 2 marks: the trade balance and current account improve (smaller deficit or larger surplus).

practice.subtopic: Current account of the balance of payments

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether a current account deficit is always a problem for a country.
parts.answer: It can be a problem if long-lasting, financed by debt, or caused by uncompetitive industries; but it may be short-term, reflect imports of capital goods that raise future output, or be offset by financial inflows, and consumers gain from more imports.
parts.working: Up to 5 marks for problem: debt and interest payments; reserves run down; downward pressure on currency → imported inflation; lost output and jobs; sign of uncompetitive industries. Up to 5 marks for not always: short-term or small relative to GDP; imports of machinery boost future growth and exports; financed by FDI; higher living standards from imported goods; may correct automatically under floating exchange rate. Max 8; judgement needed for top band.

practice.subtopic: Current account of the balance of payments

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a contractionary (deflationary) fiscal policy could reduce a current account deficit.
parts.answer: Higher taxes or lower government spending reduce disposable income and aggregate demand, so spending on imports falls; lower inflation also makes exports more competitive and firms may sell more abroad.
parts.working: 1 mark: raise taxes/cut government spending; 1 mark: lower disposable income/aggregate demand; 1 mark: less spending on imports; 1 mark: reduced inflationary pressure improves price competitiveness of exports/domestic firms seek export markets.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one disadvantage of using this policy to reduce the deficit.
parts.answer: It reduces spending on domestic goods too, causing lower economic growth and higher unemployment.
parts.working: 1 mark: disadvantage (lower growth, unemployment, cuts to public services, unpopular); 1 mark: explanation.

practice.subtopic: Current account of the balance of payments
practice.stem: A country has GDP of $360 billion and a current account deficit of $14.4 billion. Its exports of goods are $40 billion and its imports of goods are $52 billion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current account deficit as a percentage of GDP.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The value of exports of goods rises by 10 % while imports of goods are unchanged. Calculate the new balance of trade in goods.
parts.answer: −$8 billion
parts.working: M1 new exports 40 × 1.1 = $44 bn; A1 44 − 52 = −$8 bn.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a country's export revenue might fall even though the volume of its exports rises.
parts.answer: If world prices of its exports fall by a larger percentage than the rise in volume, revenue (price × quantity) falls.
parts.working: 1 mark: export prices fall (e.g. commodity prices or depreciation in foreign-currency terms); 1 mark: price fall proportionally larger than volume rise, so price × quantity falls.

practice.subtopic: Current account of the balance of payments

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether a government should use import tariffs to reduce a current account deficit.
parts.answer: Discussion. For: tariffs make imports dearer, so imports fall and the trade balance improves; they protect domestic industry and jobs. Against: other countries may retaliate and reduce Pakistan's exports; tariffs raise prices for consumers and firms that use imported inputs; the deficit may be caused by structural issues (low productivity, low savings) that tariffs do not address; exchange rate or fiscal policy may work better. Reasoned conclusion.
parts.working: Up to 8 marks (levels): two developed sides (trade balance and industry effects against retaliation, input costs and structural causes), plus a supported conclusion that considers alternatives.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A country's currency appreciates against other currencies. What is the most likely effect?
A its exports become more expensive for foreign buyers
B its imports become more expensive for domestic buyers
C foreign tourists find it cheaper to visit the country
D its exports become more price competitive
parts.answer: A its exports become more expensive for foreign buyers
parts.working: After an appreciation each unit of foreign currency buys less of the domestic currency, so exports cost more in foreign currency. Imports become cheaper (B wrong) and exports less competitive (D wrong).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define an exchange rate.
parts.answer: The price of one currency in terms of another currency.
parts.working: 1 mark: price/value of a currency; 1 mark: expressed in terms of another currency.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two causes of a depreciation of a currency in a floating exchange rate system.
parts.answer: A fall in demand for the currency, e.g. because exports fall; a rise in supply of the currency, e.g. because imports rise or interest rates are cut and savers move money abroad
parts.working: 1 mark each for two causes + 1 mark each for explanation (via demand/supply of the currency): fall in exports/foreign demand; rise in imports; lower interest rates; higher relative inflation; fall in foreign direct investment; speculation.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following would cause a currency to depreciate?
A an increase in foreign demand for the country's exports
B an increase in the demand for imports
C an increase in foreign investment in the country
D a fall in domestic inflation relative to other countries
parts.answer: B an increase in the demand for imports
parts.working: When people demand more imports they must sell domestic currency to buy foreign currency, which lowers the value of the domestic currency. A, C and D increase demand for the currency, so it would appreciate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two factors that could cause a currency to appreciate.
parts.answer: Any two of: higher interest rates attracting foreign investment; higher demand for the country's exports; higher foreign tourism; lower domestic inflation than other countries; increased capital inflows.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two correct factors.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define depreciation of a currency.
parts.answer: A fall in the value of a currency against other currencies, so that one unit of the currency buys fewer units of foreign currency (in a floating exchange rate system).
parts.working: 1 mark: fall in the value of the currency against others; 1 mark: one unit buys less foreign currency.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The exchange rate of a country's currency, the rupee, changes from Rs 280 = $1 to Rs 300 = $1. An imported machine part costs $50. Which statement is correct?
A the rupee has depreciated and the part now costs Rs 15 000
B the rupee has appreciated and the part now costs Rs 15 000
C the rupee has depreciated and the part still costs Rs 14 000
D the rupee has appreciated and the part now costs Rs 13 000
parts.answer: A the rupee has depreciated and the part now costs Rs 15 000
parts.working: More rupees are needed to buy $1, so the rupee has depreciated. Cost = 50 × 300 = Rs 15 000 (up from 50 × 280 = Rs 14 000). B gets the price right but the direction wrong.

practice.stem: A machine made in Germany is priced at €20 000. The exchange rate changes from €1 = $1.10 to €1 = $1.25.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost of the machine in US dollars before and after the change in the exchange rate.
parts.answer: $22 000 before; $25 000 after

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in the dollar price of the machine. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the likely effect of this exchange rate change on the quantity of European machinery bought by US firms.
parts.answer: The machines are dearer in dollars, so US firms buy fewer (or switch to other suppliers), depending on price elasticity of demand.
parts.working: 1 mark: higher dollar price; 1 mark: quantity demanded falls/switch to US or other suppliers (more so if demand is elastic).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between a floating exchange rate system and a fixed exchange rate system.
parts.answer: Floating: the rate is set by market demand for and supply of the currency. Fixed: the government or central bank sets the rate at a chosen level and maintains it.
parts.working: 1 mark: floating determined by market forces; 1 mark: fixed set and maintained by the government/central bank (by buying or selling currency).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two advantages of a fixed exchange rate for a country.
parts.answer: Certainty for exporters and importers, encouraging trade and investment; discipline to keep inflation low
parts.working: 1 mark each for two advantages + 1 mark each for explanation: certainty/less risk for traders and foreign investors; easier planning of prices and costs; prevents speculation; forces government to control inflation to stay competitive; stable import prices.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The exchange rate changes from $1 = Rs 270 to $1 = Rs 295. Which statement is correct?
A the rupee appreciated, so imports are cheaper
B the rupee depreciated, so imports are cheaper
C the rupee depreciated, so imports are dearer
D the rupee appreciated, so imports are dearer
parts.answer: C the rupee depreciated, so imports are dearer
parts.working: More rupees are needed to buy one dollar (270 to 295), so the rupee has fallen in value (depreciated). Imports priced in dollars now cost more rupees, so they are dearer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A Pakistani exporter receives $2,400 for a shipment. The exchange rate is Rs 285 per $1. Calculate the number of rupees the exporter receives.
parts.working: 2,400 x 285 = Rs 684,000. 1 mark for the method, 1 mark for the answer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why a depreciation of a country's currency could lead to inflation.
parts.answer: Any two developed: imported raw materials, fuel and goods cost more in domestic currency, so firms' costs and prices rise (cost-push inflation); consumers switch to domestic goods, raising demand and prices (demand-pull effect); imported consumer goods become dearer, raising the general price level.
parts.working: 2 marks per reason: 1 mark for the point, 1 mark for explaining how the price level rises.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether a depreciation of its currency will benefit an economy.
parts.answer: Exports become cheaper and imports dearer, which may raise output, jobs and improve the current account; but imported raw materials and fuel cost more, causing cost-push inflation, real incomes fall, foreign-currency debts rise, and benefits depend on price elasticity of demand for exports and imports.
parts.working: Up to 5 marks for benefits: exports cheaper in foreign currency → more sold; imports dearer → consumers switch to domestic products; higher aggregate demand, output and employment; current account improves; more tourism. Up to 5 marks for costs: imported inflation (fuel, raw materials); lower living standards; foreign debts more expensive to repay; little benefit if demand for exports/imports is price inelastic or other countries retaliate. Max 8; judgement needed for top band.

practice.stem: A hotel in Hunza charges Rs 18 000 per night. The exchange rate changes from 1 Malaysian ringgit (RM) = Rs 60 to RM 1 = Rs 66.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost per night of the hotel, in ringgit, before and after the exchange rate change. Give the second answer to the nearest ringgit.
parts.answer: RM 300 before; RM 273 after

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the likely effect of this exchange rate change on tourism to Pakistan and on Pakistan's current account.
parts.answer: Holidays in Pakistan become cheaper for Malaysian tourists, so more visit; tourist spending is an export of services, so the trade in services balance and current account improve (if demand is price elastic).
parts.working: 1 mark: rupee has depreciated against the ringgit/stay cheaper in ringgit; 1 mark: more foreign tourists; 1 mark: tourism spending is a services export/credit; 1 mark: current account improves, depending on elasticity or other changes (e.g. Pakistani travel to Malaysia becomes dearer).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A Pakistani importer buys a machine priced at €18,000. The exchange rate changes from Rs 300 to Rs 318 per €1. (a) Calculate the cost of the machine in rupees before the change. (b) Calculate the cost in rupees after the change. (c) Calculate the percentage increase in the rupee cost.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether a government should try to keep its currency strong (appreciated) rather than allowing it to depreciate.
parts.answer: Discussion. Strong currency: imports are cheaper, which lowers inflation and gives consumers and firms cheaper inputs; foreign debts in dollars are easier to repay. Weak currency: exports are cheaper and more competitive, which can improve the trade balance and support domestic industry and jobs. A strong currency can hurt exporters and tourism. Reasoned conclusion linking to the economy's structure, e.g. a net importer or exporter.
parts.working: Up to 8 marks (levels): two developed sides on the effects of a strong and a weak currency on prices, exports and debt, plus evaluation, and a supported conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is an advantage to a country of specialising in the products it can make most efficiently and trading with other countries?
A it can achieve a higher total output from its resources
B it becomes less dependent on other countries
C it develops a wider variety of domestic industries
D it avoids all transport costs
parts.answer: A it can achieve a higher total output from its resources
