parts.working: Specialisation allows resources to be used where they are most productive, increasing output; the country trades for other goods. B and C are the opposite – specialisation increases dependence and narrows the range of domestic industries.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define specialisation at a national level.
parts.answer: When a country concentrates on producing the goods and services it is best at producing (and trades for others).
parts.working: 1 mark: country concentrates on a narrow range of products; 1 mark: those it produces most efficiently/trades for the rest.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two disadvantages for a country of specialising in a narrow range of products.
parts.answer: If world demand or prices for its product fall, incomes and jobs fall sharply; it becomes dependent on imports of other goods, which may be disrupted
parts.working: 1 mark each for two disadvantages + 1 mark each for explanation: risk from fall in world demand/price; structural unemployment if the industry declines; dependence on imports (supply disruption, war); depletion of resources; competition from new low-cost producers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define division of labour.
parts.answer: Breaking down production into separate tasks, with each worker or group of workers specialising in one part of the process.
parts.working: 1 mark: production broken into separate tasks; 1 mark: workers specialise in one task.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two disadvantages of specialisation to a country.
parts.answer: Any two of: dependence on a few products, so the country is vulnerable to falls in their prices; loss of self-sufficiency, so it relies on imports; boredom and repetitive work can reduce worker motivation; traditional industries decline when a country focuses elsewhere.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two correct disadvantages.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways in which specialisation can increase a country's output.
parts.answer: Any two developed: division of labour raises productivity because workers become faster at repeated tasks; economies of scale lower the average cost of production as output grows; workers gain skills and experience in one area; resources are concentrated where they are most productive.
parts.working: 2 marks per way: 1 mark for the point, 1 mark for the explanation of higher output.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A country exports 4.2 million tonnes of rice in a year at a price of $420 per tonne. Calculate the value of its rice exports in $ billion.
parts.answer: $1.764 billion
parts.working: 4.2 million x 420 = 1,764 million = $1.764 billion. 1 mark for the method, 1 mark for the answer in billions.

practice.stem: Garments make up 82 % of the exports of a South Asian country whose total exports are worth $55 billion a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of the country's garment exports.
parts.answer: $45.1 billion

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two benefits to the country of specialising in garment production.
parts.answer: Economies of scale lower average costs, making garments competitive; large export earnings and employment, especially for women workers
parts.working: 1 mark each for two benefits + 1 mark each for explanation: economies of scale; workers become skilled/productive; export revenue/foreign currency; employment and income; attracts foreign investment.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one risk of this degree of specialisation.
parts.answer: Exports depend on one industry, so a fall in world demand or a rise in competition from lower-cost countries would cut export earnings and jobs.
parts.working: 1 mark: risk identified (fall in world demand, new competitors, trade barriers abroad, rising wages); 1 mark: explanation of effect on export earnings/jobs.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following is a disadvantage to a country of specialising in one or two products?
A it reduces the total output of the country
B it makes the country dependent on a few products, so it is vulnerable to falls in their world prices
C it always increases unemployment
D it reduces the output per worker
parts.answer: B it makes the country dependent on a few products, so it is vulnerable to falls in their world prices
parts.working: Specialisation usually increases output and productivity (A and D are wrong), and it does not always raise unemployment (C is wrong). The key disadvantage is dependence and vulnerability to price shocks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Country X can produce 60 bicycles or 120 tables per day. Country Y can produce 30 bicycles or 90 tables per day. (a) Calculate the opportunity cost of one bicycle in each country, in tables. (b) State which country should specialise in bicycles, and why.
parts.answer: (a) X: 2 tables; Y: 3 tables. (b) Country X should specialise in bicycles because it gives up fewer tables for each bicycle (lower opportunity cost).
parts.working: (a) X: 120 / 60 = 2 (2 marks: one for each country). (b) X has the lower opportunity cost, so it should specialise in bicycles (2 marks: decision and reason).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two benefits of free trade to consumers.
parts.answer: Any two developed: a wider range of goods and services becomes available; competition from imports lowers prices; imports may be of higher quality or more advanced technology.
parts.working: 2 marks per benefit: 1 mark for the benefit, 1 mark for the explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A country's exports rise from $3.6 billion to $4.1 billion. Calculate the percentage increase in exports.
parts.working: (4.1 - 3.6) / 3.6 x 100 = 13.9 %. 1 mark for the method, 1 mark for the answer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether consumers benefit when their country specialises and trades freely with other countries.
parts.answer: Consumers gain from lower prices, wider choice and better quality through competition and economies of scale; but may lose if jobs and incomes fall in declining industries, if supply is disrupted, if quality or safety standards are lower, or if foreign firms gain monopoly power.
parts.working: Up to 5 marks for benefits: lower prices from efficient production/economies of scale; wider choice including goods not produced at home; competition raises quality; higher incomes from export industries. Up to 5 marks against: consumers are also workers – job losses in industries facing imports; vulnerability to supply disruptions and price shocks; unsafe imports; dumping may eventually reduce competition; depreciation may make imports expensive. Max 8; judgement needed for top band.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse how a country that depends on exporting a single commodity, such as cotton, is made vulnerable to changes in world prices.
parts.answer: A large share of export earnings comes from one product, so a fall in its world price sharply reduces export revenue and the current account; the government loses tax revenue and jobs fall in the sector; the country cannot easily switch to other exports, so it is exposed to shocks such as bad harvests or a fall in demand abroad.
parts.working: 2 marks: one product gives most export revenue; 2 marks: a price fall cuts earnings, the current account and government revenue; 2 marks: the country cannot switch quickly, so it stays exposed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether free trade always benefits the workers in a country.
parts.answer: Discussion. Benefits: export industries grow and create jobs; wages in export sectors may rise; cheaper imported inputs help firms that employ workers. Costs: workers in import-competing industries may lose jobs; wages may fall where cheap imports compete; workers may need retraining and suffer frictional or structural unemployment. Reasoned conclusion, e.g. the gains are often large but unevenly spread, so policies such as training and social support are needed.
parts.working: Up to 8 marks (levels): two developed sides on export and import-competing workers, evaluation of who gains and loses in the short and long run, and a supported conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Three countries can each produce only textiles (T) or electronics (E) in a day. Alpha: 12 T or 6 E. Beta: 9 T or 9 E. Gamma: 20 T or 4 E. (a) Calculate the opportunity cost of one unit of electronics in textiles for Alpha, Beta and Gamma. (b) State which country should specialise in electronics and which should specialise in textiles, giving a reason. (c) Explain one benefit of this pattern of specialisation to the three countries.
parts.answer: (a) Alpha 2.0 T; Beta 1.0 T; Gamma 5.0 T per E. (b) Beta should specialise in electronics (lowest opportunity cost in electronics), and Gamma should specialise in textiles (it gives up the fewest electronics per textile, i.e. lowest opportunity cost in textiles). (c) Total output of both goods can rise when each country specialises in the good it makes at the lowest opportunity cost and trades.
parts.working: (a) 2 marks: 12/6 = 2; 9/9 = 1; 20/4 = 5. (b) 2 marks: Beta has the lowest cost of electronics (1 T), Gamma the lowest cost of textiles (0.2 E); accept the reasoning that the lowest opportunity cost determines specialisation. (c) 2 marks: developed benefit (higher total output or cheaper goods from trade).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Each option gives a country's birth rate, death rate and net migration rate, all per 1 000 of the population per year. Which combination would increase the country's population?
A birth rate 12, death rate 10, net migration −1
B birth rate 10, death rate 12, net migration +1
C birth rate 15, death rate 9, net migration −8
D birth rate 9, death rate 11, net migration 0
parts.answer: A birth rate 12, death rate 10, net migration −1
parts.working: Population change = birth rate − death rate + net migration: A 12 − 10 − 1 = +1 per 1 000 (increase). B = −1, C = −2 and D = −2 per 1 000 (decreases). C is the main trap: it has the highest natural increase (+6) but net emigration of 8 outweighs it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define birth rate.
parts.answer: The number of live births per 1 000 of the population in a year.
parts.working: 1 mark: number of (live) births. 1 mark: per 1 000 population per year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why birth rates are often higher in low-income countries than in high-income countries.
parts.answer: Any two, developed: children work on family farms or bring in income, so families want more; high infant mortality means parents have more children to ensure some survive; lack of pensions means parents rely on children in old age; limited access to or knowledge of family planning; lower female education and early marriage; cultural or religious traditions favouring large families.
parts.working: For each of two reasons: 1 mark for the reason, 1 mark for development.

practice.stem: Millions of Pakistani workers live and work in Gulf countries such as Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define net migration.
parts.answer: The difference between the number of people entering a country to live (immigrants) and the number leaving it to live elsewhere (emigrants) over a period.
parts.working: 1 mark: immigration minus emigration. 1 mark: over a period of time / people moving to live.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why workers emigrate from Pakistan to Gulf countries.
parts.answer: Higher wages abroad, so they can earn more and send money home; more job opportunities, e.g. in construction, when unemployment is high at home; demand for specific skills such as engineering or nursing; established communities and recruitment networks make moving easier.
parts.working: For each of two reasons: 1 mark for the reason, 1 mark for development.

practice.stem:
In one year, Country X had the following population data.
Population at the start of the year: 40 million
Births: 1.0 million
Deaths: 0.3 million
Immigrants: 0.15 million
Emigrants: 0.25 million

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Country X's net migration for the year.
parts.answer: −0.1 million (net emigration of 100 000)
parts.working: 0.15 − 0.25 = −0.1 million (B1; sign or 'net outflow' needed).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the population at the end of the year.
parts.answer: 40.6 million

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the birth rate per 1 000 of the population, using the population at the start of the year.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In one year a country of 2 million people records 16 000 births and 6 000 deaths, and has no migration. What is its rate of natural increase?
A 0.5%
B 0.8%
C 1.1%
D 0.05%
parts.working: Natural increase = births − deaths = 10 000; 10 000 ÷ 2 000 000 × 100 = 0.5%. B uses births only (16 000 ÷ 2 000 000 = 0.8%). C adds births and deaths (22 000 ÷ 2 000 000 = 1.1%). D is a decimal-place error: the answer is 0.5%, not 0.05%.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A country has a birth rate of 24 per 1 000 and a death rate of 9 per 1 000. There is no migration. What is the rate of natural increase of its population?
A 0.15% per year
B 1.5% per year
C 3.3% per year
D 15% per year
parts.answer: B 1.5% per year
parts.working: Natural increase = 24 − 9 = 15 per 1 000 = 15 ÷ 1 000 × 100 = 1.5% a year. D (15%) treats 15 per 1 000 as 15 per 100; C (3.3%) adds the two rates instead of subtracting (33 per 1 000).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is most likely to result from an ageing population?
A a rise in the proportion of the population of working age
B a fall in the demand for healthcare
C an increase in government spending on pensions and healthcare
D a rise in the birth rate
parts.answer: C an increase in government spending on pensions and healthcare
parts.working: An ageing population means more people over retirement age, so spending on state pensions and healthcare rises. The working-age share usually falls (A), demand for healthcare rises rather than falls (B), and ageing is usually caused by, not followed by, a low birth rate (D).

practice.stem:
A country's population is divided into age groups as follows.
Aged 0–14: 36 million
Aged 15–64: 60 million
Aged 65 and over: 4 million

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the dependency ratio as the number of dependants per 100 people of working age. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: 66.7 dependants per 100 people of working age

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two economic problems that may be caused by the country's high proportion of young dependants.
parts.answer: Any two, developed: high government spending on schools and child healthcare, which has an opportunity cost or needs higher taxes; working-age people have to support many dependants, so household saving is low and investment is limited; pressure on housing, food and other resources; in future, many young people entering the labour force may face unemployment if jobs are not created.
parts.working: For each of two problems: 1 mark for the problem, 1 mark for development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define optimum population.
parts.answer: The size of population that, with the country's existing resources and technology, gives the highest output (real GDP) per head.
parts.working: 1 mark: population size giving maximum output/income per head. 1 mark: given existing resources and technology.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a country being under-populated, and why new technology might change its optimum population.
parts.answer: Under-populated means the population is smaller than the optimum: there are too few workers to make full use of the resources, so a larger population would raise output per head. New technology raises the productivity of resources, so more people can be supported at the highest output per head; the optimum population therefore increases.
parts.working: 1 mark: population below the optimum. 1 mark: resources not fully used / more people would raise output per head. 1 mark: technology raises productivity. 1 mark: so optimum population rises.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which change would reduce a country's dependency ratio, other things being equal?
A a rise in the number of people aged 65 and over
B a fall in the number of children aged 0–14
C a fall in the number of people of working age
D a rise in the number of children aged 0–14
parts.answer: B a fall in the number of children aged 0–14
parts.working: The dependency ratio is the number of dependants (children under 15 and people aged 65 and over) divided by the working-age population. Fewer children reduce dependants. A and D increase dependants; C reduces the working-age population, so the ratio rises.

practice.stem: A country has a population of 45 million at the start of a year. During the year there are 1.1 million births, 0.5 million deaths and a net inflow of 0.2 million migrants.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the population growth rate for the year, as a percentage. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: 1 mark for a net change of 0.8 million (births minus deaths plus net migration); 1 mark for 1.8%.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a high population growth rate can make it harder to raise living standards.
parts.answer: Output per head grows more slowly when the population grows fast, so income per person rises slowly. More children increase the dependency burden on working adults. Schools, hospitals and housing come under pressure, so less is available per person. More people need jobs, which may be hard to create.
parts.working: 1 mark for each explained point (maximum 3).

practice.stem:
The table shows the average years of schooling of women and the birth rate in five countries.
Country | Average years of schooling of women | Birth rate (per 1 000)
A | 3.1 | 36
B | 5.4 | 29
C | 7.8 | 22
D | 10.2 | 14
E | 11.6 | 16

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the country with the highest birth rate.
parts.answer: Country A

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse the relationship between the average years of schooling of women and the birth rate.
parts.answer: Expected: an inverse relationship – the more years of schooling women have, the lower the birth rate. Evidence: A has 3.1 years and a birth rate of 36, while D has 10.2 years and 14. Reason: educated women marry later, have careers and know about family planning. Exception: E has more schooling (11.6) than D but a higher birth rate (16 v 14), so other factors also matter.
parts.working: 1 mark: inverse/negative relationship stated. 1 mark: comparative evidence from the table. 1 mark: economic reason (later marriage, work, opportunity cost of children, family planning). 1 mark: exception identified (E compared with D).

practice.stem: In some high-income countries, more than one in four people is now aged 65 or over.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two causes of an ageing population.
parts.answer: Falling birth rate; rising life expectancy / falling death rate (due to better healthcare, nutrition); emigration of young workers.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two causes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not an ageing population is harmful to an economy.
parts.answer: It creates costs but also some benefits and can be managed.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for 'harmful': higher dependency ratio, so a smaller share of workers supports more retired people; higher government spending on pensions and healthcare, needing higher taxes or borrowing; shortage of workers and lower labour mobility; slower growth. Up to 3 marks for 'not necessarily': older people can work longer, bringing experience; new markets for goods and services for older people; older people do voluntary work and childcare; the problem can be reduced by raising the retirement age, immigration or investment in labour-saving technology. Max 5 without a conclusion; 1 mark for a justified conclusion.

practice.stem: Money sent home by Pakistanis working abroad is one of the country's largest sources of foreign currency.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what remittances are.
parts.answer: Money sent by migrants working in another country back to their families in their home country.
parts.working: 1 mark: money/income sent home. 1 mark: by people working abroad (migrants) to their families.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not a country benefits from the emigration of its workers.
parts.answer: Benefits through remittances and lower unemployment, but loses skills.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for 'benefits': remittances raise family incomes and spending, and pay for education and housing; inflow of foreign currency helps the current account; reduces unemployment at home; returning migrants bring skills and savings. Up to 3 marks for 'does not': brain drain – loss of doctors, engineers and other skilled workers whose training was paid for at home; smaller labour force and tax base; families separated; dependence on remittances that may fall if the host economy slows. Max 5 without a conclusion; 1 mark for a justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether a country with a young population has an advantage over a country with an ageing population.
parts.answer: A balanced discussion. Young population: a larger future workforce; a demographic dividend if young people are educated and employed; lower pension costs for now. But a high number of dependent children needs spending on schools and health care, and youth unemployment may be high. Ageing population: an experienced workforce, but fewer workers support more pensioners; health and pension costs rise; saving and labour supply may fall. The conclusion depends on jobs, education and health provision.
parts.working: 5–6 marks: developed arguments on both sides and a justified conclusion. 3–4 marks: one side well developed. 1–2 marks: unsupported statements.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is NOT one of the measures used to calculate the Human Development Index (HDI)?
A life expectancy at birth
B gross national income (GNI) per head
C expected years of schooling
D the percentage of the population with internet access
parts.answer: D the percentage of the population with internet access
parts.working: The HDI combines life expectancy (health), mean and expected years of schooling (education) and GNI per head (income). Internet access is not included, although it may indicate living standards.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define real GDP per head.
parts.answer: The total output (GDP) of a country adjusted for inflation (at constant prices), divided by the population.
parts.working: 1 mark: GDP adjusted for inflation / constant prices. 1 mark: divided by population / average per person.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why real GDP per head, rather than total GDP, is used to compare living standards between countries.
parts.answer: Countries have very different population sizes; a large country can have a high total GDP but a low output per person, so dividing by population shows how much output is available on average for each person.
parts.working: 1 mark: populations differ. 1 mark: per head shows average output/income available to each person.

practice.stem:
Country P | Real GDP: $80 billion | Population: 20 million
Country Q | Real GDP: $300 billion | Population: 150 million

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the real GDP per head of each country.
parts.working: 1 mark: 80 billion ÷ 20 million = $4 000. 1 mark: 300 billion ÷ 150 million = $2 000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why Country P may not have higher living standards than Country Q, despite its higher real GDP per head.
parts.answer: Any two, developed: income may be very unequally distributed in P, so most people are poorer than the average suggests; Q may have a larger informal economy or more subsistence production not counted in GDP; P's output may include defence or pollution clean-up rather than consumer goods; P may have longer working hours, more pollution or worse public services; prices (cost of living) may be higher in P.
parts.working: For each of two reasons: 1 mark for the reason, 1 mark for development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the three dimensions of human development measured by the Human Development Index (HDI).
parts.answer: Health (a long and healthy life – life expectancy at birth); education (knowledge – mean and expected years of schooling); standard of living (income – GNI per head).
parts.working: 1 mark each: health/life expectancy; education/years of schooling; income/GNI per head.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one advantage of the HDI over real GDP per head as a measure of living standards.
parts.answer: It includes non-income measures such as health and education, so it gives a broader picture of people's well-being than income alone.
parts.working: 1 mark: includes health and/or education. 1 mark: so it reflects quality of life, not just income/output.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement about real GDP per head is correct?
A it is always larger than nominal GDP per head
B it is not affected by changes in the price level
C it adjusts output for inflation and then divides by the population
D it includes the value of people's leisure time
parts.answer: C it adjusts output for inflation and then divides by the population
parts.working: Real GDP per head = real GDP ÷ population, and real GDP removes the effect of price changes. A is not always true, because real GDP can be larger or smaller than nominal GDP. B is wrong because prices affect nominal GDP and the adjustment removes them. D is wrong because leisure is not counted in GDP.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is a limitation of using GDP per head to compare living standards?
A it cannot be calculated in real terms
B it ignores how income is distributed between people
C it includes the value of unpaid housework
D it takes no account of population size
parts.answer: B it ignores how income is distributed between people
parts.working: An average income can hide large differences between rich and poor. A is wrong because GDP per head can be calculated in real terms. C is wrong because unpaid housework is excluded from GDP. D is wrong because GDP per head divides by population.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A country has a real GDP of $360 billion and a population of 240 million. What is its real GDP per head?
A $15
B $150
C $1 500
D $15 000
parts.working: GDP per head = 360 000 000 000 ÷ 240 000 000 = $1 500. A, B and D come from errors in the powers of ten when converting billions and millions (e.g. B treats a billion as 100 million).

practice.stem: In a country, nominal GDP per head rose from Rs 400 000 to Rs 460 000 in one year. Over the same year, the general price level rose by 20%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in nominal GDP per head.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate real GDP per head in the second year at first-year prices. Give your answer to the nearest rupee.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what has happened to living standards, on average, during the year.
parts.answer: Real GDP per head has fallen (from Rs 400 000 to about Rs 383 333, roughly 4%), because prices rose faster than nominal income, so the average person can buy fewer goods and services; average living standards have fallen.
parts.working: 1 mark: real GDP per head fell / prices rose faster than income. 1 mark: so purchasing power and average living standards fell.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two limitations of the HDI as a measure of living standards.
parts.answer: Any two, developed: it is an average, so it does not show inequality between groups or regions; it ignores other aspects of well-being such as political freedom, crime, pollution, housing and working hours; years of schooling do not measure the quality of education; data in low-income countries may be inaccurate; GNI per head ignores the informal economy.
parts.working: For each of two limitations: 1 mark for the limitation, 1 mark for development.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one other indicator that could be used to measure living standards, and explain why it is useful.
parts.answer: e.g. percentage of households with access to clean drinking water – shows whether basic needs are met and affects health. Also accept: doctors per 1 000 people, housing quality, pollution levels, literacy rate, ownership of consumer durables.
parts.working: 1 mark: a valid indicator not in the HDI. 1 mark: why it reflects well-being.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two non-monetary indicators of living standards.
parts.answer: Any two of: life expectancy; literacy rate; years of schooling; infant mortality rate; access to clean water; doctors per 1 000 people; housing quality; pollution levels.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two non-monetary indicators.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why an unequal distribution of income can make real GDP per head a misleading measure of the living standard of a typical household.
parts.answer: Real GDP per head is an average. If a small group of rich people receives a large share of income, the average is pulled up, so most households earn much less than the average; GDP per head can rise while the incomes of the poor stay the same, so it overstates the living standard of a typical household.
parts.working: 1 mark: GDP per head is an average/mean. 1 mark: high incomes of a few raise the average. 1 mark: most households have below-average income. 1 mark: growth may go mainly to the rich, so typical living standards may not rise.

practice.stem: A country's real GDP per head was $2 100 in Year 1 and $2 310 in Year 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in real GDP per head.
parts.working: 1 mark for the increase of $210 and the method; 1 mark for 10.0%.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a rise in real GDP per head may not improve living standards for every household.
parts.answer: The extra income may be unequally shared, so most of the rise goes to higher-income households. Prices of essentials such as food or rent may rise faster than average, so poorer households gain little. The figure does not include unpaid work or the informal economy, and it may ignore environmental costs.
parts.working: 1 mark for each explained point (maximum 3).

practice.stem:
The table shows real GDP per head and life expectancy in five countries.
Country | Real GDP per head ($) | Life expectancy (years)
V | 1 200 | 62
W | 3 500 | 67
X | 8 000 | 74
Y | 15 000 | 72
Z | 40 000 | 82

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the country with the highest life expectancy.
parts.answer: Country Z
parts.working: B1: Z (82 years).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse the relationship between real GDP per head and life expectancy.
parts.answer: Expected: a positive relationship – countries with higher real GDP per head tend to have longer life expectancy. Evidence: V has $1 200 and 62 years; Z has $40 000 and 82 years. Reason: higher income pays for better diet, healthcare, clean water and sanitation. Exception: Y has higher GDP per head than X ($15 000 v $8 000) but lower life expectancy (72 v 74), perhaps because of inequality or poor healthcare spending.
parts.working: 1 mark: positive relationship. 1 mark: comparative evidence. 1 mark: economic reason. 1 mark: exception (Y compared with X).

practice.stem: In many low-income countries, a large share of output is produced in the informal economy (unregistered small businesses) or by families growing food for their own use.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a large informal economy can cause real GDP per head to understate living standards.
parts.answer: Output from informal businesses and subsistence farming is not recorded in official GDP, so measured GDP per head is lower than the real value of goods and services people actually enjoy.
parts.working: 1 mark: informal/subsistence output is not recorded. 1 mark: so measured GDP per head is lower than actual output/consumption.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not real GDP per head is a better measure than the HDI for comparing living standards between countries.
parts.answer: Each has strengths; the HDI is usually broader, but GDP per head is simpler.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for GDP per head being better: data are widely available and simple to calculate; measures the goods and services available; can be updated frequently; income allows people to buy health and education. Up to 3 marks for HDI being better: includes health and education, not just income; two countries with the same income can have very different life expectancy and schooling; less distorted by a small rich group's income alone. Both ignore inequality, informal output and environmental damage. Max 5 without a conclusion; 1 mark for a justified conclusion.

practice.stem: Over ten years, a country's real GDP per head rose by 50% as new factories and mines opened. Air pollution in its cities also increased.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two possible costs of economic growth for living standards.
parts.answer: Any two of: pollution and environmental damage; depletion of natural resources; longer working hours / stress; greater inequality; congestion; loss of traditional communities.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two costs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not rising real GDP per head always raises living standards.
parts.answer: Usually raises material living standards, but not always for everyone.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for 'raises': more goods and services per person; higher incomes buy better food, housing and healthcare; more tax revenue for schools and hospitals; lower unemployment and poverty. Up to 3 marks for 'not always': gains may go to a small group, so inequality rises; pollution damages health; longer hours reduce leisure; the extra output may be capital goods, defence or exports rather than consumer goods; prices of necessities may rise. Max 5 without a conclusion; 1 mark for a justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether access to clean water, sanitation and health care matters more than income per head for the living standards of people in a low-income country.
parts.answer: A balanced discussion. For services: they directly affect health, survival and wellbeing; a family without clean water or medical care loses health and earnings; basic services can be provided at low cost to large numbers of people, including the poor, whom income growth may miss. Against: income pays for food, housing and private services; government services are paid for from tax revenue that depends on income, so a richer country can provide more services over time. The conclusion should recognise that the two are closely linked and justify which matters more in the situation described.
parts.working: 5–6 marks: developed arguments on both sides and a justified conclusion. 3–4 marks: one side well developed. 1–2 marks: unsupported statements.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement describes absolute poverty?
A having an income below the average income of the country
B being unable to afford basic necessities such as food, shelter and clothing
C having an income below 60% of the median income
D being unemployed for more than one year
parts.answer: B being unable to afford basic necessities such as food, shelter and clothing
parts.working: Absolute poverty means a person cannot meet basic needs. A and C describe relative poverty, which compares a person's income with others in the same country; unemployment (D) can cause poverty but does not define it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define relative poverty.
parts.answer: Having an income that is well below the average (e.g. below a set percentage of median income) in the country, so the person cannot afford the standard of living that most people enjoy.
parts.working: 1 mark: income low compared with others / below a % of average or median income. 1 mark: in that country/society, can't afford a normal standard of living.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two causes of poverty.
parts.answer: Any two, developed: unemployment – no wage income; low wages from low-skilled jobs; lack of education and skills, which limits job opportunities; ill health or disability preventing work; old age with no pension; large family size, so income is shared among many; living in an area with few jobs; natural disasters destroying crops or homes.
parts.working: For each of two causes: 1 mark for the cause, 1 mark for explaining how it leads to low income.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two causes of poverty in rural areas.
parts.answer: Any two: low levels of education and skills; low farm productivity or low crop prices; limited access to credit; poor roads and other infrastructure; drought or other natural disasters.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid cause.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two indicators, other than income, that are used to measure poverty.
parts.answer: Any two: access to clean water; child malnutrition or stunting rates; literacy rates; access to health services; quality of housing.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid indicator.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two effects of poverty on children's education.
parts.answer: Any two, each explained: children may miss school to earn money or do household work; malnutrition reduces concentration and learning; families cannot afford uniforms, books or transport; children may repeat years or leave school early.
parts.working: 2 marks for each effect fully explained.

practice.stem: In a town, the median household monthly income is Rs 85 000. A household is counted as being in relative poverty if its income is below 60% of the median. Five households have monthly incomes of: Rs 42 000, Rs 55 000, Rs 48 500, Rs 61 000 and Rs 51 000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the relative poverty line for the town.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how many of the five households are in relative poverty.
parts.working: B1: 2 — the household on exactly Rs 51 000 is not below the line.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a household could be in relative poverty but not in absolute poverty.
parts.answer: Relative poverty compares a household's income with others; it may have enough income to buy food, shelter and clothing (so it is not in absolute poverty) but still be well below the town's typical income.
parts.working: 1 mark: relative poverty is measured against others' income. 1 mark: the household can still meet basic needs.

practice.stem: A government is planning a cash transfer scheme that pays a monthly sum to women in the poorest households.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two consequences of poverty for a household.
parts.answer: Any two of: poor diet/malnutrition; poor health and shorter life expectancy; children leaving school early; poor housing; lack of access to clean water; debt.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two consequences.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two policies, other than cash transfers, that a government could use to reduce poverty.
parts.answer: Any two, developed: free or subsidised education and training, raising skills and future earnings; free healthcare, so illness does not stop people working; a national minimum wage, raising pay of low-paid workers; policies to create jobs, e.g. spending on infrastructure; progressive taxation to redistribute income; subsidised food or housing.
parts.working: For each of two policies: 1 mark for the policy, 1 mark for explaining how it reduces poverty.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which factor is most likely to reduce poverty in the long term?
A a rise in interest rates
B wider access to primary and secondary education
C an increase in import tariffs
D a rise in value added tax (VAT) on food
parts.answer: B wider access to primary and secondary education
parts.working: Education raises skills and earning power, and its benefits pass across generations. A reduces investment and spending. C raises prices of imported goods. D raises the cost of food, which hits poor households hardest.

practice.stem: A household of six people has a total daily income of $11.50. For this question, use a poverty line of $2.15 per person per day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the daily income per person in the household. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how far each person's income is below the poverty line, in $ per day to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: $0.23 (2.15 − 1.9167 = 0.2333, rounded to 2 decimal places)
parts.working: 1 mark for the method (poverty line minus income per person); 1 mark for $0.23.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a cash transfer paid to poor households could reduce poverty.
parts.answer: Any two, each explained: it raises the household's income directly; spending on food, health and schooling improves living standards; better schooling for children can raise their future earnings; the extra spending supports local shops and jobs.
parts.working: 2 marks for each point fully explained.

practice.stem: A country has 120 million people. 18.4 million people live below the national poverty line.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the poverty headcount ratio as a percentage. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: 1 mark for the method; 1 mark for 15.3%.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the headcount ratio on its own may not show how severe poverty is.
parts.answer: It counts how many people are below the line but not how far below they are, so two countries with the same ratio may have very different poverty depth. It also says nothing about inequality among the poor.
parts.working: 1 mark: counts people but not depth of poverty; 1 mark: same ratio can hide different levels of severity; 1 mark: ignores inequality among the poor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one way in which poverty can be passed from one generation to the next.
parts.answer: Poor families may not be able to afford schooling, or need children to work, so children leave school with few skills; as adults they get low-paid jobs, so their own children are also poor (the poverty cycle).
parts.working: 1 mark: children of poor families get less education / poorer health. 1 mark: so they earn low incomes as adults and the cycle continues.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not providing free education is the most effective way to reduce poverty.
parts.answer: Education is vital in the long run, but other measures are needed too.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for 'most effective': raises skills and productivity, so future earnings rise; breaks the poverty cycle; increases occupational mobility; educated women tend to have smaller, healthier families. Up to 3 marks for 'not the most effective': takes many years to have an effect; families may still keep children at home to work, so free tuition is not enough; quality of schools may be poor; graduates need jobs to be available; people in poverty now need immediate help (cash transfers, food, healthcare); old or disabled people do not benefit. Max 5 without a conclusion; 1 mark for a justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether economic growth on its own is enough to reduce poverty.
parts.answer: A balanced discussion. For: growth creates jobs and higher incomes, and raises government revenue for welfare and public services. Against: the benefits may bypass the poor, especially in rural areas; inequality may increase; people without education or health may not gain from new jobs; targeted policies such as social protection are often needed. The conclusion should weigh these points.
parts.working: 5–6 marks: developed arguments on both sides and a justified conclusion. 3–4 marks: one side well developed. 1–2 marks: unsupported statements.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a rise in food prices affects poor households more than rich households.
parts.answer: Food takes a much larger share of a poor household's spending, so its real income falls more. Poor households have no savings to absorb the rise, so they cut spending on education or health. They may need to borrow, which adds to their debt.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three explained points.

practice.stem: A government introduced a clean water scheme. The share of the population living in poverty fell from 34% to 27%. Assume the population is 50 million throughout.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the fall in the share of the population living in poverty, in percentage points.
parts.answer: 7 percentage points (34% − 27%)
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage fall in the number of people living in poverty.
parts.answer: 20.6% (17 million fell to 13.5 million, a fall of 3.5 million; 3.5 ÷ 17 × 100 = 20.6%)
parts.working: 1 mark for 17 million and 13.5 million (or a fall of 3.5 million); 1 mark for 20.6%.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why it is difficult to attribute the whole fall in poverty to the water scheme.
parts.answer: Other factors, such as economic growth, new jobs, other government programmes or migration, may also have changed poverty levels. Without a comparison group, the effect of the scheme alone cannot be isolated.
parts.working: 1 mark for another factor that could explain the fall; 1 mark for the need for a comparison group or control.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which characteristic is most typical of a country at a low level of economic development?
A a large share of workers employed in the primary sector
B a low birth rate
C a high level of capital per worker
D a large share of workers employed in the tertiary sector
parts.answer: A a large share of workers employed in the primary sector
parts.working: Low-income countries usually have many workers in agriculture and other primary industries, with low productivity. A low birth rate (B), plenty of capital per worker (C) and a large tertiary sector (D) are typical of more developed countries.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following would NOT normally be a feature of a country at a high level of economic development?
A a high share of employment in services
B high levels of adult literacy
C high infant mortality rates
D widespread use of modern technology
parts.answer: C high infant mortality rates
parts.working: High-income countries have low infant mortality because of good health care, sanitation and nutrition. A, B and D are all typical features of high-income economies.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two reasons why countries differ in their level of economic development.
parts.answer: Any two: differences in natural resources; differences in education and skills of the population; differences in access to capital and investment; differences in political stability and institutions; differences in trade and technology.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why low levels of education can limit a country's labour productivity.
parts.answer: Workers with few skills find it hard to operate modern machinery and technology, so output per worker is low. Fewer skilled workers means less innovation and less ability to adapt production methods. Low productivity keeps wages and incomes low.
parts.working: 1 mark for each explained point.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways in which increased trade can help a developing economy to grow.
parts.answer: Any two, each explained: exports earn foreign currency to pay for imports of capital goods and technology; access to larger markets allows firms to gain economies of scale; competition from imports encourages domestic firms to become more efficient; foreign investment may bring new skills and technology.
parts.working: 2 marks for each way fully explained.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two differences in the typical export structure of low-income and high-income countries.
parts.answer: Low-income countries typically export mainly primary products such as raw materials and agricultural goods. High-income countries typically export mainly manufactured goods and services.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct difference.

practice.stem:
The table shows the percentage of the labour force employed in each sector in two countries.
Country | Primary (%) | Secondary (%) | Tertiary (%)
R | 58 | 14 | 28
S | 4 | 22 | 74

parts.label: a
parts.text: Country R has a labour force of 12 million. Calculate the number of workers employed in R's tertiary sector.
parts.answer: 3.36 million

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why Country S is likely to be more economically developed than Country R.
parts.answer: Most of R's workers are in the primary sector, often in low-productivity subsistence farming, whereas S has few workers in farming, suggesting farming is highly mechanised and productive; S's large tertiary sector (finance, education, health, tourism) indicates high incomes and demand for services; S's workers are likely to be more skilled and use more capital, so output per worker and incomes are higher.
parts.working: For each of two reasons: 1 mark for using the data, 1 mark for explaining the link to development (productivity, incomes, skills, capital).

practice.stem:
Country | GDP per head ($) | Life expectancy (years)
A | 1 500 | 60
B | 9 000 | 76

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater GDP per head is in Country B than in Country A.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage difference in life expectancy between Country B and Country A, relative to Country A. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: 1 mark for the method; 1 mark for 26.7%.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the gap in life expectancy is smaller in percentage terms than the gap in GDP per head.
parts.answer: Life expectancy depends largely on basic health care, clean water and sanitation, which can be improved at relatively low cost. It also has a biological limit. Income differences between countries are much wider because they reflect large differences in output per person.
parts.working: 1 mark: life expectancy depends on basic health and sanitation that do not need high incomes, or has a biological limit; 1 mark: income gaps are much wider because output per person differs greatly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why a high level of foreign debt can make economic development harder for a country.
parts.answer: Any two, each explained: interest repayments take a large share of the government budget, leaving less for education and health; repayments need foreign currency, which limits imports of capital goods; lenders may require cuts in public spending; a heavy debt burden lowers investor confidence and raises borrowing costs.
parts.working: 2 marks for each reason fully explained.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why technology gaps between countries can persist over time.
parts.answer: Any two, each explained: low-income countries lack finance to buy or develop modern machinery; limited research and development means little new technology is created at home; shortages of skilled workers make it hard to use new technology; the brain drain takes skilled workers to richer countries; weak institutions or weak protection of intellectual property deter investment.
parts.working: 2 marks for each reason fully explained.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the emigration of skilled workers, known as brain drain, can slow economic development in the country they leave.
parts.answer: The country loses doctors, teachers and engineers whose training it has paid for, reducing productivity and services. Fewer skilled workers means less innovation and fewer people to train others. Lost income tax and lower spending reduce government revenue and demand.
parts.working: 1 mark for each explained point.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how differences in labour productivity can cause differences in economic development between countries.
parts.answer: Where workers produce more output per hour (because of more skills, capital and technology), total output and incomes per head are higher, so the country can afford better living standards.
parts.working: 1 mark: higher output per worker. 1 mark: leads to higher incomes/GDP per head and development.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not differences in saving and investment are the main reason why some countries are more economically developed than others.
parts.answer: Important, but other factors such as education, health, population growth and institutions also matter.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for 'main reason': high saving provides funds for investment in machinery and infrastructure; more capital per worker raises productivity and output; low-income countries are stuck in a cycle of low income → low saving → low investment. Up to 3 marks for other reasons: education and health (human capital); rapid population growth spreading income thinly; reliance on primary products with volatile prices; political stability, corruption and the rule of law; access to trade, technology and foreign direct investment; natural resources and climate. Max 5 without a conclusion; 1 mark for a justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether all countries can follow the same path to economic development as the countries that developed earlier.
parts.answer: A balanced discussion. For a similar path: latecomers can adopt existing technology and methods more cheaply; they can learn from successful policies. Against: countries differ in natural resources, geography, population and institutions; world markets are more competitive and earlier developers may have advantages; the successful path depends on domestic policy choices that differ between countries. The conclusion should recognise broad common stages but different circumstances.
parts.working: 5–6 marks: developed arguments on both sides and a justified conclusion. 3–4 marks: one side well developed. 1–2 marks: unsupported statements.

practice.stem: Sector shares of GDP. Country S: primary 8%, secondary 22%, tertiary 70%. Country T: primary 52%, secondary 18%, tertiary 30%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times larger the primary sector's share of GDP is in Country T than in Country S.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a country with a large primary sector may have unstable incomes.
parts.answer: Prices of commodities such as crops and minerals often change sharply on world markets. A country that depends on a few primary exports has unstable export earnings, government revenue and incomes. Investment plans are hard to sustain when prices fall.
parts.working: 1 mark for each explained point.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a fall in the prices of a country's exports, relative to the prices of its imports, reduces its real income.
parts.answer: A country must export more to buy the same quantity of imports, so less of its output is available to its people; the purchasing power of its export earnings falls; government revenue from exports falls; investment may be cut because incomes are lower.
parts.working: 1 mark each for four linked points, maximum 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is an example of capital as a factor of production?
A a delivery van owned by a courier firm
B money kept in the owner's savings account
C fish swimming in the Arabian Sea
D the risk taken by the owner of the courier firm
parts.answer: A a delivery van owned by a courier firm
parts.working: Capital is a man-made aid to production, such as a van. Money (B) is not itself a factor of production in economics because it does not produce anything directly; fish in the sea (C) are land (a natural resource); risk-taking (D) is enterprise.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A woman in Multan uses her own savings to start a business installing solar panels on homes. What is the reward for the factor of production that she provides as the owner who organises the business and bears its risk?
A interest
B profit
C rent
D wages
parts.answer: B profit
parts.working: Organising production and bearing risk is enterprise, rewarded by profit. Interest (A) is the reward to capital, rent (C) to land and wages (D) to labour; she would receive wages only if she were employed by someone else.

practice.stem: A tea estate in the hills of Sri Lanka grows tea bushes on sloping fields that receive heavy rainfall.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define land as a factor of production.
parts.answer: Land is all the natural resources used in production, such as the surface of the earth, soil, minerals, water and climate.
parts.working: 1 mark: natural resources / gifts of nature. 1 mark: example or 'used to produce goods and services'.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify two examples of land used by the tea estate.
parts.answer: Any two of: the fields/soil, the rainfall, the climate/sunlight, rivers or streams used for water.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two natural resources. Do not accept tea-processing machines (capital) or pickers (labour).

practice.stem: A family bakery in Lahore makes bread and cakes. It rents a shop, employs six bakers, uses two large ovens and is run by its owner, who takes the business decisions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the four factors of production used by the bakery, giving one example of each from the information.
parts.answer: Land – the site the shop stands on; labour – the six bakers; capital – the ovens; enterprise – the owner who organises the business and takes decisions/risks.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct factor with a matching example.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the reward to labour and the reward to capital.
parts.answer: Labour: wages (salaries). Capital: interest.
parts.working: 1 mark: wages. 1 mark: interest.

practice.stem: A country has a total population of 50 million. Of these, 32 million are of working age, and 20 million people are in the labour force (employed or actively seeking work).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the labour force as a percentage of the total population.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which the quantity of labour in this country could increase.
parts.answer: e.g. (1) Raising the retirement age keeps older workers in the labour force for longer. (2) Providing childcare encourages more women of working age to seek work, raising the participation rate. Also: net immigration of workers; higher wages attracting people into work; a larger population of working age over time.
parts.working: For each of two ways: 1 mark for the way, 1 mark for explaining how it adds to the number of people/hours available for work.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the reward to enterprise as a factor of production?
A interest
B profit
C rent
D wages
parts.answer: B profit
parts.working: Enterprise (the entrepreneur) takes the risk of organising production and is rewarded with profit. Interest (A) is the reward to capital, rent (C) to land and wages (D) to labour.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which change would increase the occupational mobility of labour?
A a government-funded scheme retraining coal miners as electricians
B a rise in house prices in the capital city
C stricter licence requirements before a person can work as a nurse
D workers becoming more specialised in a single narrow task
parts.answer: A a government-funded scheme retraining coal miners as electricians
parts.working: Occupational mobility is the ease of moving between jobs; retraining gives miners the skills for a new occupation. Higher house prices (B) reduce geographical, not occupational, mobility. Stricter licences (C) and narrower specialisation (D) make it harder to change jobs, so they reduce occupational mobility.

practice.stem: Hospitals in rural Balochistan have many vacancies for doctors, while hospitals in Karachi receive many more applications than they have posts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define geographical mobility of labour.
parts.answer: The ease with which workers can move from one area or region to another to take up a job.
parts.working: 1 mark: moving between places/areas. 1 mark: to find or take a job / for work.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why doctors may be geographically immobile.
parts.answer: Any two, developed: family and social ties keep doctors in the city; differences in housing costs or lack of suitable housing; fewer good schools and facilities for their children in rural areas; lack of information about vacancies; cost of moving; differences in language or culture.
parts.working: For each of two reasons: 1 mark for the reason, 1 mark for explaining why it discourages moving to the rural area.

practice.stem: A garment factory in Dhaka, Bangladesh, sends its machine operators on a training course and replaces old sewing machines with faster computer-controlled ones.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how training improves the quality of labour.
parts.answer: Training gives workers new skills and knowledge, so each worker can produce more output or better-quality output in the same time (higher productivity).
parts.working: 1 mark: increases skills/knowledge. 1 mark: leads to more or better output per worker / higher productivity.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse how an improvement in the quality of capital can increase the factory's output.
parts.answer: Faster machines sew more garments per hour; they break down less often, so less production time is lost; computer control reduces mistakes and wasted cloth; so with the same workers and hours, total output rises and average cost may fall.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for a logical chain: better technology → each machine produces more per hour (1) → fewer breakdowns/less waste (1) → each worker using the machine is more productive (1) → total output rises with the same inputs (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two functions of an entrepreneur.
parts.answer: Organising: bringing together land, labour and capital to produce. Risk-bearing: putting money into the business without knowing whether it will make a profit. (Also: making decisions on what, how and how much to produce; innovating with new products or methods.)
parts.working: For each of two functions: 1 mark for identifying it, 1 mark for development.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why profit is described as the reward for risk-taking.
parts.answer: The entrepreneur is paid only what is left after all other factors have been paid; this may be a loss, so profit is the return that compensates for taking that uncertain risk.
parts.working: 1 mark: profit is the residual / not guaranteed / may be a loss. 1 mark: without the chance of profit no one would take the risk of starting a business.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which change would increase the quality, rather than the quantity, of a country's labour force?
A a rise in the age at which workers retire
B the arrival of many unskilled immigrant workers
C free vocational training courses for school leavers
D a rise in the birth rate
parts.answer: C free vocational training courses for school leavers
parts.working: The quality of labour is the skills, education and health of workers; vocational training raises skills and so productivity. A, B and D all increase the number of workers available (quantity), not their skills.

practice.stem: Over-fishing in the sea off the coast of Gwadar has reduced the stocks of several fish species. Local fishing crews now catch less each trip.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why fish stocks are classified as land rather than capital.
parts.answer: Fish in the sea are a natural resource (a gift of nature) and are not made by people, so they are land; capital is man-made, such as boats and nets.
parts.working: 1 mark: natural resource / not man-made. 1 mark: contrast with capital being man-made (e.g. boats).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not a fall in the quantity of one factor of production, such as fish stocks, must reduce a country's total output.
parts.answer: Output in the fishing industry is likely to fall, but total output need not fall if resources are reallocated or other factors substitute.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for 'must reduce': fewer fish means less catch with the same labour and boats; fishing workers may become unemployed; related industries (processing, exports) lose output; incomes and spending in the area fall. Up to 3 marks for 'need not': other factors can be substituted (fish farming/aquaculture using capital); workers can move to other industries; productivity elsewhere may rise; fish stocks can recover if fishing is controlled. Max 5 without a reasoned conclusion; 1 mark for a justified conclusion (e.g. depends on how mobile the workers are).

practice.stem: A government is considering paying part of the removal costs of workers who move from high-unemployment regions to regions with labour shortages.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two costs to a worker of moving to a new region for a job.
parts.answer: Any two of: removal/transport costs; higher housing costs; loss of contact with family and friends; children changing school; cost of finding a new home.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two costs (financial or non-financial).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not the government should subsidise removal costs to improve the geographical mobility of labour.
parts.answer: Arguments both ways leading to a supported conclusion.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for 'should': fills vacancies so output rises; reduces regional unemployment and benefit spending; workers earn higher incomes and pay more tax; firms in shortage areas can expand. Up to 3 marks for 'should not': opportunity cost of government spending; moving costs are often not the main barrier (family ties, housing shortages); depopulation of poorer regions; may only help workers who would have moved anyway; better to bring jobs to the workers. Max 5 without a conclusion; 1 mark for a justified conclusion.

practice.stem: A coastal city-state has increased its land area from 580 km² to 735 km² by reclaiming land from the sea.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in the city-state's land area. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why land is often said to be fixed in supply, yet the quantity of land available for production can change.
parts.answer: The total surface of the earth is fixed, so in the economy as a whole land is in fixed supply. But the land available for production can increase through reclamation, irrigation of deserts, clearing forests or discovering new mineral deposits, and can decrease through soil erosion, flooding, desertification or depletion of resources.
parts.working: 1 mark: total area of the earth/natural resources is fixed. Up to 3 marks for ways the usable quantity changes, e.g. reclamation (1), irrigation/fertilisers improving land (1), discovery of new resources (1), erosion/depletion/climate change reducing it (1).

practice.stem: At the start of 2026 the machinery and equipment used by a country's manufacturing firms was valued at $48.0 billion. During 2026 firms spent $6.2 billion on new machinery, while machinery worth $3.8 billion wore out or became out of date (depreciation).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net increase in the value of machinery in 2026 and express it as a percentage of the value at the start of the year.
parts.answer: Net increase = $2.4 billion, which is 5.0% of the starting value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why an increase in the quantity of capital may not increase output by as much as expected.
parts.answer: e.g. not enough skilled workers to operate the machines; unreliable electricity or poor transport; weak demand for the extra output.
parts.working: 2 marks for each of two developed reasons: shortage of skilled labour/training to use the machines; machines lie idle because of power cuts or lack of raw materials; poor infrastructure (roads, ports) limits output; little demand, so firms do not use the extra capacity; the new machines may replace old ones rather than add to capacity; poor management/enterprise.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Discuss whether or not a country should spend more on improving the quality of its labour, rather than on increasing the quantity of capital, in order to raise output.
parts.answer: Improving labour quality can raise productivity widely and lasts, but takes a long time; capital can raise output faster but needs skilled workers. Best answer: both are complementary; conclusion depends on the country's current shortages.
parts.working: Labour quality (up to 4): education and training raise productivity of every worker; skilled workers can use existing and new capital better; helps occupational mobility and adaptability; benefits spread across all industries; can attract foreign firms. Capital (up to 4): machines can raise output quickly; new technology embodies higher productivity; may be needed where infrastructure is poor; training takes many years and trained workers may emigrate (brain drain); education has an opportunity cost. Conclusion (needed for top band): e.g. the two are complements; which comes first depends on whether the shortage is of skills or of equipment. Levels: 1–3 one-sided or undeveloped; 4–6 both sides developed; 7–8 both sides plus justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
On a production possibility curve diagram, what does a point inside the curve show?
A All resources are fully and efficiently employed.
B Some resources are unemployed or used inefficiently.
C An output that the economy cannot reach with its present resources.
D The economy has experienced economic growth.
parts.answer: B Some resources are unemployed or used inefficiently.
parts.working: A point inside the PPC means more of both goods could be made, so some resources are idle or used inefficiently. Points on the curve show full, efficient use (A); points outside are unattainable (C); growth is shown by an outward shift of the curve (D).

practice.stem:
The table shows the maximum combinations of rice and textiles that a country can produce when all its resources are fully employed.
Point | Rice (million tonnes) | Textiles (million metres)
A | 0 | 100
B | 20 | 95
C | 40 | 85
D | 60 | 65
E | 80 | 35
F | 90 | 0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the opportunity cost of increasing rice production from 40 million tonnes to 60 million tonnes.
parts.answer: 20 million metres of textiles
parts.working: 85 − 65 = 20 million metres of textiles (B1). Must be expressed in textiles.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the opportunity cost of one extra million tonnes of rice when moving from point D to point E.
parts.answer: 1.5 million metres of textiles
parts.working: M1: (65 − 35) ÷ (80 − 60) = 30 ÷ 20. A1: 1.5 million metres of textiles per million tonnes of rice.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the opportunity cost of rice rises as more rice is produced.
parts.answer: Resources are not equally suited to producing both goods. As more rice is grown, the country must use workers and land that are better suited to textiles, so more textiles must be given up for each extra tonne of rice.
parts.working: 1 mark: factors of production are not equally suitable / not perfectly mobile between uses. 1 mark: less suitable resources are moved, so more textiles are lost per extra unit of rice.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State whether producing 40 million tonnes of rice and 70 million metres of textiles would be an efficient use of resources. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: No. Point C shows 40 million tonnes of rice can be produced with 85 million metres of textiles, so 40 and 70 is inside the curve: resources are unemployed or used inefficiently.
parts.working: 1 mark: not efficient / inside the PPC. 1 mark: comparison with point C (85 million metres possible), so some resources are underused.

practice.stem: An earthquake destroys many factories, roads and bridges in one region of a country. Farmland in the region is much less affected.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the effect of the earthquake on the country's production possibility curve.
parts.answer: The PPC shifts inwards (to the left), because the quantity of capital has fallen, so the maximum possible output falls.
parts.working: 1 mark: inward shift. 1 mark: reason – fewer resources/capital destroyed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the shift may not be the same for all goods, using a PPC with manufactured goods and farm goods on the axes.
parts.answer: Factories were damaged more than farmland, so the maximum output of manufactured goods falls more than that of farm goods; the curve shifts in further on the manufactured goods axis.
parts.working: 1 mark: manufacturing capital lost more than farmland. 1 mark: so the curve pivots/shifts in more on the manufactured-goods axis.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how foreign aid for rebuilding could change the position of the PPC over time.
parts.answer: Aid could pay for new factories, roads and bridges, increasing the capital stock again, so the PPC shifts back outwards, possibly beyond its original position if newer technology is used.
parts.working: 1 mark: aid funds rebuilding of capital / infrastructure. 1 mark: PPC shifts outwards again.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A country is producing at a point on its production possibility curve. What must be true?
A All its resources are fully employed.
B It is producing equal quantities of the two goods.
C It can produce more of both goods without any extra resources.
D There is no opportunity cost of producing more of either good.
parts.answer: A All its resources are fully employed.
parts.working: A point on the PPC shows the maximum output with all resources fully (and efficiently) employed. C describes a point inside the curve, D is wrong because on the curve more of one good means less of the other, and B is not required: any point on the curve is possible.

practice.stem:
A country's production possibility curve passes through these combinations (smartphones in millions, maize in million tonnes):
0 smartphones, 50 maize
10 smartphones, 45 maize
20 smartphones, 36 maize
30 smartphones, 22 maize
40 smartphones, 0 maize
The country is currently producing 20 million smartphones and 30 million tonnes of maize.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State whether the current combination is on, inside or outside the production possibility curve, and what this shows about the economy.
parts.answer: Inside the curve; some resources are unemployed or used inefficiently.
parts.working: Inside the PPC (B1) because with 20 million smartphones it could produce 36 million tonnes of maize; this shows unemployed/underused resources (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the extra maize the country could produce without reducing its output of smartphones.
parts.answer: 6 million tonnes
parts.working: 36 − 30 = 6 million tonnes (B1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons why an economy may produce inside its production possibility curve.
parts.answer: e.g. unemployment of workers; factories or land left idle because of low demand or power shortages; inefficient methods.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two developed reasons: unemployment (workers able and willing to work but without jobs); idle capital, e.g. factories closed by power shortages or low demand; land left unused; inefficient production methods or poor management; strikes or disruption such as floods.

practice.stem: A country has 2 million workers. In one year each worker can produce either 5 tonnes of wheat or 2 machines (the same for every worker). At present 1.2 million workers grow wheat, 0.6 million make machines and the rest are unemployed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum quantity of wheat the country could produce if all workers grew wheat.
parts.answer: 10 million tonnes
parts.working: 2 million × 5 = 10 million tonnes (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the country's current output of wheat and of machines.
parts.answer: 6 million tonnes of wheat and 1.2 million machines
parts.working: 1.2 million × 5 = 6 million tonnes (B1); 0.6 million × 2 = 1.2 million machines (B1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the extra machines that could be made if all the unemployed workers were employed making machines.
parts.answer: 0.4 million (400 000) machines
parts.working: Unemployed = 2 − 1.2 − 0.6 = 0.2 million; 0.2 million × 2 = 0.4 million (B1).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain whether the current combination of wheat and machines is on or inside the country's production possibility curve.
parts.answer: Inside, because 0.2 million workers are unemployed, so more of one good could be produced without less of the other.
parts.working: Inside the PPC (B1); because not all resources (workers) are employed, so output of one good could rise with no fall in the other (B1).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which change would shift a country's production possibility curve outwards?
A a fall in the country's unemployment rate
B the discovery of new reserves of copper
C the emigration of many skilled engineers
D moving workers from farming into manufacturing
parts.answer: B the discovery of new reserves of copper
parts.working: New copper reserves increase the quantity of land (natural resources), so the maximum possible output rises and the PPC shifts out. Lower unemployment (A) moves the economy from inside towards the curve without shifting it; emigration of skilled workers (C) shifts it inwards; moving workers between industries (D) is a movement along the curve.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define a production possibility curve.
parts.answer: A curve showing the maximum combinations of two goods (or types of goods) that an economy can produce when all its resources are fully and efficiently used.
parts.working: 1 mark: maximum output combinations of two goods. 1 mark: with all resources fully/efficiently employed (given resources and technology).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A country decides to produce more capital goods and fewer consumer goods. Explain, by describing a production possibility curve with capital goods on one axis and consumer goods on the other, the effect of this decision now and in the future.
parts.answer: Now: the economy moves along its PPC towards the capital goods axis – more capital goods, fewer consumer goods, so the opportunity cost is consumer goods given up today. In the future: the extra machinery and infrastructure increase productive capacity, so the PPC shifts outwards and more of both goods can be produced.
parts.working: 1 mark: movement along the existing curve. 1 mark: fewer consumer goods now / opportunity cost. 1 mark: increase in capital stock raises productive capacity. 1 mark: PPC shifts outwards in the future.

practice.stem: A small country's production possibility curve for computers and wheat is a straight line. If it produces only computers it can make 400 000 computers a year; if it produces only wheat it can grow 2 000 000 tonnes a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the opportunity cost of producing one tonne of wheat, in computers.
parts.answer: 0.2 computers
parts.working: M1: 400 000 ÷ 2 000 000. A1: 0.2 computers per tonne of wheat.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what a straight-line PPC shows about the country's factors of production.
parts.answer: The opportunity cost is constant, which means the factors of production are equally suited to producing computers and wheat.
