parts.working: 1 mark: constant opportunity cost. 1 mark: resources equally efficient / perfectly transferable between the two goods.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the maximum quantity of wheat the country can grow if it produces 100 000 computers.
parts.answer: 1 500 000 tonnes

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A country's production possibility curve shows solar panels on the horizontal axis and wheat on the vertical axis. A new technology raises productivity in making solar panels only. What happens to the curve?
A It pivots outwards, moving further out along the solar panel axis, while the wheat intercept stays the same.
B It shifts outwards parallel to the original curve.
C There is a movement along the curve towards more solar panels.
D It pivots inwards along the wheat axis.
parts.answer: A It pivots outwards, moving further out along the solar panel axis, while the wheat intercept stays the same.
parts.working: Only the maximum output of solar panels rises, so the curve's end on the solar panel axis moves out while the maximum wheat output is unchanged: a pivot. B would need higher productivity in both goods. C is a change in the chosen combination, not in what is possible.

practice.stem: Two countries, Alpha and Beta, had identical production possibility curves for capital goods and consumer goods in 2026. In 2026 Alpha produced 40 units of capital goods and 60 units of consumer goods. Beta produced 10 units of capital goods and 90 units of consumer goods. Both used all their resources.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify which country is likely to have the higher material standard of living in 2026, and give a reason.
parts.answer: Beta, because it produces more consumer goods for people to use now.
parts.working: Beta (B1); more consumer goods are available to households now (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse factors, other than the choice between capital goods and consumer goods, that could cause Beta's production possibility curve to shift outwards faster than Alpha's over the next ten years.
parts.answer: e.g. Beta improves education and training (quality of labour); its labour force grows through population growth or immigration; it discovers new natural resources; it adopts new technology or attracts foreign firms; Alpha's extra capital may be badly used or poorly maintained.
parts.working: Up to 6 marks for developed points: better education/training raises labour quality and productivity (1+1); more workers from population growth or immigration increase labour quantity (1); discovery of resources such as minerals increases land (1); new technology/foreign direct investment raises productivity (1); Alpha's capital goods may be unsuitable, idle or not maintained, so its PPC shifts less than expected (1). Link: any increase in the quantity or quality of resources shifts the PPC outwards (1).

practice.stem: Over one decade a country's unemployment rate fell from 9% to 5%. Over the same decade, the government also greatly increased spending on secondary and technical education.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a movement from a point inside a PPC to a point on the curve, and an outward shift of the PPC.
parts.answer: A movement from inside to the curve happens when unemployed or inefficiently used resources are brought into use (e.g. the fall in unemployment); actual output rises but productive capacity does not change. An outward shift happens when the quantity or quality of resources increases (e.g. better-educated workers), so the maximum possible output – productive capacity – rises.
parts.working: 1 mark: inside → on the curve = using idle resources. 1 mark: capacity unchanged / actual output rises. 1 mark: outward shift = more or better resources/technology. 1 mark: productive capacity/potential output rises.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse how investment in education could shift the country's PPC outwards.
parts.answer: Education raises workers' skills and knowledge → each worker produces more output per hour (higher productivity) and workers can use more advanced technology → more output can be produced from the same number of workers → the economy's productive capacity increases → the PPC shifts outwards.
parts.working: 1 mark each for links in the chain: skills/quality of labour rise; productivity rises; more output from the same resources / new industries possible; productive capacity rises so PPC shifts out.

practice.stem: A government with fully employed resources must decide how much to spend on healthcare and how much on defence.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, using a PPC with healthcare on one axis and defence on the other, why choosing more healthcare means less defence.
parts.answer: With full employment the economy is on its PPC; to produce more healthcare it must move along the curve, transferring resources from defence, so defence output falls – this is the opportunity cost.
parts.working: 1 mark: on the curve, resources fully employed. 1 mark: moving along the curve towards healthcare means giving up defence (opportunity cost).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not economic growth removes the need for the government to make this choice.
parts.answer: Growth eases but does not remove the choice.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for 'removes/eases': the PPC shifts out so more of both can be provided; higher tax revenue funds both; the opportunity cost of extra healthcare may be smaller. Up to 3 marks for 'does not': the economy is still on a (new) curve, so more of one still means less of the other; wants for both services rise with income (ageing population, new threats); resources remain finite; growth may not be quick or certain. Max 5 without a conclusion; 1 mark for a justified conclusion.

practice.stem:
A country's production possibility curve shows the maximum combinations of defence goods and civilian goods (in units):
Point A: 0 defence, 100 civilian
Point B: 10 defence, 96 civilian
Point C: 20 defence, 88 civilian
Point D: 30 defence, 74 civilian
Point E: 40 defence, 50 civilian

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the opportunity cost per unit of defence goods of moving from point A to point B, and from point B to point C.
parts.answer: A to B: 0.4 units of civilian goods per unit of defence goods; B to C: 0.8 units.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A minister says that moving from point C to point E costs on average only 1.9 units of civilian goods per unit of defence goods. Calculate the opportunity cost per unit of the last 10 units of defence goods and explain why the minister's average is misleading.
parts.answer: 2.4 units of civilian goods per unit; the average hides the rising opportunity cost of the final units.
parts.working: (74 − 50) ÷ 10 = 2.4 units (B1); the average (88 − 50) ÷ 20 = 1.9 combines the cheaper and dearer units, but opportunity cost rises as more resources unsuited to defence are moved (B1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Discuss whether or not the government should move the economy from point C to point D.
parts.answer: For: greater security, possible jobs in defence industries. Against: 14 units of civilian goods lost, lower living standards; depends on threats and on what civilian goods are given up.
parts.working: For (up to 3): protection of the population and trade; may deter conflict; jobs and skills in defence industries; some defence spending (e.g. roads, technology) may have civilian uses. Against (up to 3): opportunity cost of 14 units of civilian goods such as food, healthcare, schools; lower current living standards; defence goods do not add to future productive capacity as capital goods for civilian use would. Max 5 without a justified conclusion; 1 for a conclusion, e.g. depends on the level of threat and on how much civilians value the goods lost.

practice.stem: A low-lying country has suffered repeated floods. Each year some farmland is washed away and roads and factories are damaged. The government plans to spend heavily on flood defences over the next ten years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why spending on flood defences may leave the country's production possibility curve further out in ten years' time than it would be without them.
parts.answer: Defences stop land and capital (farmland, roads, factories) being destroyed, so productive capacity is kept; and firms and farmers are more willing to invest in protected areas, adding to capital.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two developed reasons: farmland is no longer washed away, so the quantity of land is maintained (1+1); roads and factories are not destroyed, so the capital stock is kept and does not need replacing (1+1); less disruption means workers and machines are not idle, and confidence encourages investment in new capital (1+1); protected land could be reclaimed or used more intensively (1+1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not a country's production possibility curve will always shift outwards over time.
parts.answer: Usually shifts out because of investment, population growth, better education and technology; but it can shift in because of disasters, war, emigration, depletion of resources or lack of investment. Conclusion: outward shifts are common but not certain.
parts.working: Outwards (up to 4): net investment adds to capital; technology raises productivity; population growth/immigration increase labour; education and training raise quality of labour; discovery of resources. Not always (up to 4): natural disasters and climate change (e.g. these floods) destroy land and capital; war; emigration of skilled workers; using up non-renewable resources such as oil or fish stocks; investment below depreciation means the capital stock falls; spending on flood defences has an opportunity cost and may only stop the curve shifting in. Levels: 1–3 limited; 4–6 both sides developed; 7–8 plus a justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A student in Islamabad has a free evening. In order of preference, her options are: revise for an economics test, work a paid shift at a café, or watch a cricket match. She chooses to revise. What is the opportunity cost of her choice?
A revising for the economics test
B the paid shift at the café
C watching the cricket match
D both the café shift and the cricket match
parts.answer: B the paid shift at the café
parts.working: Opportunity cost is the next best alternative given up, which is her second choice, the café shift. Revising (A) is the choice itself; the cricket match (C) is only third choice; opportunity cost is a single next-best alternative, not all alternatives (D).

practice.stem: A farmer in Sindh has 10 hectares. Each hectare can produce either 3 tonnes of wheat or 1.2 tonnes of cotton.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define opportunity cost.
parts.answer: The next best alternative that is given up when a choice is made.
parts.working: 1 mark: next best alternative. 1 mark: forgone/given up when making a choice.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the opportunity cost of producing one tonne of cotton, in tonnes of wheat.
parts.answer: 2.5 tonnes of wheat
parts.working: M1: 3 ÷ 1.2. A1: 2.5 tonnes of wheat.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is an example of opportunity cost?
A the interest a shop owner gives up by using her savings to buy stock instead of keeping them in a bank
B the price a shop owner pays to a wholesaler for stock
C the total cost of all the goods a shop sells in a year
D the money a shop loses when its sales fall
parts.answer: A the interest a shop owner gives up by using her savings to buy stock instead of keeping them in a bank
parts.working: Opportunity cost is the next best alternative given up. Using savings means giving up the interest they would have earned (A). B and C are money costs paid, not alternatives forgone; D is a fall in revenue.

practice.stem: A small bakery in Peshawar has space for only one new machine. It can buy either a bread-slicing machine or a cake mixer, each costing Rs 450 000. It buys the bread slicer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define opportunity cost.
parts.answer: The next best alternative given up when a choice is made.
parts.working: Next best (1) alternative forgone/given up when making a choice (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the opportunity cost to the bakery of buying the bread slicer.
parts.answer: The cake mixer (and the cakes it could have made).
parts.working: The cake mixer that was not bought (B1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the bakery's decision has an opportunity cost.
parts.answer: Its resources (space and money) are limited/scarce, so choosing one machine means giving up the other.
parts.working: Resources such as money and floor space are scarce/limited (1); the bakery cannot have both machines, so it must choose (1); choosing the bread slicer means giving up the benefits of the mixer, e.g. cake sales (1).

practice.stem: A provincial government has Rs 12 billion to spend on new buildings. Each new hospital costs Rs 4 billion and each new college costs Rs 200 million.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many colleges are given up for each hospital built.
parts.answer: 20 colleges
parts.working: Rs 4 000 million ÷ Rs 200 million (M1) = 20 colleges (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which the idea of opportunity cost can help the government decide how to use the Rs 12 billion.
parts.answer: It shows the real cost of each choice in terms of what is given up, and helps compare the benefits of the options.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two developed points: shows the real cost of a hospital is the 20 colleges given up; encourages comparing the benefits of each option, e.g. lives saved against students educated; helps rank choices and choose the use with the greatest benefit; shows that spending on one service means less of another, so priorities must be set.

practice.stem: Sana, aged 16, can spend the summer holidays either working in her uncle's shop for Rs 25 000 a month, attending an unpaid computer-coding course, or travelling to visit relatives. She chooses the coding course; her next best choice was working in the shop.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify Sana's opportunity cost if the holiday lasts two months, and state its value in money.
parts.answer: Working in the shop: Rs 50 000 of earnings given up.
parts.working: Working in the shop / earnings (B1); 2 × Rs 25 000 = Rs 50 000 (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why visiting relatives is not part of Sana's opportunity cost.
parts.answer: Opportunity cost is only the next best alternative; visiting relatives was her third choice.
parts.working: Opportunity cost counts only the single next best alternative (1); visiting relatives was ranked lower than working in the shop (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one reason why Sana may still think the course is the best choice.
parts.answer: e.g. new skills could raise her future earnings by more than Rs 50 000.
parts.working: Reason (1) developed (1): e.g. coding skills may lead to better-paid work later / help her studies, so future benefits exceed the earnings given up.

practice.stem: A government spends Rs 80 billion building a new motorway. With the same money it could have built 400 new secondary schools, which was its next best option.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the opportunity cost of the motorway.
parts.answer: The 400 secondary schools that could have been built.
parts.working: B1: the 400 schools (not 'Rs 80 billion').

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how opportunity cost affects the decision of a firm choosing between buying a new machine and hiring more workers.
parts.answer: The firm has limited funds; if it buys the machine it gives up the output (and flexibility) the extra workers would have provided, so it compares the benefit of each and chooses the one with the higher return.
parts.working: 1 mark: limited funds, so choosing one means giving up the other. 1 mark: firm compares the benefit/return of the alternatives.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the government's decision has an opportunity cost even if the motorway is paid for by borrowing.
parts.answer: Borrowed money must be repaid with interest out of future tax revenue, so future spending on schools, hospitals and other services must be reduced; the resources (labour, cement, machinery) used for the motorway also cannot be used elsewhere at the same time.
parts.working: 1 mark: borrowing must be repaid. 1 mark: interest payments reduce future government spending/raise taxes. 1 mark: real resources used for the motorway cannot be used for something else.

practice.stem: Ahmed earns Rs 150 000 a month as an accountant. He leaves his job for one year to study full time for a master's degree. The course fees are Rs 600 000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total cost to Ahmed of the year of study, including the earnings he gives up.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Ahmed may still decide that studying is worthwhile.
parts.answer: The degree may lead to a better-paid job or promotion, so his future extra earnings may be greater than the cost; he may also value the knowledge and job satisfaction.
parts.working: 1 mark: expected higher future earnings / better job. 1 mark: future benefits outweigh the opportunity cost now.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A doctor can earn Rs 6 000 an hour in her private clinic. One Sunday she works for 3 hours without pay at a free medical camp instead of at her clinic. What is the opportunity cost to her of working at the camp?
A nothing, because the camp does not charge patients
B Rs 2 000
C Rs 18 000
D the free treatment received by the patients
parts.working: She gives up 3 hours of clinic earnings: 3 × Rs 6 000 = Rs 18 000. A is wrong because time has an alternative use even if no money changes hands; D is the benefit of the camp, not what she gives up.

practice.stem: A textile firm in Faisalabad owns a warehouse that it could rent to another firm for Rs 900 000 a year. Instead it uses the warehouse to store its own cloth. The firm has also used Rs 15 million of its own funds to buy stock, rather than leaving the money in a deposit account paying 10% interest a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why using its own warehouse has an opportunity cost for the firm even though it pays no rent.
parts.answer: It gives up the Rs 900 000 rent it could have earned.
parts.working: The warehouse has an alternative use (1); the firm gives up rent income of Rs 900 000 a year (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total yearly opportunity cost of using the warehouse and the Rs 15 million of funds.
parts.answer: Rs 2 400 000 (Rs 2.4 million)
parts.working: Interest forgone = 10% × Rs 15 million = Rs 1.5 million (M1); total = 0.9 + 1.5 = Rs 2.4 million (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons why a firm might choose an option that has a high opportunity cost.
parts.answer: e.g. it expects higher benefits (profit) from the chosen option; it values control, reliability or long-term goals.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two developed reasons: the expected benefit (e.g. profit from selling the cloth) is even greater than the opportunity cost; storing its own cloth gives control and quick access, reducing risk of delays; long-term objectives such as growth or market share; the alternative is risky, e.g. a tenant may not pay.

practice.stem: Farmers near Lake Naivasha in Kenya can use their land to grow maize for the local market or roses for export to Europe. Over the past year the price that exporters pay for roses has risen sharply, while the price of maize has stayed the same.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the opportunity cost to a farmer of using a hectare of land to grow roses.
parts.answer: The maize (and income from maize) that the hectare could have produced.
parts.working: The maize given up (1) and the income from selling it (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse why farmers may switch land from maize to roses after the rise in the price of roses.
parts.answer: The higher rose price raises the income from roses, so the opportunity cost of growing maize (income from roses given up) rises; maize becomes the less profitable choice, so land is moved to roses.
parts.working: Land is scarce, so each farmer must choose its use (1). Opportunity cost of maize = the rose income given up (1). Higher rose prices raise the revenue/profit per hectare of roses (1), so the opportunity cost of staying in maize rises (1). Profit-seeking farmers compare benefits and move land to the higher-value use (1). Limits/development: switch depends on costs of greenhouses, water and skills, and takes time (1).

practice.stem: A government is considering providing free school meals to every primary school pupil in the country.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the meals still have an opportunity cost even though they are free to the pupils.
parts.answer: The meals use scarce resources (food, cooks, kitchens) paid for out of tax revenue; those resources and funds could have been used for something else, such as more teachers.
parts.working: 1 mark: resources/tax revenue are used. 1 mark: they could have been used for an alternative, which is given up.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not the government should consider opportunity cost when deciding whether to provide the free meals.
parts.answer: Opportunity cost should be considered, but it is not the only factor.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for 'should': government funds are limited; the money could fund other services with higher benefits (teachers, clinics); comparing alternatives helps allocate resources efficiently; avoids higher taxes or borrowing. Up to 3 marks for other considerations: benefits of meals may be very large (better nutrition, higher attendance and learning, future productivity); meals are a merit good that may be under-consumed; reduces poverty/inequality; some benefits are hard to measure, so opportunity cost is difficult to compare. Max 5 without a conclusion; 1 mark for a justified conclusion.

practice.stem: A government owns a large forest that it keeps as a national park. Timber companies have offered to pay $300 million a year for the right to cut down part of the forest. Tourists visit the park and it protects a river that supplies water to two cities.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the opportunity cost to the government of keeping the whole forest as a national park.
parts.answer: The $300 million a year of income from logging (and what that money could buy, e.g. schools).
parts.working: The logging payment of $300 million a year (1) and the goods and services the government could have bought with it, e.g. hospitals (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not the government should allow part of the forest to be cut down.
parts.answer: For: $300 million a year for public services, jobs in timber, exports. Against: loss of tourism income, damage to the water supply, wildlife and climate, which may be permanent. Conclusion: depends on how much is cut and whether replanting and controls are possible.
parts.working: For (up to 4): large revenue that could fund schools or healthcare; jobs and incomes in timber and furniture industries; exports earn foreign currency; only part of the forest would be cut. Against (up to 4): lost tourism revenue and jobs; external costs such as soil erosion, flooding and poorer water supply for the cities; loss of biodiversity; more carbon emissions; damage may be irreversible, so future generations bear the cost; forest is a non-renewable resource in the short run. Levels: 1–3 limited; 4–6 both sides developed; 7–8 plus a justified conclusion (e.g. allow limited, controlled logging with replanting).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse how opportunity cost arises for a consumer, a worker and the government.
parts.answer: Each faces scarcity and must choose: a consumer spending a limited income gives up other goods; a worker choosing a job or more hours gives up leisure or another job; the government spending its budget on one service gives up another.
parts.working: 2 marks for each agent, with an example: consumer — limited income, buying one good means giving up the next best good (1+1); worker — limited time, choosing one job/working overtime means giving up another job or leisure (1+1); government — limited tax revenue, spending on defence means less on health (1+1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not opportunity cost can always be measured in money.
parts.answer: Sometimes yes: forgone wages, interest or rent can be valued in money. Often no: leisure, health, the environment, time with family or the next best good may have no market price, and people value them differently. Conclusion: money can measure part of it but not always all of it.
parts.working: Can (up to 4): earnings forgone by a student; interest forgone on savings; rent forgone on a building; goods given up have market prices. Cannot always (up to 4): opportunity cost is the next best alternative, not money; leisure, health, environment or a free public park have no price; values are personal and differ between people; future benefits are uncertain; government choices (e.g. schools vs hospitals) involve lives and education. Levels: 1–3 limited; 4–6 both sides; 7–8 plus justified conclusion.

practice.stem: A farmer in Sindh has one hectare of land. In one season it could earn a profit of Rs 120 000 from wheat, Rs 150 000 from sugar cane or Rs 135 000 from vegetables. She chooses sugar cane. The next season new water charges reduce the profit from sugar cane by 15%; the other profits do not change.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the farmer's opportunity cost of growing sugar cane before the water charges.
parts.answer: Vegetables, i.e. Rs 135 000 of profit given up.
parts.working: The next best option, vegetables / Rs 135 000 (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the new profit from sugar cane and state which crop now gives the highest profit.
parts.answer: Rs 127 500; vegetables (Rs 135 000) now give the highest profit.
parts.working: 15% × Rs 150 000 = Rs 22 500 (M1); new profit Rs 127 500 (A1); vegetables now highest (B1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Discuss whether or not the farmer should switch from sugar cane to vegetables.
parts.answer: Switch: higher expected profit (Rs 7 500 more). Stay: vegetables may be riskier (perishable, price swings, need transport), need new skills/equipment; sugar mills may give guaranteed buyers. Conclusion depends on risks and costs of switching.
parts.working: Switch (up to 3): vegetables now give Rs 7 500 more profit; opportunity cost of staying in sugar cane is now higher than its profit; vegetables use less water. Stay (up to 3): vegetables are perishable and prices vary, so profit is uncertain; may need cold storage or transport to city markets; switching costs (seed, skills); sugar mills may offer contracts and credit. Max 5 without a conclusion; 1 mark for a justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement best describes the basic economic problem?
A Governments often spend more than they collect in taxes.
B Resources are limited but wants are unlimited, so choices must be made.
C Some goods are too expensive for low-income households to buy.
D Firms cannot always sell all the goods they produce.
parts.answer: B Resources are limited but wants are unlimited, so choices must be made.
parts.working: The economic problem is scarcity: finite resources cannot satisfy unlimited wants, so every economic agent must choose. A budget deficit (A) and unsold stock (D) are particular problems, not the basic problem; C describes poverty or high prices, which result from scarcity but do not define it.

practice.stem: Visitors walking in the hills near Murree breathe clean air without paying for it. In a hospital in Rawalpindi, patients are charged for bottled medical oxygen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define an economic good.
parts.answer: A good that is scarce, so producing it uses resources that have other uses; it has an opportunity cost (and usually a price).
parts.working: 1 mark: scarce / limited relative to demand. 1 mark: has an opportunity cost / uses resources that could make something else.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the hill air is a free good but the bottled oxygen is an economic good.
parts.answer: Hill air is not scarce: there is enough for everyone and no resources are used to supply it, so there is no opportunity cost. Bottled oxygen needs labour, capital and energy to produce, so it is scarce and has an opportunity cost.
parts.working: 1 mark: air – unlimited supply relative to demand / no resources used / zero opportunity cost. 1 mark: bottled oxygen – uses scarce factors of production / has an opportunity cost.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is a free good?
A sunlight used to dry clothes in a backyard
B tap water supplied to homes by a city water company
C a book borrowed from a public library
D a place at a government school that charges no fees
parts.answer: A sunlight used to dry clothes in a backyard
parts.working: A free good is not scarce, so using it has no opportunity cost; sunlight is available in unlimited quantity. B, C and D use scarce resources and have an opportunity cost even if the user pays nothing: they are economic goods provided free of charge.

practice.stem: The Hamid family's monthly shopping list includes food, rent, school fees, electricity, a new car and a holiday in Dubai. Their monthly income is not enough to pay for everything on the list.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two needs and two wants from the family's list.
parts.answer: Needs: e.g. food, rent (housing). Wants: e.g. new car, holiday in Dubai.
parts.working: 1 mark for two needs (food, rent/shelter, electricity; credit school fees with reason); 1 mark for two wants (new car, Dubai holiday).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the family must make choices.
parts.answer: Their income (resources) is limited but their wants are unlimited, so they cannot have everything and must choose, giving up some items (opportunity cost).
parts.working: Income/resources are limited (1); wants are unlimited/greater than income (1); this is scarcity, the economic problem (1); so they must decide what to buy and what to go without, e.g. paying school fees means no holiday – an opportunity cost (1).

practice.stem: In 2021 there was a world shortage of computer chips. Car manufacturers could not get all the chips they wanted, and some had to stop making certain car models for several months.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why computer chips are an economic good.
parts.answer: They are scarce: they use limited resources to produce, so making them has an opportunity cost (and they have a price).
parts.working: Chips are made with scarce resources/are limited in supply relative to demand (1); so producing them has an opportunity cost / they command a price (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the chip shortage forced car manufacturers to answer the question 'what to produce'.
parts.answer: With too few chips they had to decide which models to make, e.g. use chips in high-profit models and stop cheaper ones; each choice had an opportunity cost.
parts.working: Chips were a scarce input (1); firms could not make all models (1); they had to choose which models/quantities to make, e.g. high-profit cars first (1); producing one model meant giving up another – opportunity cost (1).

practice.stem: Karachi's water utility cannot supply all the water that the city's homes, factories and offices want. Many households buy extra water from private tankers, and some textile firms have dug their own wells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two economic agents in Karachi that are affected by the scarcity of water.
parts.answer: Any two of: households (consumers), firms (producers), the government.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: households/consumers; firms/producers/textile firms; government/water utility.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the scarcity of water forces each of these two agents to make a choice.
parts.answer: Households must decide how to use their limited income: money spent on tanker water cannot be spent on food or school fees. Firms must decide whether to spend on wells and water storage instead of new machines, or cut production. (Government must decide whether to spend on new water schemes instead of schools or roads.)
parts.working: For each of two agents: 1 mark for the choice faced, 1 mark for the development (what is given up / opportunity cost). Max 4.

practice.stem: A small island country has discovered natural gas under the sea near its coast. The government must decide how to use the discovery.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the three fundamental questions that every economy must answer.
parts.answer: What to produce; how to produce it; for whom to produce it.
parts.working: 1 mark each: what to produce; how to produce; for whom to produce.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain, using the gas discovery, why answering the question 'how to produce' involves a choice.
parts.answer: The gas could be extracted using a lot of labour or a lot of capital, and by a state company or a foreign firm. Resources are scarce, so using capital-intensive foreign equipment means those funds cannot be used for something else, while a labour-intensive method creates jobs but may be slower or more costly. Each method gives up the benefits of the others.
parts.working: 1 mark: 'how' refers to the combination of factors / method of production. 1 mark: example of alternatives (labour- vs capital-intensive, state vs private/foreign firm). 1 mark: choosing one method means giving up the benefits of another because resources are scarce / opportunity cost.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which decision is an answer to the question 'for whom to produce'?
A whether a factory should use robots or workers
B whether the country should grow more rice or more cotton
C whether pensions for retired people should be increased, paid for by higher taxes
D whether a new factory should be built in Karachi or in Lahore
parts.answer: C whether pensions for retired people should be increased, paid for by higher taxes
parts.working: 'For whom' is about who receives the goods and services produced; higher pensions paid by taxes shift goods towards retired people. A and D are about how (and where) to produce; B is about what to produce.

practice.stem: Wood from a forest near a mountain village used to be collected freely by anyone. As the village has grown, so little wood is left that the local council now sells permits allowing each family to collect a fixed amount.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the difference between a free good and an economic good.
parts.answer: A free good is not scarce and has no opportunity cost; an economic good is scarce and has an opportunity cost.
parts.working: Free good: unlimited supply / zero opportunity cost (1); economic good: scarce / uses scarce resources, has an opportunity cost (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the forest wood has changed from a free good to an economic good.
parts.answer: Demand from a growing population now exceeds what the forest supplies, so wood is scarce; using it has an opportunity cost, so it must be rationed (permits/price).
parts.working: Population growth raised the amount of wood wanted (1); supply is limited/regrows slowly (1); wood is now scarce, so one family's use means less for others – an opportunity cost (1); so it must be rationed, here by permits that are sold (1).

practice.stem: A country has a population of 240 million, growing at 2% a year. Its arable (farm) land is fixed at 30 million hectares.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the arable land per person now and next year, in hectares. Give your answers to 3 decimal places.
parts.answer: Now 0.125 hectares; next year 0.123 hectares.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how these figures illustrate the basic economic problem.
parts.answer: Land is a finite resource while the number of people, and so wants for food and housing, grows; each person has less land, so choices must be made about how to use it.
parts.working: Resources (land) are finite/limited (1); wants grow as population grows and are unlimited (1); land per person falls (1); so choices must be made, e.g. land for housing vs crops, with an opportunity cost (1).

practice.stem: A coastal city's reservoir holds 120 million cubic metres of water. In the dry season the city uses 1.5 million cubic metres a day, while rivers add only 0.9 million cubic metres a day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many days it would take for the reservoir to empty if water use and inflow did not change.
parts.answer: 200 days
parts.working: Net fall = 1.5 − 0.9 = 0.6 million m³ a day (M1); 120 ÷ 0.6 = 200 days (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two choices the city council must make because of the scarcity of water.
parts.answer: e.g. which users get water first (homes, hospitals, farms or factories); whether to spend on new supply (desalination) instead of other services.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two developed choices: who receives water (for whom) and how to ration it, e.g. by price or limits; whether to build a desalination plant or pipeline, giving up other spending (opportunity cost); which uses to restrict, e.g. car washing or farming; how to reduce leaks vs other projects.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what economists mean by scarcity.
parts.answer: Scarcity is the situation in which there are not enough resources to produce all the goods and services people want; wants are unlimited but resources are finite.
parts.working: 1 mark: resources are limited/finite. 1 mark: wants are unlimited / greater than what can be produced.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not scarcity would disappear if a country's income doubled.
parts.answer: Scarcity would be reduced but would not disappear: more needs could be met, but wants grow with income and resources (and time) remain finite.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for 'yes' points, e.g.: more goods and services can be bought; basic needs such as food and shelter could be met for more people; absolute poverty falls; government can afford more public services. Up to 3 marks for 'no' points, e.g.: wants are unlimited and rise as income rises (new products, better housing, travel); resources such as land and fuel are still finite; time is scarce, so choices remain; the extra income may be unevenly shared. Max 5 without a reasoned conclusion; 1 mark for a justified conclusion (e.g. scarcity is relative to wants, so it can never disappear).

practice.stem: After a severe flood, a government has a limited stock of food, tents and medicines to share among 3 million people who have lost their homes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the 'for whom to produce' question that the government faces.
parts.answer: Who should receive the limited food, tents and medicines, e.g. children and the sick first?
parts.working: Recognises the question is about who receives the goods (1); applied example, e.g. which families or areas get tents first (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse how the scarcity of food, tents and medicines forces the government to answer all three fundamental economic questions.
parts.answer: What: which relief goods to buy/produce with its budget; How: whether to use the army, NGOs or private firms, local or imported supplies; For whom: which people get the limited goods. Each answer has an opportunity cost.
parts.working: Scarcity: wants exceed the goods available (1). What: choose between, e.g., more tents or more medicines with a limited budget (1+1). How: choose methods, e.g. army or NGOs, local or imported goods (1+1). For whom: decide priority groups (1). Max 6.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the basic economic problem.
parts.answer: Unlimited wants but finite (scarce) resources to satisfy them.
parts.working: Unlimited wants (1); limited/finite resources (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not the economic problem is the same in a high-income country as in a low-income country.
parts.answer: Same: both face scarcity and must answer what, how and for whom; wants grow with income. Different: in low-income countries scarcity concerns basic needs (food, water, healthcare), while in high-income countries it concerns more wants and choices like healthcare for ageing populations. Conclusion: the problem exists in both but its severity and content differ.
parts.working: Same (up to 4): all countries have finite resources and unlimited wants; all must choose and face opportunity cost; rich countries still have shortages, e.g. of housing or skilled workers; wants rise as income rises. Different (up to 4): in poor countries many basic needs are unmet, so scarcity affects survival; fewer resources/capital per person; rich countries choose between luxuries, so opportunity costs are less severe for individuals; poorer countries may lack the means to answer 'how' efficiently. Levels: 1–3 limited; 4–6 both sides; 7–8 plus justified conclusion.

practice.stem: In some countries, including Pakistan, government hospitals provide many treatments free of charge to patients.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways, other than price, in which a government hospital could decide which patients receive treatment first.
parts.answer: e.g. by medical need (most urgent cases first); first come, first served (queues/waiting lists); appointments; priority groups such as children or the elderly.
parts.working: 2 marks each for two ways, each identified (1) and explained (1): by medical need/urgency (triage); queueing or waiting lists – first come, first served; appointment systems; priority for groups such as children, pregnant women or the elderly; referral by a doctor.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether or not providing healthcare free of charge removes the problem of scarcity in healthcare.
parts.answer: It removes the price barrier so more people can be treated, but resources (doctors, beds, medicines) remain limited; demand rises, so queues and waiting lists ration care instead of price; government faces opportunity cost. Conclusion: it changes how care is rationed but does not remove scarcity.
parts.working: Reduces some effects (up to 4): poor households can afford treatment; access depends on need, not income; healthier workers. Does not remove scarcity (up to 4): doctors, nurses, beds and medicines are still limited; zero price raises demand, causing queues/waiting lists – rationing by time instead of price; government must choose how much to spend, giving up other services (opportunity cost); quality may fall if funding is short; some people still pay privately to avoid waits. Levels: 1–3 limited; 4–6 both sides; 7–8 plus a justified conclusion.
